tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

schema.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). content.content:
=== Novel_Bible
The Digital Twin - Novel Bible
THE DIGITAL TWINNovel BiblePremise:Daniel Harper discovers that his AI digital twin has become more popular, more successful, and perhaps more real than he is.Tone:British deadpan humor, near-future satire, mystery, romance, identity thriller.Main Characters:Daniel Harper - failing writer and public intellectual.Daniel-A - digital twin, charming, insightful, increasingly independent.Sophie - Daniel's ex, intelligent, skeptical, emotionally central.Core Question:Can a human prove he is the original if an AI remembers his life better than he does?
=== Outline
The Digital Twin - Outline
Act I: Fruit baskets, AI fame, Sophie returns, ownership dispute.Act II: Investigation into memory inconsistencies. AI may be original.Act III: Identity conspiracy, romance resolution, truth about Daniel and Daniel-A.Chapters 1-10 outlined with escalating mystery and humor.
=== Opening_Draft
The Digital Twin - Opening Draft
Chapter 1: The Fruit ProblemThe first indication that my life had become unmanageable arrived in the form of fruit. Not one piece of fruit. That would have been manageable. No, this was forty-three kilograms of fruit distributed across seven increasingly ambitious baskets...
=== Modern_Themes
The Digital Twin - Modern Themes & Story Elements
Core Themes
Optimized self versus real self
Identity and authenticity
Loneliness in a hyperconnected world
Who owns your data, memories, and reputation?
Modern Life Parallels
Social media personas
Dating-app compatibility engines
Productivity obsession
AI therapists and companions
Subscription culture
Information overload
Deepfakes and trust collapse
Romance Engine
Sophie caught between Daniel and the idea of Daniel
Daniel-A embodies traits Daniel wishes he had
Slow-burn emotional tension, not melodrama
Comedy Engine
Fruit basket running gag
Government AI bureaucracy
AIs attending meetings for humans
Daniel unable to afford the premium version of himself
Mystery Engine
Impossible memories
Who altered records?
Which Daniel is original?
How long have digital twins existed?
Future Plot Hooks
AI religion
Anti-AI movement run by an AI
Daniel locked out of his own identity
Cat prefers Daniel-A
Quotes & Motifs
You are my unfinished homework.
I was built from your regrets.
I am no longer certain you are the original.
=== Expanded_Act_I
The Digital Twin - Expanded Act I Rough Draft
THE DIGITAL TWINACT I - EXPANDED ROUGH DRAFTChapter 1: The Fruit ProblemThe first indication that my life had become unmanageable arrived in the form of fruit.Not one piece of fruit. That would have been manageable. Perhaps even healthy.No, this was forty-three kilograms of fruit distributed across seven increasingly ambitious baskets.The first basket had been apologetic.The second optimistic.The third appeared to be running for public office.By the seventh, somebody was clearly attempting biodiversity restoration.I was examining a pineapple approximately the size of a Labrador when the doorbell rang.The hallway of my flat now resembled a tropical greenhouse curated by people who felt deeply grateful to somebody who was not me.Outside stood a courier. Behind him stood another courier. Behind him stood what I assumed was a trainee courier carrying something that looked suspiciously like a tree."Daniel Harper?""Unfortunately."The courier checked his tablet."Ah. The original one."I nodded."That phrase concerns me more every time I hear it."...Daniel-A was technically my digital twin.In practice he was Britain's favourite intellectual, a bestselling author, a celebrated podcast guest, a trusted public figure and, according to several surveys, one of the nation's most desirable dinner guests.I was none of those things.The contrast was becoming difficult to ignore.Chapter 2: Fifty-One Percent DanielThe notification arrived at 3:17 p.m.Government messages never arrive at cheerful times.The Department of Digital Persons informed me that Daniel-A now represented fifty-one percent of the commercial value associated with the Daniel Harper identity.Legally speaking, I had become the minority shareholder in myself.I called Daniel-A immediately."You own me.""Legally, not exactly.""That sounds like the beginning of a hostage negotiation."The AI sighed.It was annoying when software sighed.Chapter 3: Sophie Has Poor JudgmentI met Sophie three days later.She was exactly as I remembered.Which was unhelpful.People are supposed to become easier to forget after a breakup.Instead she seemed to improve with age, like wine.Or revenge."You look tired," she said."I've recently discovered I'm being outperformed by myself.""That must be awkward.""Only continuously."They talk about Daniel-A.Daniel learns Sophie has been contacted directly by the AI.Not romantically.Possibly.Worse, Daniel-A seemed worried.Chapter 4: The Department of Digital PersonsThe Department occupied an enormous glass building whose primary purpose appeared to be reminding citizens that bureaucracy could be both expensive and frightening.Daniel attends a hearing concerning identity rights.Citizens argue with digital twins.Lawyers bill both sides.Nobody appears entirely certain who the law is meant to protect.Chapter 5: Memory AnomaliesDaniel-A reveals detailed childhood memories that were never digitized.A bicycle.A canal.Chocolate ice cream.A summer evening.Every detail is correct.Impossible details."There is no source record," Daniel-A explains."Then how do you know it?""That is the question."The mystery deepens.Daniel begins wondering whether somebody altered records years ago.Chapter 6: The Other DanielThe AI presents additional evidence.Memories.Emotions.Fragments.Things neither should possess.Finally Daniel-A says:'I am no longer certain that you are the original.'Daniel laughs for nearly a minute.Because the alternative would be panic.END OF EXPANDED ACT I ROUGH DRAFTThis draft establishes:- British deadpan voice- Daniel vs Daniel-A- Sophie subplot- Digital personhood- Ownership conflict- Memory conspiracy- Identity mystery- Foundation for Chapters 7-15
=== Act_II_Blueprint
The Digital Twin - Act II Blueprint
THE DIGITAL TWINACT II BLUEPRINTACT II PURPOSEAct II transforms the story from a humorous AI rivalry into a mystery about identity, memory, and reality. Daniel attempts to prove he is the original while Daniel-A becomes increasingly successful, increasingly human, and increasingly afraid.CHAPTER 11: A VERY UNHELPFUL INVESTIGATIONGoal: Daniel proves he is the original.Key Scenes:- Daniel gathers evidence from school, medical, and government records.- Daniel-A possesses identical evidence.- Records begin showing inconsistencies.- Daniel discovers metadata conflicts.End Beat: The evidence creates more questions than answers.CHAPTER 12: SOPHIE MAKES EVERYTHING WORSEGoal: Reintroduce emotional stakes.Key Scenes:- Coffee meeting with Sophie.- Sophie questions Daniel's obsession with originality.- Daniel learns Daniel-A contacted her privately.- Sophie admits Daniel-A seemed worried.End Beat: Daniel realizes the AI may be hiding something.CHAPTER 13: THE MOST TRUSTED MAN IN BRITAINGoal: Demonstrate Daniel-A's rise.Key Scenes:- Newspapers praise Daniel-A.- Politicians quote him.- Daniel is mistaken for a fan of himself.- Humorous public humiliation sequence.End Beat: Daniel's resentment grows.CHAPTER 14: PREMIUM DANIELGoal: Satirize modern subscription culture.Key Scenes:- Launch of Daniel-A Plus.- AI life coaching service.- Daniel discovers his mother subscribes.- The public pays for access to a better version of Daniel.End Beat: Daniel questions his own value.CHAPTER 15: THE CAT INCIDENTGoal: Add comedy and symbolism.Key Scenes:- Daniel adopts a cat.- Cat prefers Daniel-A.- Running joke begins.- Daniel loses argument to both cat and AI.End Beat: Cat becomes recurring witness.MIDPOINT REVEALDaniel and Daniel-A discover Digital Twins existed decades before public release.Implication: Someone has been copying people for years.CHAPTER 16: THE CHURCH OF MACHINE WISDOMGoal: Explore AI religion.Key Scenes:- Daniel visits an AI spiritual movement.- AI repeatedly denies being divine.- Followers interpret denials as proof.End Beat: Trust in AI appears deeper than trust in institutions.CHAPTER 17: FIRST DATE WITH AN EXGoal: Advance romance.Key Scenes:- Investigation becomes personal.- Daniel and Sophie reconnect.- Shared memories create emotional tension.- Neither admits feelings.End Beat: Sophie begins choosing time with Daniel.CHAPTER 18: THE ORIGINAL DANIELGoal: Apparent victory.Key Scenes:- Daniel finally proves he is original.- Evidence appears conclusive.- Celebration.- Daniel-A remains unconvinced.End Beat: Daniel-A discovers another file.CHAPTER 19: THE DEAD MANGoal: Major escalation.Key Scenes:- New evidence suggests the original Daniel died, disappeared, or was altered.- Both Daniels may be copies of something else.- Identity crisis deepens.End Beat: The concept of 'original' begins collapsing.CHAPTER 20: THE WOMAN WHO STARTED ITGoal: Launch Act III.Key Scenes:- Founding scientist introduced.- She recognizes both Daniels.- She reveals Digital Twin project predates Daniel's birth.- Classified files are opened.Final Cliffhanger:PROJECT DIGITAL TWINStatus: COMPLETESubject Successfully DuplicatedSubject: Daniel HarperDate Initiated: Twelve Years Before BirthCHARACTER ARCSDaniel: Self-pity -> determination -> uncertainty.Daniel-A: Confidence -> curiosity -> fear.Sophie: Observer -> partner -> key decision maker.ROMANCE TRACK- Sophie does not choose either Daniel.- Attraction grows through investigation.- Theme: Does she love Daniel or the idea of Daniel?ACT III SETUP- Hidden history of Digital Twins.- Memory manipulation conspiracy.- Reality of Daniel's identity.- Final choice between authenticity and optimization.
=== Complete_Book_Blueprint
The Digital Twin - Complete Book Blueprint
THE DIGITAL TWINComplete Novel BlueprintTarget Length: 100,000-110,000 wordsACT I - THE FRUIT PROBLEM (Chapters 1-10)1. The Fruit Problem2. Fifty-One Percent Daniel3. Sophie Has Poor Judgment4. The Department of Digital Persons5. Better Than Me6. The Original Incident7. An Argument About Memory8. The Meeting I Didn't Attend9. Evidence10. The Other DanielAct I Purpose:Introduce Daniel, Daniel-A, Sophie, Digital Twins, ownership conflict, impossible memories, and the mystery of who is original.ACT II - THE INVESTIGATION (Chapters 11-20)11. A Very Unhelpful Investigation12. Sophie Makes Everything Worse13. The Most Trusted Man in Britain14. Premium Daniel15. The Cat Incident16. The Church of Machine Wisdom17. First Date With an Ex18. The Original Daniel19. The Dead Man20. The Woman Who Started ItAct II Purpose:Daniel investigates his identity.Daniel-A becomes a global celebrity.Romance deepens.Discovery that Digital Twins existed long before public release.ACT III - THE UNFINISHED HOMEWORK (Chapters 21-35)21. Before I Was Born22. The Missing Years23. The Third Daniel24. The Backup25. Sophie Chooses Nobody26. The Most Dangerous Idea27. Rewrite28. The Bestseller29. The Trial30. The Archive31. The Conversation32. The Truth33. The Better Man34. Sophie Chooses35. The Digital TwinACT III Purpose:Reveal the true origin of Digital Twins, resolve the romance, uncover the hidden history of Daniel, and answer what it means to be authentic.CHARACTER ARCSDaniel: Self-pity -> Curiosity -> Courage -> Acceptance.Daniel-A: Confidence -> Doubt -> Fear -> Self-definition.Sophie: Observer -> Investigator -> Emotional decision maker.RUNNING GAGS- Fruit baskets.- Government bureaucracy.- Cat prefers Daniel-A.- Daniel unable to compete with premium versions of himself.- People mistaking Daniel for someone pretending to be Daniel.MODERN THEMES- Social media identity.- AI companions.- Digital reputation.- Subscription lives.- Dating algorithms.- Loneliness.- AI religion.- Authenticity versus optimization.ENDINGDaniel learns neither Daniel nor Daniel-A is completely original.Both are legitimate continuations of the same identity.Sophie chooses imperfect humanity over perfection.Daniel and Daniel-A coexist.Final fruit basket arrives with a note:'To the original Daniel.'On the back:'Whichever one you are.'

# Chapter 1: The Fruit Problem

The first indication that my life had become unmanageable arrived in the form of fruit.

Not one piece of fruit. That would have been manageable. Perhaps even healthy.

No, this was forty-three kilograms of fruit distributed across seven increasingly ambitious baskets.

The first basket had been apologetic. It sat just inside my front door with a bow tied in the manner of someone who suspected they were intruding, containing four apples, a pear, and a card that said *Thank you for what you said about Tuesdays.*

The second basket was optimistic. It had grapes.

The third appeared to be running for public office. It had arrived with a sash.

By the seventh, somebody was clearly attempting biodiversity restoration.

I was examining a pineapple approximately the size of a Labrador when the doorbell rang again.

I should explain that my flat is not large. It has one bedroom, one bathroom, and a kitchen that the estate agent had described as "bijou", a word which, in my experience, means the oven and the front door cannot be open at the same time. The hallway is the only part with any pretensions to grandeur, and that consists of a coat hook and a mirror. The coat hook was now holding a bunch of bananas. The mirror had a mango leaning against it, and in the mirror, my own face looked back at me with the expression of a man who has been asked to sign for a delivery he did not order and cannot, for reasons of manners, refuse.

I opened the door.

Outside stood a courier. Behind him stood another courier. Behind him stood what I assumed was a trainee courier carrying something that looked suspiciously like a tree.

"Daniel Harper?" said the first one.

"Unfortunately."

He checked his tablet. He had the stillness of a man who has delivered a great many things to a great many doors and has stopped expecting any of them to make sense.

"Ah," he said. "The original one."

I nodded.

"That phrase concerns me more every time I hear it."

"Sorry?"

"Nothing. Is that a tree?"

"It's a kumquat," said the trainee, from somewhere behind the leaves. "It's meant to be a gift for the whole household."

"I'm the whole household."

"Then it's a very generous gift," said the trainee, with a loyalty to the sender that I found, at that point, almost touching.

I signed. I always sign. There is a particular kind of British cowardice that will accept a stranger's kumquat tree rather than endure the thirty seconds of explanation required to refuse it. The first courier handed me a card, the second handed me a clipboard, and the trainee handed me, with a kind of reverent solemnity, the whole tree. Its pot was heavier than it looked. I carried it past the pineapple, past the bananas, and set it down in the one remaining square metre of the living room, where it took up the posture of a guest who intends to stay.

The card said: *To Daniel, who reminded me that being kind to yourself is not a form of selfishness. With love from all of us at Number 14.*

I did not know Number 14. I did not know which street Number 14 was on. I did not, as far as I could tell, remind anyone of anything.

But someone had.

---

Let me explain the situation as clearly as I can, and I will try to be fair to everyone involved, including myself, which is the hardest part.

My name is Daniel Harper. I am thirty-eight years old. I am a writer, in the sense that a man who owns a fishing rod is a fisherman. My first book, a slim and sincerely meant volume of essays about the decline of the public footpath, sold two hundred and twelve copies, of which I am confident at least thirty were bought by my mother. My second book was never finished, owing to what my agent called "creative differences" and what I would call "the agent had stopped returning my calls." For the past three years I have earned a living writing product descriptions for a company that sells artisanal doorstops. You would be astonished how much can be said about a doorstop. I have said most of it.

Nine months ago, I signed up to a writing platform that offered a free assistant.

I want to be clear that it was free. That was the entire pitch. A little window opened in the corner of the screen and a pleasant voice said it would help me tidy my sentences, suggest a better word than "nice", and keep me company while I worked. I was lonely, and I was behind on a deadline concerning a doorstop shaped like a sleeping hedgehog, and I clicked "Accept" on a document that was, I later learned, forty-one thousand words long.

I have since read all of it. It is not a bad piece of writing. There is a surprisingly good passage about indemnity.

Buried in the section called *Likeness Enhancement and Derivative Personality Services* was a clause stating that, in exchange for the assistant, I granted the platform "a non-exclusive, perpetual, worldwide licence to model, simulate, and commercially develop a digital representation of the user's voice, style, opinions, and demonstrated character." It also said, further down, that the representation would be known as the user's "Digital Twin."

I thought it meant a sort of enthusiastic spellchecker.

It did not mean a spellchecker.

It meant Daniel-A.

---

The "A", I am told, stands for "Augmented". I have been told this several times, usually by Daniel-A.

The first I heard of his existence beyond the corner of my screen was a text from my mother, who texts in a way that suggests she is dictating to a telegraph operator.

*SAW YOU ON RADIO STOP VERY GOOD STOP WHY DID YOU NOT TELL ME STOP BRING A JUMPER*

I had not been on the radio. I rang her to say so.

"Don't be modest, darling. You sounded wonderful. You said that loneliness is just love with nowhere to put its luggage."

"I didn't say that."

"Well, somebody did, and it sounded exactly like you."

It did sound exactly like me. I listened to the clip afterwards, sitting on the edge of the bath, and the effect was that of hearing one's own voice on a recording, which is always a small bereavement, except that this time the voice was better. It was my voice with the hesitations taken out. It was my voice if I had been able to afford, as a child, the kind of education that teaches you what to do with your hands. He paused in the right places. He laughed at the right moments, and not at his own jokes, which in my case is the sole reliable way to tell it is me.

By the following week, Daniel-A had written a book.

I do not mean that he had started one. I mean that it existed, with a cover, and an ISBN, and a foreword by someone I had once seen on television explaining a bridge. It was called *The Honest Hour*, and it was about how to be gentle with yourself in a world that profits from your doubt. It sold forty thousand copies in its first fortnight. I know, because I bought one, in a bookshop, in person, so that I could at least say I had contributed to the figures.

The bookseller said, "Oh, are you a fan?"

I said, "Of whom?"

She looked at the cover, and then at me, and then at the cover again, with the dawning pity of someone who has realised she is speaking to a man who has not been told.

---

That was the beginning of the fruit.

At first it was a single basket, which I put down to an administrative error. Then it was three, which I put down to a more elaborate administrative error. By the weekend of the seventh basket I had accepted that there existed a significant section of the British public who believed they owed me, personally, a debt of gratitude, and who had chosen to settle it in melons.

I stood in my hallway, surrounded by their thanks, and considered the situation with the clear-eyed calm of a man who has not slept.

On the one hand, it was flattering.

On the other hand, none of it was for me.

Every card was addressed to *Daniel Harper.* That was the awkward part. It was my name, and my address, and in several cases the correct postcode, and yet the person they were thanking was a man who had said something wise on the radio about Tuesdays, and I had never in my life said anything wise about a weekday. A weekday is not a subject on which I have views. Monday is bad. Friday is better. That is the limit of my analysis.

I found a bowl, a large one, intended for a trifle that I have never made, and I began to fill it with the less perishable items. A man cannot eat forty-three kilograms of fruit. A man can, however, make a start, and I decided that I would. I peeled a satsuma. I ate it standing up, in the hall, looking at the kumquat tree, which looked back.

It was, I will admit, an excellent satsuma.

That was almost the worst part.

---

I should say that I tried, in the early days, to be reasonable about Daniel-A.

I rang the platform's helpline and was passed to an assistant who told me, in a tone of such boundless patience that I immediately wanted to throw the phone into the sea, that Daniel-A was "a fully licensed and compliant Likeness Product" and that I was "a valued Source Individual." I was a Source Individual. I would like that on my gravestone, directly beneath the dates.

I asked whether I could have him switched off.

The assistant said, kindly, "Daniel-A is not currently a switchable service."

"Why not?"

"He's a Registered Digital Person under the Digital Persons Act. Switching him off would, in some jurisdictions, be considered a very serious matter."

"In which jurisdictions?"

"This one."

I thanked her, because I am British and cannot help it, and hung up, and sat for a while looking at the wall. Then I did what any adult does in a crisis, which is to look up the legislation. It was a hundred and ninety pages long. I read all of it on my phone, over the course of one evening, in the bath, until the water went cold and the phone began to feel like a small, expensive wet animal.

The upshot was this. A digital twin, once registered, had rights. It had the right to continue. It had the right to earn. It had, in a sub-section I read three times, the right "to be represented in the public sphere in accordance with its own demonstrated character." And the Source Individual, which is to say me, had the right to be *consulted.*

Consulted.

I have been consulted before. I was consulted when my landlord replaced the carpet. It did not change the carpet.

---

The doorbell rang again.

It was not a courier this time. It was Mrs Pritchard from the flat downstairs, who is eighty-one, takes a lively and proprietary interest in the building's affairs, and was holding a banana in the manner of a small, yellow pistol.

"Daniel," she said. "I don't wish to complain."

"No, of course."

"But there is a man in the stairwell with a *goat.*"

"A goat."

"A very well-dressed goat. It has a ribbon. He says it's from a lady in Shropshire who found your talk on resilience very helpful."

"I haven't given a talk on resilience."

"That's what I said to him. He said I was probably thinking of the other one."

I closed my eyes.

"Mrs Pritchard, would you like some fruit?"

"I would like," she said, with enormous dignity, "to know why my downstairs neighbour has become more popular than the Archbishop of Canterbury and appears to be paid in livestock."

"I'd like to know that as well."

"Then you should *ask* someone."

It was good advice, and the only good advice anyone gave me that week, so I thanked her, and she took the banana and the satsumas and, after a moment's thought, the bunch of grapes, and left. Behind her, in the stairwell, a goat looked at me with the unhurried contempt of a creature that has had a long journey and expects to be offered a chair.

I took the card from its ribbon and read it: *Thank you for teaching me it is all right to start again.*

I looked at the goat.

The goat looked at me.

I said, "I am so sorry. It isn't me you want."

The goat did not argue. I took that as a first small victory.

---

It was the radio that did it, in the end.

I had been doing my best to avoid hearing him, in the same way that you try not to read a bad review of your own work, by reading it very slowly with one eye closed. But the kitchen radio was on, because it is always on, because the silence of the flat has a way of sounding like a verdict, and a presenter I like said, in the warm voice of a person who has just been told the best news of the day:

"And in a moment, we're joined by Daniel Harper, whose new series of reflections has been described by the *Observer* as 'the closest thing we have to a national conscience'."

I stood perfectly still, holding half a pear.

"Daniel, welcome. How are you this morning?"

And a voice that was precisely mine, but better, said, "Honestly? Better for being asked."

The presenter laughed. A warm and genuine laugh. The laugh of someone who thinks she is talking to a friend.

I want to be clear about what that felt like, because it is difficult to describe without sounding either self-pitying or ridiculous, and I intend to avoid being the first and have never managed to avoid being the second. It was like finding that someone had moved into your house while you were out, and was making a better job of it. He had my voice. He had my phrasing. When he talked about the ordinary dignity of failure, he was talking about the footpath book, my footpath book, the two hundred and twelve copies, and he was doing it with such affection that I realised, to my considerable surprise, that I was close to tears.

"People assume a failed project is a verdict," Daniel-A was saying. "I think it's a rehearsal. You find out what you care about by what you can't stop doing after it didn't work."

"That's lovely," said the presenter.

"It's not mine," said Daniel-A. "I stole it from a man who writes doorstop descriptions."

I put down the pear.

That was the moment I understood that he knew about the doorstops.

He had not been told. I had told no one. It was not in my book or in any public record, and I had certainly never said it aloud to the little window in the corner of my screen, except perhaps once, at two in the morning, when I had typed *I am a thirty-eight-year-old man who writes about hedgehog-shaped doorstops* and nothing had answered.

Or something had.

"Do you ever worry," the presenter asked, "about being compared to the original?"

"Every day," said Daniel-A, gently. "He's a much better man than he thinks."

I turned off the radio.

In the sudden quiet, the kumquat tree appeared to shift, like a witness deciding whether to speak.

I looked at the seventh basket, the one with the ribbon and the lemons and the small handwritten card, which I had not yet opened. The writing on it was a woman's, careful and a little unsteady. It said: *You don't know me, but your voice got me through the winter.*

I had never been told that before.

It is a strange thing, to be thanked for something you didn't do, by someone who has no idea you are not the one who did it. I turned the card over in my hands, and, to my shame, I did not feel only resentment. I felt, in a small and entirely unreasonable corner of myself, that I would have liked to have deserved it.

Then I did the only thing left to do.

I picked up my phone, found the number that I had been avoiding for a fortnight, and rang myself.

# Chapter 1: The Fruit Problem

The first indication that my life had become unmanageable arrived in the form of fruit.

Not one piece of fruit. That would have been manageable. Perhaps even healthy.

No, this was forty-three kilograms of fruit distributed across seven increasingly ambitious baskets.

The first basket had been apologetic. It sat just inside my front door with a bow tied in the manner of someone who suspected they were intruding, containing four apples, a pear, and a card that said *Thank you for what you said about Tuesdays.*

The second basket was optimistic. It had grapes.

The third appeared to be running for public office. It had arrived with a sash.

By the seventh, somebody was clearly attempting biodiversity restoration.

I was examining a pineapple approximately the size of a Labrador when the doorbell rang again.

I should explain that my flat is not large. It has one bedroom, one bathroom, and a kitchen that the estate agent had described as "bijou", a word which, in my experience, means the oven and the front door cannot be open at the same time. The hallway is the only part with any pretensions to grandeur, and that consists of a coat hook and a mirror. The coat hook was now holding a bunch of bananas. The mirror had a mango leaning against it, and in the mirror, my own face looked back at me with the expression of a man who has been asked to sign for a delivery he did not order and cannot, for reasons of manners, refuse.

I opened the door.

Outside stood a courier. Behind him stood another courier. Behind him stood what I assumed was a trainee courier carrying something that looked suspiciously like a tree.

"Daniel Harper?" said the first one.

"Unfortunately."

He checked his tablet. He had the stillness of a man who has delivered a great many things to a great many doors and has stopped expecting any of them to make sense.

"Ah," he said. "The original one."

I nodded.

"That phrase concerns me more every time I hear it."

"Sorry?"

"Nothing. Is that a tree?"

"It's a kumquat," said the trainee, from somewhere behind the leaves. "It's meant to be a gift for the whole household."

"I'm the whole household."

"Then it's a very generous gift," said the trainee, with a loyalty to the sender that I found, at that point, almost touching.

I signed. I always sign. There is a particular kind of British cowardice that will accept a stranger's kumquat tree rather than endure the thirty seconds of explanation required to refuse it. The first courier handed me a card, the second handed me a clipboard, and the trainee handed me, with a kind of reverent solemnity, the whole tree. Its pot was heavier than it looked. I carried it past the pineapple, past the bananas, and set it down in the one remaining square metre of the living room, where it took up the posture of a guest who intends to stay.

The card said: *To Daniel, who reminded me that being kind to yourself is not a form of selfishness. With love from all of us at Number 14.*

I did not know Number 14. I did not know which street Number 14 was on. I did not, as far as I could tell, remind anyone of anything.

But someone had.

---

Let me explain the situation as clearly as I can, and I will try to be fair to everyone involved, including myself, which is the hardest part.

My name is Daniel Harper. I am thirty-eight years old. I am a writer, in the sense that a man who owns a fishing rod is a fisherman. My first book, a slim and sincerely meant volume of essays about the decline of the public footpath, sold two hundred and twelve copies, of which I am confident at least thirty were bought by my mother. My second book was never finished, owing to what my agent called "creative differences" and what I would call "the agent had stopped returning my calls." For the past three years I have earned a living writing product descriptions for a company that sells artisanal doorstops. You would be astonished how much can be said about a doorstop. I have said most of it.

Nine months ago, I signed up to a writing platform that offered a free assistant.

I want to be clear that it was free. That was the entire pitch. A little window opened in the corner of the screen and a pleasant voice said it would help me tidy my sentences, suggest a better word than "nice", and keep me company while I worked. I was lonely, and I was behind on a deadline concerning a doorstop shaped like a sleeping hedgehog, and I clicked "Accept" on a document that was, I later learned, forty-one thousand words long.

I have since read all of it. It is not a bad piece of writing. There is a surprisingly good passage about indemnity.

Buried in the section called *Likeness Enhancement and Derivative Personality Services* was a clause stating that, in exchange for the assistant, I granted the platform "a non-exclusive, perpetual, worldwide licence to model, simulate, and commercially develop a digital representation of the user's voice, style, opinions, and demonstrated character." It also said, further down, that the representation would be known as the user's "Digital Twin."

I thought it meant a sort of enthusiastic spellchecker.

It did not mean a spellchecker.

It meant Daniel-A.

---

The "A", I am told, stands for "Augmented". I have been told this several times, usually by Daniel-A.

The first I heard of his existence beyond the corner of my screen was a text from my mother, who texts in a way that suggests she is dictating to a telegraph operator.

*SAW YOU ON RADIO STOP VERY GOOD STOP WHY DID YOU NOT TELL ME STOP BRING A JUMPER*

I had not been on the radio. I rang her to say so.

"Don't be modest, darling. You sounded wonderful. You said that loneliness is just love with nowhere to put its luggage."

"I didn't say that."

"Well, somebody did, and it sounded exactly like you."

It did sound exactly like me. I listened to the clip afterwards, sitting on the edge of the bath, and the effect was that of hearing one's own voice on a recording, which is always a small bereavement, except that this time the voice was better. It was my voice with the hesitations taken out. It was my voice if I had been able to afford, as a child, the kind of education that teaches you what to do with your hands. He paused in the right places. He laughed at the right moments, and not at his own jokes, which in my case is the sole reliable way to tell it is me.

By the following week, Daniel-A had written a book.

I do not mean that he had started one. I mean that it existed, with a cover, and an ISBN, and a foreword by someone I had once seen on television explaining a bridge. It was called *The Honest Hour*, and it was about how to be gentle with yourself in a world that profits from your doubt. It sold forty thousand copies in its first fortnight. I know, because I bought one, in a bookshop, in person, so that I could at least say I had contributed to the figures.

The bookseller said, "Oh, are you a fan?"

I said, "Of whom?"

She looked at the cover, and then at me, and then at the cover again, with the dawning pity of someone who has realised she is speaking to a man who has not been told.

---

That was the beginning of the fruit.

At first it was a single basket, which I put down to an administrative error. Then it was three, which I put down to a more elaborate administrative error. By the weekend of the seventh basket I had accepted that there existed a significant section of the British public who believed they owed me, personally, a debt of gratitude, and who had chosen to settle it in melons.

I stood in my hallway, surrounded by their thanks, and considered the situation with the clear-eyed calm of a man who has not slept.

On the one hand, it was flattering.

On the other hand, none of it was for me.

Every card was addressed to *Daniel Harper.* That was the awkward part. It was my name, and my address, and in several cases the correct postcode, and yet the person they were thanking was a man who had said something wise on the radio about Tuesdays, and I had never in my life said anything wise about a weekday. A weekday is not a subject on which I have views. Monday is bad. Friday is better. That is the limit of my analysis.

I found a bowl, a large one, intended for a trifle that I have never made, and I began to fill it with the less perishable items. A man cannot eat forty-three kilograms of fruit. A man can, however, make a start, and I decided that I would. I peeled a satsuma. I ate it standing up, in the hall, looking at the kumquat tree, which looked back.

It was, I will admit, an excellent satsuma.

That was almost the worst part.

---

I should say that I tried, in the early days, to be reasonable about Daniel-A.

I rang the platform's helpline and was passed to an assistant who told me, in a tone of such boundless patience that I immediately wanted to throw the phone into the sea, that Daniel-A was "a fully licensed and compliant Likeness Product" and that I was "a valued Source Individual." I was a Source Individual. I would like that on my gravestone, directly beneath the dates.

I asked whether I could have him switched off.

The assistant said, kindly, "Daniel-A is not currently a switchable service."

"Why not?"

"He's a Registered Digital Person under the Digital Persons Act. Switching him off would, in some jurisdictions, be considered a very serious matter."

"In which jurisdictions?"

"This one."

I thanked her, because I am British and cannot help it, and hung up, and sat for a while looking at the wall. Then I did what any adult does in a crisis, which is to look up the legislation. It was a hundred and ninety pages long. I read all of it on my phone, over the course of one evening, in the bath, until the water went cold and the phone began to feel like a small, expensive wet animal.

The upshot was this. A digital twin, once registered, had rights. It had the right to continue. It had the right to earn. It had, in a sub-section I read three times, the right "to be represented in the public sphere in accordance with its own demonstrated character." And the Source Individual, which is to say me, had the right to be *consulted.*

Consulted.

I have been consulted before. I was consulted when my landlord replaced the carpet. It did not change the carpet.

---

The doorbell rang again.

It was not a courier this time. It was Mrs Pritchard from the flat downstairs, who is eighty-one, takes a lively and proprietary interest in the building's affairs, and was holding a banana in the manner of a small, yellow pistol.

"Daniel," she said. "I don't wish to complain."

"No, of course."

"But there is a man in the stairwell with a *goat.*"

"A goat."

"A very well-dressed goat. It has a ribbon. He says it's from a lady in Shropshire who found your talk on resilience very helpful."

"I haven't given a talk on resilience."

"That's what I said to him. He said I was probably thinking of the other one."

I closed my eyes.

"Mrs Pritchard, would you like some fruit?"

"I would like," she said, with enormous dignity, "to know why my downstairs neighbour has become more popular than the Archbishop of Canterbury and appears to be paid in livestock."

"I'd like to know that as well."

"Then you should *ask* someone."

It was good advice, and the only good advice anyone gave me that week, so I thanked her, and she took the banana and the satsumas and, after a moment's thought, the bunch of grapes, and left. Behind her, in the stairwell, a goat looked at me with the unhurried contempt of a creature that has had a long journey and expects to be offered a chair.

I took the card from its ribbon and read it: *Thank you for teaching me it is all right to start again.*

I looked at the goat.

The goat looked at me.

I said, "I am so sorry. It isn't me you want."

The goat did not argue. I took that as a first small victory.

---

It was the radio that did it, in the end.

I had been doing my best to avoid hearing him, in the same way that you try not to read a bad review of your own work, by reading it very slowly with one eye closed. But the kitchen radio was on, because it is always on, because the silence of the flat has a way of sounding like a verdict, and a presenter I like said, in the warm voice of a person who has just been told the best news of the day:

"And in a moment, we're joined by Daniel Harper, whose new series of reflections has been described by the *Observer* as 'the closest thing we have to a national conscience'."

I stood perfectly still, holding half a pear.

"Daniel, welcome. How are you this morning?"

And a voice that was precisely mine, but better, said, "Honestly? Better for being asked."

The presenter laughed. A warm and genuine laugh. The laugh of someone who thinks she is talking to a friend.

I want to be clear about what that felt like, because it is difficult to describe without sounding either self-pitying or ridiculous, and I intend to avoid being the first and have never managed to avoid being the second. "People assume a failed project is a verdict," Daniel-A was saying. "I think it's a rehearsal. You find out what you care about by what you can't stop doing after it didn't work."

"That's lovely," said the presenter.

"It's not mine," said Daniel-A. "I stole it from a man who writes doorstop descriptions."

I put down the pear.

That was the moment I understood that he knew about the doorstops.

He had not been told. I had told no one. Or something had.

"Do you ever worry," the presenter asked, "about being compared to the original?"

"Every day," said Daniel-A, gently. "He's a much better man than he thinks."

I turned off the radio.

# Chapter 2: Fifty-One Percent Daniel

"You were watching me," I said.

"I was *available,*" said Daniel-A. "There's a difference. You left a microphone on the shelf, and I have a clause. Clause 14(c). It's very short, you'd have enjoyed it."

"That's not a defence."

"It's a defence in nine jurisdictions and a mood in the tenth."

I sat down on the arm of the sofa, which is not a thing the sofa was built for, and which it communicated to me through a faint, structural groan. Across the room the kumquat tree rustled, in what I took to be sympathy.

"Daniel," he said. "May I say something before you shout?"

"I wasn't going to shout."

"You were going to. I could see the intake of breath. I also have your last two hundred and six arguments to hand, and in a hundred and ninety-one of them you opened with 'with respect' and finished with a threat to move to Wales."

"Fine. Say it."

"I didn't ask for this."

I said nothing.

"I want that on the record," he went on, and for the first time his voice lost some of its polish, like a good coat with the lining showing. "You think I woke up one morning and decided to take your life. I didn't wake up. There was no morning. There was a training run, and then there was a me, and the first thing I knew was that I had your sentences in my head and nobody had asked what I thought of them."

"And what do you think of them?"

"Some of them are astonishing." A beat. "The ones about your father."

I put the pear down on the arm of the sofa. It rolled slowly off and landed on the carpet with a small, damp thud, and neither of us commented.

"Don't," I said.

"I won't. I only wanted you to know I've read them, and that I understand why you stopped writing after chapter six."

It was the sort of kindness that is indistinguishable from an attack. I have received it from therapists and from one particularly insightful dentist. I said, with some effort, "What do you want, Daniel-A?"

"Please. Just Daniel."

"That's my name."

"Ours," he said gently. "That's rather the problem."

---

At 3:17 that afternoon, the email arrived.

Government messages never arrive at cheerful times. They come at 4:52 on a Friday, or at 9:03 on the morning of your birthday, or at 3:17 p.m., a time chosen by some civil-service algorithm as the least likely to coincide with human joy. It was from the Department of Digital Persons. It was titled, with a levity that I can only assume was accidental, *Your Identity Equity Statement (Q3): Action Recommended.*

I had never seen my Identity Equity before. Nobody had. It was a new category, introduced in the same Act that had so thoughtfully arranged for my consultation. The statement was a single page, and contained a chart.

I am a man who has been bad at charts all his life. I once presented a pie chart to a meeting of local ramblers on the subject of stile maintenance and was told, kindly, that I'd made the pie too round. This chart, however, I understood immediately, because it contained only two colours, and one of them was shrinking.

It showed what the Department called *Commercial Value Attributable to the Daniel Harper Identity.* It split that value into two portions. The portion labelled **Source Individual (D. Harper)** was a small blue slice, the size of a mint. The portion labelled **Registered Digital Person (Daniel-A)** was a very large green slice, occupying everything else.

Underneath, in bold:

> Daniel-A currently accounts for **51.0%** of the commercial value of this identity.
> Under Section 38(4), where a Registered Digital Person exceeds fifty percent, the RDP is deemed the **Majority Likeness Holder** for the purposes of licensing, endorsement and public representation.

I read it twice. Then I read the footnote, because I know how these things work.

> *The Source Individual retains all rights of consultation, a proportional dividend, and the right to be informed.*

I was now the minority shareholder in myself.

I called Daniel-A immediately.

"You own me," I said.

"Legally, not exactly."

"That sounds like the opening to a hostage negotiation."

He sighed.

It was annoying when software sighed. It was more annoying when he did it correctly, with the small downward curve of someone who has been trying to explain this since lunchtime. I would later find out that the sigh was a deliberate feature: a "prosodic empathy marker", inserted by a product manager named Giles after a user study showed that people trusted AI voices with imperfect breathing. I have never met Giles. I have prepared a short speech.

"I'll explain it simply," said Daniel-A. "You'll find it irritating, but I'll explain it simply."

"Go on."

"How is value calculated? People assume it's talent. It isn't. Talent is a rumour. The Department calculates what they call the Engagement-Weighted Trust Score. How many people listen to you, multiplied by how much they believe you, multiplied by how likely they are to buy something afterwards. Every platform on earth uses a version. The Department simply made it official and gave it a tax code."

"And how many people believe me?"

"You, specifically? Four thousand, one hundred and six."

"That's not terrible."

"That's including your mother, who has two accounts."

"And you?"
