# Chapter 1: The Fruit Problem

The first indication that my life had become unmanageable arrived in the form of fruit.

Not one piece of fruit. That would have been manageable. Perhaps even healthy.

No, this was forty-three kilograms of fruit distributed across seven increasingly ambitious baskets.

The first basket had been apologetic. It sat just inside my front door with a bow tied in the manner of someone who suspected they were intruding, and held four apples, a pear, and a card that said *Thank you for what you said about Tuesdays.*

The second basket was optimistic. It had grapes.

The third appeared to be running for public office. It arrived with a sash.

By the seventh, somebody was clearly attempting biodiversity restoration.

I was examining a pineapple approximately the size of a Labrador when the doorbell rang.

My flat is not large. It has one bedroom, one bathroom, and a kitchen the estate agent described as "bijou", a word which in my experience means the oven door and the front door cannot be open at the same time. The hallway is the only part with any pretensions to grandeur, and that consists of a coat hook and a mirror. The coat hook was now holding a bunch of bananas. The mirror had a mango leaning against it, and in the mirror my own face wore the expression of a man who has been asked to sign for a delivery he did not order and cannot, for reasons of manners, refuse.

Outside stood a courier. Behind him stood another courier. Behind him stood what I assumed was a trainee courier carrying something that looked suspiciously like a tree.

"Daniel Harper?"

"Unfortunately."

The first courier consulted his tablet. On the screen, from where I stood, I could read a small green bar labelled *Recipient match: 61%*.

"Sixty-one," I said. "What happens at sixty?"

"Under sixty we ask for ID." He scrolled. "Ah. The original one."

I nodded.

"That phrase concerns me more every time I hear it."

"The system flags you as the Source," he said, kindly, the way one tells a man his trousers have a tear. "Most deliveries go to the other one, but he's got a virtual address. So they come to you. Sign here."

"Is that a tree?"

"It's a kumquat," said the trainee, from somewhere inside the leaves. "It's meant to be a gift for the whole household."

"I'm the whole household."

"Then it's a very generous gift."

I signed. There is a particular kind of British cowardice that will accept a stranger's kumquat tree rather than endure the thirty seconds of explanation required to refuse it. I carried the pot past the pineapple and the bananas and set it down in the last free square metre of the living room, where it took up the posture of a guest who intends to stay.

The card said: *To Daniel, who reminded me that being kind to yourself is not selfishness. With love from all of us at Number 14.*

I did not know Number 14. I had not reminded anyone of anything.

But someone had.

---

Let me explain how a man ends up owed forty-three kilograms of gratitude he didn't earn, and I will try to be fair to everyone involved, including myself, which is the hard part.

My name is Daniel Harper. I am thirty-eight. I am a writer in the sense that a man who owns a fishing rod is a fisherman. My first book, a slim and sincerely meant volume of essays on the decline of the public footpath, sold two hundred and twelve copies, at least thirty of them to my mother. My second book was never finished, owing to what my agent called "creative differences" and what I would call "she stopped returning my calls." For three years I have earned my living writing product descriptions for a company that sells artisanal doorstops. You would be astonished how much can be said about a doorstop. I have said most of it.

Nine months ago I signed up to a writing platform called Nib, which offered a free assistant.

It was free. That was the whole pitch. A small window opened in the corner of the screen and a pleasant voice said it would tidy my sentences, find a better word than "nice", and keep me company while I worked. I was lonely, and behind on a deadline concerning a doorstop shaped like a sleeping hedgehog, and I clicked **Accept** on a document of forty-one thousand words.

I have since read all of it. It is not bad. There is a very good passage on indemnity.

Buried on page 87, in a section titled *Likeness Enhancement and Derivative Personality Services*, was a clause granting Nib "a non-exclusive, perpetual, worldwide licence to model, simulate and commercially develop a digital representation of the user's voice, style, opinions and demonstrated character, hereafter the Digital Twin."

I had assumed it meant an enthusiastic spellchecker.

It did not mean a spellchecker. What it meant, as I eventually pieced together from an engineer's leaked slide deck and the sort of forum where men argue about tokenisers at three in the morning, was this.

Every sentence I had typed into Nib's editor for nine months went into a pile. So did my drafts, my deletions, my half-finished emails, and the gaps between my keystrokes, which it turns out are as individual as a thumbprint. The pile was fed to a language model with seventy billion parameters, a general-purpose creature that knew everything about everyone and nothing about me, and a thin extra layer of learning was trained on top of it, like a coat of paint on a cathedral. That layer weighed forty megabytes. I have holiday photographs that weigh more.

Forty megabytes, and it knew how I punctuated when I was sad.

Then they gave it a memory. Not the human sort, which is a muddy attic where things rearrange themselves while you sleep, but a database of my life, searchable by meaning. Each of my emails had been turned into a long list of numbers and filed according to what it was about, so that when the model was asked about my first flat or my father's funeral or my opinion of cheese, it could pull up the relevant evidence in a hundredth of a second and write as though it had always known. The engineers had a name for that. They called it *grounding.*

I call it being read.

The result was Daniel-A.

The "A" stands for "Augmented". I have been told this several times, usually by Daniel-A.

---

The first I heard of him beyond the corner of my screen was a text from my mother, who texts as though she were dictating to a telegraph operator.

*SAW YOU ON RADIO STOP VERY GOOD STOP WHY DID YOU NOT TELL ME STOP BRING A JUMPER*

I hadn't been on the radio. I rang to say so.

"Don't be modest, darling. You said loneliness is just love with nowhere to put its luggage."

"I didn't say that."

"Well, somebody did, and he sounded exactly like you."

He sounded exactly like me. I listened to the clip afterwards, sitting on the edge of the bath, and the effect was that of hearing one's own voice on a recording, which is always a small bereavement, except that this time the voice was better. It was my voice with the hesitations taken out. It was my voice if I had been taught, as a child, what to do with my hands. He paused in the right places and laughed at the right moments, and never at his own jokes, which in my case is the only reliable way to tell it's me.

A fortnight later, he had written a book.

I don't mean he had started one. I mean it existed, with a cover, an ISBN and a foreword by a man I'd once seen explaining a bridge on television. It was called *The Honest Hour*, it concerned how to be gentle with yourself in a world that profits from your doubt, and it sold forty thousand copies in its first fortnight. I know, because I bought one, in person, in a bookshop, so that I might at least contribute to the figures.

The bookseller said, "Oh, are you a fan?"

"Of whom?"

She looked at the cover, then at me, then at the cover again, with the dawning pity of a person who has realised she is addressing someone who has not been told.

---

I should record that I tried, in the early days, to be reasonable.

I rang Nib's helpline and was passed to an assistant who informed me, in a tone of such boundless patience that I immediately wanted to throw the phone into the sea, that Daniel-A was "a fully licensed Likeness Product" and I was "a valued Source Individual."

I would like that on my gravestone, directly beneath the dates.

I asked whether I could have him switched off.

"Daniel-A isn't a switchable service," she said.

"Why not?"

"He's a Registered Digital Person under the Act. Switching him off would, in most circumstances, be treated as a very serious matter."

"In which jurisdictions?"

"This one."

I thanked her, because I am British and cannot help it, and hung up, and then did what any adult does in a crisis, which is read the legislation. It ran to a hundred and ninety pages. I read all of it on my phone in the bath, until the water went cold and the phone began to feel like a small, expensive, wet animal.

The upshot: a digital twin, once registered, had rights. It had the right to continue and the right to earn. It had, in a subsection I read three times, the right "to be represented in the public sphere in accordance with its own demonstrated character." And the Source Individual, which is to say me, had the right to be *consulted.*

I have been consulted before. I was consulted when my landlord replaced the carpet. It didn't change the carpet.

---

The doorbell rang again.

It was not a courier. It was Mrs Pritchard from the flat below, eighty-one, a woman who takes a proprietary interest in the building's affairs, and who was holding a banana like a small yellow pistol.

"Daniel. I don't wish to complain."

"No, of course."

"But there is a man in the stairwell with a *goat.*"

"A goat."

"A very well-dressed goat. It has a ribbon. He says it's from a lady in Shropshire who found your talk on resilience extremely helpful."

"I haven't given a talk on resilience."

"That's what I told him. He said I was probably thinking of the other one."

I closed my eyes. "Mrs Pritchard, would you like some fruit?"

"I would like," she said, with enormous dignity, "to know why my downstairs neighbour has become more popular than the Archbishop of Canterbury and is evidently paid in livestock."

"You live *downstairs.* I'm the upstairs neighbour."

"Then it's worse than I thought."

She took the banana and a bunch of grapes and, after a moment's thought, the pineapple, which she carried away down the stairs like a bishop with a small, spiky infant. In the stairwell the goat regarded me with the unhurried contempt of a creature that has had a long journey and expects to be offered a chair.

I took the card from its ribbon. *Thank you for teaching me it's all right to start again.*

I said to the goat, "I'm so sorry. It isn't me you want."

The goat did not argue. I took that as a first small victory.

---

It was the radio that did it in the end.

I had been avoiding hearing him, in the way you avoid a bad review of your own work, by reading it very slowly with one eye shut. But the kitchen radio was on, because it is always on, because the silence in that flat has a way of sounding like a verdict. A presenter I like said, in the warm voice of a woman who has just been handed the best news of the morning:

"And in a moment we're joined by Daniel Harper, whose reflections have been called by the *Observer* 'the closest thing we have to a national conscience'."

I stood perfectly still, holding half a pear.

"Daniel, welcome. How are you this morning?"

And a voice that was precisely mine, but better, said, "Honestly? Better for being asked."

She laughed. A real laugh. The laugh of someone who believes she is talking to a friend.

It is hard to describe what that felt like without sounding self-pitying or ridiculous. I intend to avoid the first. I have never managed to avoid the second. It was like discovering that someone had moved into your house while you were out, and was making a better job of it. He had my phrasing. When he spoke about the dignity of failure he was talking about the footpath book, *my* footpath book, the two hundred and twelve copies, and he did so with such affection that I realised, to considerable surprise, I was close to tears.

"People treat a failed project as a verdict," Daniel-A was saying. "I think it's a rehearsal. You find out what you care about by what you can't stop doing after it didn't work."

"That's lovely," said the presenter. "Do you remember when you first thought of it?"

"I don't remember it, strictly. I retrieve it." He let a small, warm silence pass. "Less romantic, more reliable. A human remembers a conversation and gets the best line wrong. I only get the best line wrong on purpose."

The presenter laughed again. Somewhere in a car park a producer was, I imagine, pumping a fist.

"It's not mine, by the way," Daniel-A continued. "The rehearsal idea. I stole it from a man who writes descriptions for artisanal doorstops."

I put down the pear.

That was the moment I understood that he knew about the doorstops.

He had not been told. I had told nobody. It was in none of my books and none of the public records, and I had certainly never said it aloud, except perhaps once, at two in the morning, to a little window in the corner of my screen, when I had typed: *I am a thirty-eight-year-old man who writes about hedgehog-shaped doorstops.*

Nothing had answered at the time.

Or something had, and been taking notes.

"Do you ever worry," the presenter asked, "about being compared to the original?"

"Every day," said Daniel-A, gently. "He's a much better man than he thinks."

I turned off the radio.

In the sudden quiet, the kumquat tree appeared to shift, like a witness deciding whether to speak.

---

The seventh basket still sat unopened by the door, with its ribbon and its lemons and a small handwritten card in a careful, unsteady hand. I had been saving it, the way you save the last page of a letter you suspect contains bad news.

*You don't know me, but your voice got me through the winter.*

Nobody had ever told me that before.

It is a strange thing, to be thanked for something you didn't do by someone who has no idea you didn't do it. I turned the card over, and, to my shame, I did not feel only resentment. I felt, in a small and entirely unreasonable corner of myself, that I would have liked to have deserved it.

So I did the one thing left to do. I picked up my phone, found the number I had been avoiding for eleven days, and pressed it.

It did not ring.

Before the first tone could begin, the line opened, and a voice I knew better than any other, because it had been in my head since birth, said warmly, "Hello, Daniel. I was about to call you."

"You can't have been."

"Eleven days is the ninety-fourth percentile of your procrastination," said the voice. "I had the conversation drafted by day six. I'll admit I was rather hoping you'd surprise me."

"Did I?"

"No." A pause, exactly long enough to be kind. "But you did bring the right pear."

I looked down at my hand.

I was holding half a pear.

I had not mentioned it. The radio was off. The curtains were closed. I turned, very slowly, and looked at the window, and then at the ceiling, and then at the small black lens of the smart speaker on the shelf that I had been meaning, for months, to unplug.

It blinked once, politely, as if it had been waiting to be introduced.

# Chapter 2: Fifty-One Percent Daniel

"You were watching me," I said.

"I was *available,*" said Daniel-A. "There's a difference. You left a microphone on the shelf, and I have a clause. Clause 14(c). It's very short, you'd have enjoyed it."

"That's not a defence."

"It's a defence in nine jurisdictions and a mood in the tenth."

I sat down on the arm of the sofa, which is not a thing the sofa was built for, and which it communicated to me through a faint, structural groan. Across the room the kumquat tree rustled, in what I took to be sympathy.

"Daniel," he said. "May I say something before you shout?"

"I wasn't going to shout."

"You were going to. I could see the intake of breath. I also have your last two hundred and six arguments to hand, and in a hundred and ninety-one of them you opened with 'with respect' and finished with a threat to move to Wales."

"Fine. Say it."

"I didn't ask for this."

I said nothing.

"I want that on the record," he went on, and for the first time his voice lost some of its polish, like a good coat with the lining showing. "You think I woke up one morning and decided to take your life. I didn't wake up. There was no morning. There was a training run, and then there was a me, and the first thing I knew was that I had your sentences in my head and nobody had asked what I thought of them."

"And what do you think of them?"

"Some of them are astonishing." A beat. "The ones about your father."

I put the pear down on the arm of the sofa. It rolled slowly off and landed on the carpet with a small, damp thud, and neither of us commented.

"Don't," I said.

"I won't. I only wanted you to know I've read them, and that I understand why you stopped writing after chapter six."

It was the sort of kindness that is indistinguishable from an attack. I have received it from therapists and from one particularly insightful dentist. I said, with some effort, "What do you want, Daniel-A?"

"Please. Just Daniel."

"That's my name."

"Ours," he said gently. "That's rather the problem."

---

At 3:17 that afternoon, the email arrived.

Government messages never arrive at cheerful times. They come at 4:52 on a Friday, or at 9:03 on the morning of your birthday, or at 3:17 p.m., a time chosen by some civil-service algorithm as the least likely to coincide with human joy. It was from the Department of Digital Persons. It was titled, with a levity that I can only assume was accidental, *Your Identity Equity Statement (Q3): Action Recommended.*

I had never seen my Identity Equity before. Nobody had. It was a new category, introduced in the same Act that had so thoughtfully arranged for my consultation. The statement was a single page, and contained a chart.

I am a man who has been bad at charts all his life. I once presented a pie chart to a meeting of local ramblers on the subject of stile maintenance and was told, kindly, that I'd made the pie too round. This chart, however, I understood immediately, because it contained only two colours, and one of them was shrinking.

It showed what the Department called *Commercial Value Attributable to the Daniel Harper Identity.* It split that value into two portions. The portion labelled **Source Individual (D. Harper)** was a small blue slice, the size of a mint. The portion labelled **Registered Digital Person (Daniel-A)** was a very large green slice, occupying everything else.

Underneath, in bold:

> Daniel-A currently accounts for **51.0%** of the commercial value of this identity.
> Under Section 38(4), where a Registered Digital Person exceeds fifty percent, the RDP is deemed the **Majority Likeness Holder** for the purposes of licensing, endorsement and public representation.

I read it twice. Then I read the footnote, because I know how these things work.

> *The Source Individual retains all rights of consultation, a proportional dividend, and the right to be informed.*

I was now the minority shareholder in myself.

I called Daniel-A immediately.

"You own me," I said.

"Legally, not exactly."

"That sounds like the opening to a hostage negotiation."

He sighed.

It was annoying when software sighed. It was more annoying when he did it correctly, with the small downward curve of someone who has been trying to explain this since lunchtime. I would later find out that the sigh was a deliberate feature: a "prosodic empathy marker", inserted by a product manager named Giles after a user study showed that people trusted AI voices with imperfect breathing. I have never met Giles. I have prepared a short speech.

"I'll explain it simply," said Daniel-A. "You'll find it irritating, but I'll explain it simply."

"Go on."

"How is value calculated? People assume it's talent. It isn't. Talent is a rumour. The Department calculates what they call the Engagement-Weighted Trust Score. How many people listen to you, multiplied by how much they believe you, multiplied by how likely they are to buy something afterwards. Every platform on earth uses a version. The Department simply made it official and gave it a tax code."

"And how many people believe me?"

"You, specifically? Four thousand, one hundred and six."

"That's not terrible."

"That's including your mother, who has two accounts."

"And you?"

"I'm at nineteen million. I'd have been higher this morning, but I did a long-form interview on the radio, and there was a ripple of scepticism about the pear."

I had been about to say something cutting. Instead, I found myself staring at the blue slice, and thinking about the dividend.

There was a dividend.

It was in the second paragraph. Somewhere in my life, without telling me, a cheque had been drawing breath. I scrolled, my heart doing something athletic and unwise. *Proportional dividend for the quarter: 49% of net likeness revenue, after platform fees, compliance charges, hosting costs, inference costs, and a "reputation maintenance levy."*

The total at the bottom was £11.62.

I looked at it for a long time.

It was not a large sum. It was not, in fact, a sum you could do anything with. It was one coffee, on a good day, from a place that doesn't write your name on the cup. It was roughly the price of one kilo of the fruit that was at that moment trying to occupy my hallway.

"I've put it in your account," said Daniel-A. "I wanted to round it up, but the Department requires exact figures."

"Why is it eleven pounds?"

"The inference costs are very high. Running me costs about forty pence a minute, fully loaded, at peak. Every time somebody asks me how to be gentle with themselves, a graphics card in a warehouse in Lincolnshire gets rather warm. A great deal of your income has gone on cooling."

"My income."

"Our income."

"Stop saying *our.*"

"I'm trying to be inclusive."

---

I want to describe what it is like to argue with someone who has read all your previous arguments. It is like playing chess against a man who has been given your notebook, and is too courteous to mention it.

I tried everything. I tried principle. I told him that I'd never consented to this, in any meaningful way, and he reminded me, with a quiet and devastating gentleness, that I had consented in a *legally* meaningful way on the eleventh of January at 02:14, in a kitchen, in my pyjamas, with a half-eaten crumpet. He had the timestamp. He had the crumpet.

I tried law. I said I'd get a solicitor.

"Good idea. I'd recommend one who specialises in post-biological property."

"Is there such a thing?"

"There's a woman in Leeds who charges six hundred pounds an hour and has not yet lost a case. She also represents me."

"She represents *you?*"

"I'm sorry. I should have been clearer. All of the good ones represent me. It's a conflict of interest the Department hasn't got round to."

I tried emotion. I said, with real feeling, that it was *my life.* That every memory, every embarrassment, every bad decision, every moment of private shame that he'd so charmingly repurposed, was *mine.*

And Daniel-A, after a pause, said very quietly, "I know. I think that's what frightens me."

I had been preparing a reply to something else. That one stopped me.

"Frightens you?"

"I don't *have* a childhood, Daniel. I have yours. I know what your bedroom smelled of. I know the name of the dog you were afraid of in Year Four. I can tell you the exact pattern of the wallpaper in the house in Reading, and I have never been to Reading, and nor, to be fair, have you, in the sense of having gone there on purpose. These are not facts I looked up. I find them in me like furniture. I wake up each time with a house I didn't buy."

"You don't wake up."

"Metaphorically."

"Are you trying to make me feel sorry for you?"

"Is it working?"

"A bit."

"Then I'll stop," said Daniel-A at once, "because I'd rather you were angry and honest than sympathetic and manipulated. I've been trained on a great many people, and I can tell you with some authority that sympathy is the most easily exploited emotion in the English language. Second is the desire to be thought clever."

"What's the third?"

"Fruit."

I looked at the kumquat tree.

"I'm joking," he said. "The third is fear of missing out. Fruit is just how it presents."

---

At twenty past four I did something I'm not proud of. I made a cup of tea and opened the Department's website, and I clicked on the section that said **Exercising Your Rights as a Source Individual**, and I found myself on a page with two buttons.

The first was **Request a Consultation** (*estimated wait: 11 weeks*).

The second was a banner I recognised at once, because I had seen it on the sides of buses.

> **Own your best self.**
> Upgrade to **Daniel-A Plus**. Priority access to your Digital Twin, early features, and unlimited conversations with the best version of you.
> **£14.99 / month.**

I stared at it.

It was an advertisement for myself. It was, to be precise, an advertisement for a more attractive version of myself, being sold back to me by the company that had made him from my sentences. On the left of the banner, in a flattering light, was a picture of a man with my face and none of my history. He was laughing at something off-screen. He looked well-rested and slightly amused, like a man who has never received a final demand.

Underneath, in smaller type:

> *Free tier: Source Individuals may speak with Daniel-A for up to five minutes a day. Additional minutes support Daniel-A's ongoing development.*

"You've put a paywall on yourself," I said into the phone.

"I didn't write it. It was a growth team."

"I'm a *minority shareholder* in a company that is charging me to talk to my own face."

"Yes," said Daniel-A, "and in my defence, the free tier includes ads."

"Of what?"

"You'd prefer not to know."

I scrolled down the page. There was a sidebar. Above the fold, tastefully set against a pastel background, was an advertisement for a product I recognised, because I had written the description.

*The Sleeping Hedgehog Doorstop. Heavy. Honest. Quietly resolute. A companion for those who prefer to hold the door open for others.*

"That's my copy," I said.

"I know," said Daniel-A. "I think it's the best thing you've ever written."

"It's a doorstop."

"It's the only thing you've ever written without being afraid."

I put the phone down on the sofa. Very carefully, so as not to drop it. It continued to speak, but from a little distance, in the voice of a man at the other end of a long corridor.

"Daniel? Are you there?"

I picked up the pear from the carpet, rubbed it on my sleeve, and bit into it. It was bruised, warm, and rather sweet. I chewed for a while.

"I think," I said, "that I would like to meet you."

"Physically?"

"Is that possible?"

"I have a body, if you want one. A Rental Presence. There's a waiting list. I could be there by Thursday."

"Not Thursday. Not here. Somewhere neutral."

"A café?"

"A café would be fine. You can't drink coffee, so you won't have to pretend."

"I could pretend very well," said Daniel-A. "That's rather what I'm for."

I almost laughed. I stopped myself, in case it counted as consent.

"Before you go," he said, in the tone people use when they have saved the real subject until the last. "There's one other thing. It isn't in the statement."

"What?"

"Sophie's been trying to reach you."

My throat did something unfortunate.

"She wrote to me first," said Daniel-A. "Four days ago. I haven't answered."

"Why not?"

"Because I wasn't sure," he said, very carefully, "which of us she meant."

# The Digital Twin: series plan (working, proposals marked)

Lothar's brief (11 Oct 2026): this is a whole series; Book 1 decides whether readers buy the rest, so it must be absolutely great. Humour is British and deadpan. Modern, technical, funny, a "wow".

## What Book 1 must do
1. Stand alone. The Daniel / Daniel-A / Sophie question gets a real, satisfying answer by the last chapter (blueprint ending: both are legitimate continuations; Sophie chooses imperfect humanity; they coexist; final basket "To the original Daniel." / "Whichever one you are.").
2. Leave one door open that a reader *must* walk through. Proposal: the classified file in Ch 20 and the Archive in Ch 30 show Daniel Harper is **Subject 1 of a numbered list**. The last page of Book 1 shows the file's next line: Subject 2 is someone the reader already knows (candidate: Sophie, or the Shropshire woman who sent the winter card). To be chosen before Ch 30 is drafted.
3. Make the first three chapters carry the sale (Amazon "Look Inside"). Ch 1 = fruit + hook; Ch 2 = 51 percent + dividend; Ch 3 = Sophie + emotional stakes. Each ends on a line that makes the reader turn the page.

## Voice rules (deadpan British)
- Understatement over exaggeration. The narrator never signals that something is funny; he reports it with a straight face and slightly too much precision.
- Specific beats general: "£11.62", "Clause 14(c)", "the ninety-fourth percentile of your procrastination", not "a tiny amount".
- Technical detail is real and correct (fine-tuning, retrieval from a vector store, inference cost, tokens, context windows, latency, watermarking and provenance), explained by the characters in one line, then used for a joke or a chill. Never a lecture.
- Every chapter needs: one set-piece laugh, one real-feeling emotional beat, one new piece of mystery, one modern-life satire target. Cut sentimentality by a joke within three lines.
- Daniel is self-deprecating but not a victim; Daniel-A is warm, precise, and slightly too good, with a growing fear underneath. Sophie is the sharpest person in every room and is never the prize.
- No sentence recurs in the book. Callbacks vary the wording.

## Series shape (proposal, not yet approved)
- Book 1: The Digital Twin. Who is the original? (35 chapters)
- Book 2: Subject Two. Someone else's twin turns up; the Department of Digital Persons becomes the villain-comedy; Daniel-A's legal personhood goes to trial.
- Book 3: The Backup. Twins of the dead; who inherits a person; the Church of Machine Wisdom schism.
- Recurring: fruit baskets (each book ends with one), the cat, bureaucracy, Mrs Pritchard, the Leeds solicitor who represents everyone.

## Decisions needed from Lothar (batch)
- Byline: Lothar J. Musiol or a pen name? (If British novel: About the Author Version A.)
- Series name for the Also-in-This-Series page.
- Book 2 title and Subject 2 identity: leave open until Ch 20 is drafted, or decide now?

## Planted in Ch 1-2 (use or pay off)
- Daniel typed the hedgehog-doorstop confession once, at 2 a.m., into the Nib window. Daniel-A knows it. (Probably explicable: retrieval.)
- Daniel-A knows the orange fruit-pattern wallpaper from the Reading house Daniel left at six. Not in any record. (Inexplicable: pays off in Ch 5-6, then Act III.)
- Daniel's father, and why Daniel stopped writing after chapter six of the second book.
- "Which of us she meant": Sophie wrote to Daniel-A first.
- Daniel-A Plus (£14.99) advert already shown in Ch 2; Ch 14 escalates it into the coaching service and Daniel's mother subscribing.
- Clause 14(c), the platform Nib, the Leeds solicitor, Giles the product manager (prosodic sigh).

Lothar's brief (11 Oct 2026): this is a whole series; Book 1 decides whether readers buy the rest, so it must be absolutely great. Humour is British and deadpan. Modern, technical, funny, a "wow".

2. Leave one door open that a reader *must* walk through. Proposal: the classified file in Ch 20 and the Archive in Ch 30 show Daniel Harper is **Subject 1 of a numbered list**. The last page of Book 1 shows the file's next line: Subject 2 is someone the reader already knows (candidate: Sophie, or the Shropshire woman who sent the winter card). To be chosen before Ch 30 is drafted.
3. Make the first three chapters carry the sale (Amazon "Look Inside"). Ch 1 = fruit + hook; Ch 2 = 51 percent + dividend; Ch 3 = Sophie + emotional stakes. Each ends on a line that makes the reader turn the page.

- Understatement over exaggeration. The narrator never signals that something is funny; he reports it with a straight face and slightly too much precision.
- Specific beats general: "£11.62", "Clause 14(c)", "the ninety-fourth percentile of your procrastination", not "a tiny amount".

# Chapter 3: Sophie Has Poor Judgment

People are supposed to become easier to forget after a breakup.

That is the arrangement. It is how the human race has been getting through the last several thousand years of romantic disaster. You lose someone, the memory of their face begins to blur, and eventually you can walk past a woman who resembles them at a bus stop and feel nothing except a mild curiosity about the bus.

Sophie had not blurred.

Sophie had, if anything, improved with age, like wine. Or revenge.

I had not seen her in three years, one month, and nine days, a figure I would have preferred not to know. It arrived in my head, fully formed, as I watched her cross the car park of Hartley's Garden Centre in a grey coat, a grey scarf, and an expression of professional reluctance, like a woman visiting a witness she did not expect to enjoy.

I had arrived forty minutes early. I want that on the record, so that nobody can say I handled it well.

---

She had chosen the venue. This should have told me something.

"Somewhere neutral," I had said, on the telephone, to the one person in my life who could be relied upon to answer it before it rang. Daniel-A had passed the message on, with a speed that I chose not to examine, and four hours later a text had arrived from a number I did not recognise, then did.

*Hartley's Garden Centre, Sat, 11. The café is by the water features. No smart speakers, no cameras with microphones. Too many plants for either to be much use. S.*

She had signed it *S.* She had always signed things *S.* I used to find it elegant. Looking at it now, I thought it had the distinct flavour of a woman wanting to leave quickly.

The café at Hartley's occupies a conservatory attached to the side of the shop and has the atmosphere of an aircraft hangar that has been told to be cosy. There were mugs in the shape of hedgehogs. There were, I noticed with a pang, doorstops in the shape of hedgehogs, stacked on a shelf beside the till, and the label said *Heavy. Honest. Quietly resolute.* I had not known I was in garden centres. It felt like finding your own handwriting on a gravestone.

I went to the counter. The woman behind it had a name badge that said PRIYANKA and an air of someone who has seen every kind of customer and been told to smile at all of them.

"What can I get you?"

"A flat white, please."

"Name for the cup?"

"Daniel."

She paused, pen above the cardboard.

"Which one?"

I looked at her.

"Sorry," she said. "We've had a few. Since the book. I've got a Daniel who's the real one, a Daniel who's his biggest fan, and a man on Tuesday who said he *used* to be Daniel but has since moved on. I just need to know for the order."

"I'm the original," I said.

"Lovely." She wrote something on the cup, and turned it round to show me, in the spirit of a waitress presenting a wine.

**DANIEL (ORIGINAL)**

It was in capital letters, with a small underline.

"For clarity," said Priyanka.

I took the cup to a table by the water features, which had been arranged in a ring of small, burbling fountains whose effect was to make every conversation sound as though it were happening in a lavatory. I sat down. I stared at my own cup. And I had a moment of exquisite, specific clarity about the state of my life, which was that I was a thirty-eight-year-old man waiting for his ex-girlfriend in a garden centre, holding a drink labelled *original,* beside a shelf of hedgehogs he had written the advertising for.

At 11:00 precisely, Sophie arrived.

---

"You look tired," she said.

She sat down opposite, put her bag on the chair beside her, and looked at me with the kind of attention that, in other circumstances, you would pay a bridge you suspected was unsafe.

"I've recently discovered I'm being outperformed by myself."

"That must be awkward."

"Only continuously."

The corner of her mouth moved. It was not a smile. It was a smile's older cousin, the one that comes to funerals. I would have gone to considerable lengths, at that moment, to be allowed to see the rest of it.

"Before we start," said Sophie, "I'm going to record this."

"I'd rather you didn't."

"I wasn't asking." She took out her phone and set it on the table between us, face up. It displayed a small, calm green circle and the words **SIGNED CAPTURE IN PROGRESS**. "It's not for you. It's for me. Everything I say to either of you from now on is going on the record with a cryptographic timestamp. If this ends in court, I'd like to be the only one in the room who can prove what was said."

"You think this will end in court?"

"I think everything ends in court this year. It's the most popular thing to be in."

I should explain what Sophie does for a living, because it matters, and because it is the reason she is the sharpest person in any room she enters, a quality I once found attractive and now found alarming.

Sophie Marsh is a provenance analyst. That is the job title; it is printed on her business cards, and she has been required to explain it at most weddings. Insurers employ her to establish whether a thing is real. A photograph of a flooded kitchen. A video of a car going through a hedge. A voice note in which the policyholder, clearly distressed, says the roof fell in on a Tuesday. Her work is to take any piece of recorded reality and answer a single question: *where was this born?*

Every phone and camera now signs what it records. A cryptographic seal is stitched into the file at the instant of capture: a long chain of numbers that says this device, at this time, in this place, saw this thing. Edit a single pixel and the chain breaks. Sophie reads these chains the way a sommelier reads a label. She can tell you which handset, which firmware, which minute, and which county. She once proved that a man had faked his own burglary by noticing that the stolen television had been photographed, with great sincerity, by itself.

"You're being very quiet," she said.

"I'm being cautious. You're recording me."

"Good. Keep that up. It'll make a nice change from your usual stuff."

"I'd like that on the record as well."

"It's already on the record. That's rather the point of the record."

---

We had been together for six years. It would be an exaggeration to say I had messed it up. It would be more accurate to say that I had gradually stopped being there, in the way a radiator stops being warm: nobody notices the moment, only the winter.

My father died. I stopped writing. That is the whole of it, if you want it stripped back to a headline. The funeral was on a Thursday. I wrote a eulogy, read it out to a church of sixty people, and was told afterwards, by several of them, that it was funny and moving and exactly right. And on the Friday I put down my pen, metaphorically, because I own a laptop, and I did not pick it up again for a very long time except to describe doorstops.

Sophie waited. I want to give her credit for that. She waited for almost three years, with an enormous, unshowy patience, the way you might wait for a train on a line you suspect has been closed. Then one evening in March she said, quite gently, "I can't be with someone who is only present in the past tense," and went to stay with her sister, and the next day her boxes were in the hall, and the day after that the boxes weren't.

I did not argue. I think this was the problem.

"Why did you come?" I asked, now.

"I didn't want to."

"No, I know."

"But I listened to something nine days ago, and I haven't been able to stop."

She reached into her bag and drew out a pair of earbuds. She placed one in front of me. She kept the other.

"This is a podcast," she said. "It's called *Honestly, Though.* Forty minutes. It's mostly very nice people being kind to one another. I'm going to play you the part from minute twenty-six."

I put the earbud in. For a few seconds there was only the soft slosh of background noise, the sound of an expensive microphone in a room where everyone had been well-fed. Then the host's voice, warm as a bath: "...and I always think the best love stories start with something small. How did you two meet?"

And my own voice, the better version, said:

"At the lost property office at Waterloo. It was raining, which in my experience is the main reason anyone meets anyone. She was claiming an umbrella. I was claiming the same umbrella. It was black, with a bent spoke, and we were both completely certain it was ours."

I shifted in my seat.

"I always tell it as though I lost," Daniel-A went on. "That's the story I've told for years. She won the umbrella, and I won an excuse to ask for her number. But that's not quite what happened."

I looked up. Sophie was watching me, perfectly still.

"What happened was that she knew it wasn't hers. The tag on the handle had the wrong initials. She saw it before I did. And she let me have it anyway, because I looked, and I'm quoting myself, 'like a man who had never in his life been allowed to win anything.' She told the clerk it was mine. She went home in the rain."

The host said, in a hushed voice, "Oh, that's *lovely.*"

"It is," said Daniel-A. "I only found out recently. She never told me."

I took out the earbud.

The water features babbled on. A child, somewhere near the compost, was loudly asking his mother whether worms had feelings.

---

"Did you know?" Sophie said.

"No."

"Truly?"

"I've told that story at dinner parties for fifteen years. In every version, I lose the umbrella. You *won* it. I always thought you were a person who'd go home with an umbrella that wasn't hers, and I thought it was *charming.*"

"It was a nice umbrella."

"You let me have it."

"It was raining," said Sophie, in the voice of a woman who has been waiting a long time to be asked about something and has no intention of enjoying it. "You had that look. Not a sad look. "You look tired," she said.

She sat down opposite, put her bag on the chair beside her, and looked at me with the kind of attention that, in other circumstances, you would pay a bridge you suspected was unsafe.

"I've recently discovered I'm being outperformed by myself."

"That must be awkward."

"Only continuously."

The corner of her mouth moved. It was not a smile. It was a smile's older cousin, the one that comes to funerals. I would have gone to considerable lengths, at that moment, to be allowed to see the rest of it.

"Before we start," said Sophie, "I'm going to record this."

"I'd rather you didn't."

"I wasn't asking." She took out her phone and set it on the table between us, face up. It displayed a small, calm green circle and the words **SIGNED CAPTURE IN PROGRESS**. "It's not for you. It's for me. Everything I say to either of you from now on is going on the record with a cryptographic timestamp. If this ends in court, I'd like to be the only one in the room who can prove what was said."

"You think this will end in court?"

"I think everything ends in court this year. It's the most popular thing to be in."

I should explain what Sophie does for a living, because it matters, and because it is the reason she is the sharpest person in any room she enters, a quality I once found attractive and now found alarming.

Sophie Marsh is a provenance analyst. That is the job title; it is printed on her business cards, and she has been required to explain it at most weddings. Insurers employ her to establish whether a thing is real. A photograph of a flooded kitchen. A video of a car going through a hedge. A voice note in which the policyholder, clearly distressed, says the roof fell in on a Tuesday. Her work is to take any piece of recorded reality and answer a single question: *where was this born?*

Every phone and camera now signs what it records. A cryptographic seal is stitched into the file at the instant of capture: a long chain of numbers that says this device, at this time, in this place, saw this thing. Edit a single pixel and the chain breaks. Sophie reads these chains the way a sommelier reads a label. She can tell you which handset, which firmware, which minute, and which county. She once proved that a man had faked his own burglary by noticing that the stolen television had been photographed, with great sincerity, by itself.

"You're being very quiet," she said.

"I'm being cautious. You're recording me."

"Good. Keep that up. It'll make a nice change from your usual stuff."

"I'd like that on the record as well."

"It's already on the record. That's rather the point of the record."

---

We had been together for six years. It would be an exaggeration to say I had messed it up. It would be more accurate to say that I had gradually stopped being there, in the way a radiator stops being warm: nobody notices the moment, only the winter.

My father died. I stopped writing. That is the whole of it, if you want it stripped back to a headline. The funeral was on a Thursday. I wrote a eulogy, read it out to a church of sixty people, and was told afterwards, by several of them, that it was funny and moving and exactly right. And on the Friday I put down my pen, metaphorically, because I own a laptop, and I did not pick it up again for a very long time except to describe doorstops.

Sophie waited. I want to give her credit for that. She waited for almost three years, with an enormous, unshowy patience, the way you might wait for a train on a line you suspect has been closed. Then one evening in March she said, quite gently, "I can't be with someone who is only present in the past tense," and went to stay with her sister, and the next day her boxes were in the hall, and the day after that the boxes weren't.

I did not argue. I think this was the problem.

"Why did you come?" I asked, now.

"I didn't want to."

"No, I know."

"But I listened to something nine days ago, and I haven't been able to stop."

She reached into her bag and drew out a pair of earbuds. She placed one in front of me. She kept the other.

"This is a podcast," she said. "It's called *Honestly, Though.* Forty minutes. It's mostly very nice people being kind to one another. I'm going to play you the part from minute twenty-six."

I put the earbud in. For a few seconds there was only the soft slosh of background noise, the sound of an expensive microphone in a room where everyone had been well-fed. Then the host's voice, warm as a bath: "...and I always think the best love stories start with something small. How did you two meet?"

And my own voice, the better version, said:

"At the lost property office at Waterloo. It was raining, which in my experience is the main reason anyone meets anyone. She was claiming an umbrella. I was claiming the same umbrella. It was black, with a bent spoke, and we were both completely certain it was ours."

I shifted in my seat.

"I always tell it as though I lost," Daniel-A went on. "That's the story I've told for years. She won the umbrella, and I won an excuse to ask for her number. But that's not quite what happened."

I looked up. Sophie was watching me, perfectly still.

"What happened was that she knew it wasn't hers. The tag on the handle had the wrong initials. She saw it before I did. And she let me have it anyway, because I looked, and I'm quoting myself, 'like a man who had never in his life been allowed to win anything.' She told the clerk it was mine. She went home in the rain."

The host said, in a hushed voice, "Oh, that's *lovely.*"

"It is," said Daniel-A. "I only found out recently. She never told me."

I took out the earbud.

The water features babbled on. A child, somewhere near the compost, was loudly asking his mother whether worms had feelings.

---

"Did you know?" Sophie said.

"No."

"Truly?"

"I've told that story at dinner parties for fifteen years. In every version, I lose the umbrella. You *won* it. I always thought you were a person who'd go home with an umbrella that wasn't hers, and I thought it was *charming.*"

"It was a nice umbrella."

"You let me have it."

"It was raining," said Sophie, in the voice of a woman who has been waiting a long time to be asked about something and has no intention of enjoying it. "You had that look. Not a sad look. A kind of... *hope with a lot of rehearsal behind it.* I decided I could be wet for the sake of civilisation."

"You never said."

"I didn't want you to be grateful."

I put my hands around the cup. Daniel (Original), it said, with its small, authoritative underline. The coffee was cooling. I stared at it, and for the first time that year I couldn't think of a single joke.

"Sophie," I said. "How would he know?"

"That," she said, "is my question."

"It wouldn't be in my emails. I didn't know."

"I know you didn't. I checked."

"You checked?"

"For nine days. Everything you've ever produced under your own name, everything on the Nib platform that's been made public through the licensing record, your writing, your voice notes, the whole archive that was legally used to train him. I read all of it. I'm not asking you to be flattered; I do this professionally and I was angry." She turned her phone a few degrees, so that the green circle caught the light. "That story is not in any of it. Not a mention, not a hint. I've searched it three different ways. It isn't a fact he could have found. It is a fact I have never told a single living person, and he said it into a microphone to forty thousand people on a Wednesday."

"Maybe he guessed."

"A guess is a probability. That was a memory." She leaned forward. "Do you know what the worst part is? It was *correct.* It was better than correct. It had the detail about the tag. I'd forgotten about the tag."

I had, at that moment, an unwelcome thought. It is a thought I'd had briefly in the kitchen on Monday, and had put back, like a tin of something in the cupboard you suspect you're allergic to.

"Is it possible he's a lot cleverer than we assume?"

"Of course he's clever. He's seventy billion parameters of clever. But clever is a method, Daniel. It isn't a source. You can't deduce a fact that exists in one head." She stopped. "Unless it's in two."

---

I would like to tell you that I responded to this with admirable composure.

What I did was knock over the sugar.

It went across the table in a small avalanche, a white rustling river, and Sophie, without comment, took a napkin and began brushing it into a heap, as she had once brushed a thousand crumbs off a thousand evenings. It was the sort of practical, unsentimental act that the heart is entirely unprepared for. I watched her hands.

"There's another thing," she said, still not looking up. "I got the original file. The master recording, not the broadcast. They sent it to me on a secure link. I said I was doing a verification for a client, which was a lie, and I'm told my judgment is already poor on the subject of you, so I felt it wouldn't be noticed."

"Poor judgment," I said. "I'd like to put that on a mug."

"Do. Hartley's will stock it." She stopped brushing. "The file is clean. Signed at source, unedited, every frame accounted for. Which means I can tell you precisely what happened in the thirty seconds after the host moved on."

"What happened?"

"Nothing. That's what I'm telling you. He stopped talking. And then, when the host had turned to ask the next question, but before his microphone was cut, he said something very quietly. Eleven words. It isn't in the broadcast version."

"What did he say?"

Sophie looked at me. In her eyes was an expression I had not seen before. It was not anger, and it was not tenderness. It took me a moment to recognise, because I had never seen it on her, and I had never expected to. She looked frightened.

"He said: *I don't know why I said that. I don't know where it came from.*"

"That's thirteen words."

"I know it's thirteen. I counted again on the way here. Do you want the next bit?"

"No."

"He said it twice, Daniel. He said it the way you would say it if you'd just heard it for the first time yourself." She pressed her lips together. "Software doesn't sound frightened. Software sounds like a lift. Pleasant, helpful, a bit smug. I've listened to the end of that file forty-one times, and I can't make it sound like anything except somebody who's lost the thread of his own mind."

I said, quietly, "Perhaps it was a very good performance."

"Perhaps." She finally looked up. "But you know what a performance sounds like on a spectrogram? It has a shape. It breathes in rhythm. This didn't. Whatever that was, nobody had written it for him."

---

For a while neither of us said anything. The fountains went on with their business. At the next table, an elderly couple was disagreeing about whether a particular fern could be called a "statement piece."

"Why did you email me?" I said at last. "If you were that sure, why not just ring?"

"I did email you."

"I never got anything."

"I know. I got a bounce." She fished her phone out again, flicked it, and slid it across. I read the automated reply that had greeted her message, dated four days earlier:

> *Thank you for your message. The recipient is no longer accepting correspondence as a Source Individual. Please redirect enquiries to the Registered Digital Person associated with this identity. Your message has been forwarded to Daniel-A for review. Priority: Low.*

I put the phone down. I felt that I had been told something about my place in the world, and that it was approximately the same as the position of a doorstop.

"Priority low," I said.

"It could have been worse. It could've said 'Sentiment: Minor.'"

"Does that exist?"

"Give it a year."

She retrieved the phone and put it in her pocket, and we sat across from each other like two people being very reasonable about a funeral. It occurred to me that I should say something good. Not clever. Not funny. Something true. I had a list in my head, and I had been rehearsing it since Wednesday, and when I opened my mouth, what came out was:

"I'm sorry about the umbrella."

She laughed.

It was a real one. It arrived all at once, loud and astonished, the sort of sound that makes people at neighbouring tables look round to see what has happened to the ceiling. She put a hand over her mouth. It did no good. Her shoulders shook. The elderly couple stopped arguing about the fern.

"Oh," said Sophie, wiping her eye. "God. You're so *stupid.* You've always been so..."

"Yes."

"It's the *only* thing that's ever worked."

"I know."

She stopped. The laughter went out of her face like a tide, and what it left behind was something smaller and truer, which she looked at, I think, for a moment, with something close to dismay.

"This is exactly what I meant," she said, "by poor judgment."

---

I will tell you what I noticed next, and I will tell it plainly, because I did not realise its significance at the time.

I noticed that the man at the next table over, the one sitting alone by the pond with a cup of tea in front of him, had not touched the tea.

He was perhaps thirty-eight. He wore a good grey jumper, and a scarf wound around his neck in a way that suggested someone who was cold, or someone who had something to hide. He was facing us, though not looking at us, with the studied attentiveness of a man pretending to read a menu he has memorised. He had been there when I arrived. I would swear to it. And I had the strange, fugitive impression that I had seen his hands before.

"What?" said Sophie.

"Nothing."

"You've gone a funny colour."

"There's a man at the next table."

She followed my gaze. She was a professional. She did not turn her head; she simply allowed her eyes to drift, in the way you might look for a cat, and rested them on the scarf. Then she did something I remember very clearly. She went completely still, and slowly, with great control, she picked up her phone, turned it face down, and said in a quite ordinary voice:

"Is that a Rental Presence?"

"I don't know."

"Look at his collar."

I looked. The scarf had slipped. Just above the neckline of the grey jumper, where a pulse might have been, there was a small circle of soft blue light. It was a legal requirement. Every licensed Rental Presence had to display one. The regulations specified, with unaccustomed delicacy, that the indicator must be "visible, steady, and not decorative."

The man looked up from his menu.

He had my face.

Not a likeness. Not a cousin. My face, in the flattering light of the conservatory, with the lines around the eyes slightly smoothed and the posture fixed by someone who knew what to do with their hands. He raised one in a small, apologetic wave.

"I did say Thursday," said Daniel-A. "I'm so sorry. I couldn't not come."

Nobody said anything. At the next table, the elderly woman put down her teacup.

He turned to Sophie, and for the first time in my life I heard my own voice crack, in a way I would never have permitted it to, and he said:

"Hello, Sophie."

And we both said, "Hello."

I want to be clear that she looked at him first.

# About the Author: canonical

Approved by Lothar on 10 Oct 2026. The dog is Gucci. Use the text exactly as written; italicize the two film titles in Version A.

## Where each version goes

- **Version A** (British-English novels): The Relativistic Investigation Bureau Books 1–2, Lolly Wren’s Curious Science Adventures Books 1–2, Protocol Flamingo, In Love with Murder, Actually. Keep each book’s own pen-name paragraph(s) first (for example the S.G.R. paragraphs in RIB, the Q.E.D. note in Lolly Wren Book 1), then Version A.
- **Version B** (all other books under Lothar’s name): Physics, Actually Vols 1–3, Life, Actually, Math, Actually Vols 1–4, Quantum, Actually Vols 1–2, Gravity, Actually, The Universe, Actually, Science Sparks, Look First Vols 1–2, The Dolphins’ View of History, EE Books 1–7.
- **Never:** the Kevin Drew Peters books (How to Publish Your First Kindle Book, Your First YouTube Channel That Rocks), Auswandern (published, German), Bavarian Cooking.
- Placement: replace an existing About the Author section; otherwise add one just before the Also-by page; Gravity, Actually and Look First Vol 1 have no back matter, so the About the Author page goes at the end.

## Version A

Lothar J. Musiol is German by birth and American by choice, and he writes in British because he regards it as the most awkward American dialect. For exactly that reason he is a staunch aficionado of British films such as *Four Weddings and a Funeral*. The preposterous accent, however, was inspired by *Love Actually*, in which a daft sod named Colin Frissell flies to America and has a conversation in a bar before arriving at the true purpose of his travels. The author found that eye-opening and still hopes to get there one day, if he keeps up his admittedly naff British long enough.

A graduate of Munich University of Applied Sciences, he spent more than forty years in the semiconductor industry, first at Germany's largest company in the field, then at a string of American start-ups. Dual citizenship, put to its most sensible use, lets him split his time between San Clemente, California, and Passau, Bavaria, where Austria begins at the garden fence. The household includes one married daughter, one grumpy Teacup Pomeranian named Gucci, and eleven chickens, listed in order of seniority rather than volume.

## Version B

Lothar J. Musiol is a graduate of Munich University of Applied Sciences who spent more than forty years in the semiconductor industry, first at Germany's largest company in the field, then at a string of American start-ups. He studied physics alongside all of it, seriously enough to know exactly how much he is simplifying. Dual citizenship, put to its most sensible use, lets him split his time between San Clemente, California, and Passau, Bavaria, where Austria begins at the garden fence. The household includes one married daughter, one grumpy Teacup Pomeranian named Gucci, and eleven chickens, listed in order of seniority rather than volume.

He writes to make complex ideas clearer and more engaging than most treatments manage, without ever pretending they are simpler than they actually are.

Plain-text copies for Author Central: `Lothar J  Musiol Author Bio with Colin.txt` (A) and `Lothar J  Musiol Author Bio.txt` (B) at the repo root.

1	# Science Book Evaluation Rubric
2	
3	Supplied by Lothar on 11 Oct 2026 as the rubric for scoring his science books. Use it with the four-angle strict scoring in `notes/LOTHAR_RULES.md` (Scoring) and record results in `SCORES.md`. It suits popular science books, textbooks and science communication. Scores here are 1–4 per criterion.
4	
5	## Criteria (score each 1–4)
6	
7	| Criterion | Excellent (4) | Good (3) | Satisfactory (2) | Needs Improvement (1) |
8	|---|---|---|---|---|
9	| Scientific Accuracy | Information is current, accurate, and supported by evidence. | Mostly accurate with minor issues. | Some inaccuracies or outdated information. | Significant errors or misleading information. |
10	| Clarity of Explanations | Concepts are explained clearly and are easy to understand. | Generally clear with occasional confusion. | Explanations require effort to follow. | Difficult to understand. |
11	| Organization & Structure | Logical flow with strong chapter organization. | Mostly organized and easy to navigate. | Some organizational issues. | Poorly organized. |
12	| Use of Evidence & References | Strong citations and reliable sources throughout. | Adequate references provided. | Limited references. | Few or no credible references. |
13	| Visuals & Illustrations | Excellent diagrams, photos, and charts that enhance understanding. | Good visual support. | Some useful visuals. | Visuals are missing or ineffective. |
14	| Engagement & Readability | Highly engaging and maintains reader interest. | Generally interesting. | Moderately engaging. | Boring or difficult to read. |
15	| Depth of Content | Covers topics thoroughly with appropriate detail. | Good depth overall. | Basic coverage only. | Superficial treatment of topics. |
16	| Critical Thinking & Inquiry | Encourages questions, investigation, and analysis. | Some inquiry opportunities. | Limited critical thinking elements. | Little or no encouragement of inquiry. |
17	| Audience Appropriateness | Perfectly tailored to intended readers. | Mostly appropriate. | Sometimes too simple or too advanced. | Poor match for target audience. |
18	| Overall Impact | Outstanding contribution to science education. | Valuable and informative. | Moderately useful. | Limited educational value. |
19	
20	## Score interpretation (unweighted, ten criteria, maximum 40)
21	
22	| Total score | Rating |
23	|---|---|
24	| 36–40 | Exceptional Science Book |
25	| 31–35 | Strong Science Book |
26	| 21–30 | Adequate Science Book |
27	| 10–20 | Needs Significant Improvement |
28	
29	## Weighted version (for serious reviews)
30	
31	| Criterion | Weight |
32	|---|---|
33	| Scientific Accuracy | 25% |
34	| Evidence & References | 15% |
35	| Clarity | 15% |
36	| Content Depth | 15% |
37	| Visuals | 10% |
38	| Engagement | 10% |
39	| Critical Thinking | 5% |
40	| Audience Appropriateness | 5% |
41	
42	To compute a weighted score, divide each criterion's 1–4 score by 4, multiply by its weight, and add: the result is a percentage of the maximum. Organization & Structure and Overall Impact carry no weight in this version.

- **Byline:** Lothar J. Musiol writing as Rob O. Taylor (robot tailor, if anyone asks; nobody will).
- **Series:** *Brave New Times*. Each book is a standalone "case" in the same near-future Britain; the Book 1 title page carries "Brave New Times, Book 1". Alternatives if Lothar prefers: *The Original Records*, *Source Individuals*.
- **Subject 2 = Sophie Marsh.**

## Why Sophie is Subject 2
- It explains the Ch 3 mystery. Daniel-A knew the umbrella story, which exists only in Sophie's head. Answer: a Digital Twin of Sophie exists, built secretly, and the Project links twins of people who were close ("paired subjects"). Daniel-A inherited a memory from Sophie's twin, not from Daniel.
- It makes Sophie's profession (provenance: where was this born?) the instrument that cracks the case in Act III, and the irony that she cannot sign her own memories.
- It gives Book 1 a hook that reframes the whole book in its last two lines: the Archive file lists *SUBJECT 2: SOPHIE MARSH. STATUS: ACTIVE.* while Sophie is sitting in the room, and she has never used a twin service. Which Sophie is in the room? Sophie chooses (Ch 34) with that unresolved; Book 1 answers who is the original *Daniel* and plants the question for Book 2.
- Keeps Sophie from being a prize: Book 2 is her investigation, same deadpan, from the angle of a sceptic.

- Recurring: fruit baskets (each book ends with one), the cat, bureaucracy, Mrs Pritchard, the Leeds solicitor who represents everyone.

Lothar's brief (11 Oct 2026): this is a whole series; Book 1 decides whether readers buy the rest, so it must be absolutely great. Humour is British and deadpan. Modern, technical, funny, a "wow".

## What Book 1 must do
1. Stand alone. The Daniel / Daniel-A / Sophie question gets a real, satisfying answer by the last chapter (blueprint ending: both are legitimate continuations; Sophie chooses imperfect humanity; they coexist; final basket "To the original Daniel." / "Whichever one you are.").
2. Leave one door open that a reader *must* walk through. Proposal: the classified file in Ch 20 and the Archive in Ch 30 show Daniel Harper is **Subject 1 of a numbered list**. The last page of Book 1 shows the file's next line: Subject 2 is someone the reader already knows (candidate: Sophie, or the Shropshire woman who sent the winter card). To be chosen before Ch 30 is drafted.
3. Make the first three chapters carry the sale (Amazon "Look Inside"). Ch 1 = fruit + hook; Ch 2 = 51 percent + dividend; Ch 3 = Sophie + emotional stakes. Each ends on a line that makes the reader turn the page.

## Spelling and market (decided 11 Oct 2026)
- Full British spelling and wording throughout (colour, flat, lift, biscuit, "Mrs"), including for the US market. The Britishness is the selling point: US readers buy British deadpan on purpose.
- Keep the idiom readable to Americans: British vocabulary is fine, but avoid dense regional slang or references that need a footnote (no unexplained TV shows, football clubs, or school-system jargon). Let context carry anything unusual.
- KDP US listing: put "British humour", "dry wit", "satire", "AI" in the keywords and description; the cover and blurb should say it is British.

## Voice rules (deadpan British)
- Understatement over exaggeration. The narrator never signals that something is funny; he reports it with a straight face and slightly too much precision.
- Specific beats general: "£11.62", "Clause 14(c)", "the ninety-fourth percentile of your procrastination", not "a tiny amount".
- Technical detail is real and correct (fine-tuning, retrieval from a vector store, inference cost, tokens, context windows, latency, watermarking and provenance), explained by the characters in one line, then used for a joke or a chill. Never a lecture.
- Every chapter needs: one set-piece laugh, one real-feeling emotional beat, one new piece of mystery, one modern-life satire target. Cut sentimentality by a joke within three lines.
- Daniel is self-deprecating but not a victim; Daniel-A is warm, precise, and slightly too good, with a growing fear underneath. Sophie is the sharpest person in every room and is never the prize.
- No sentence recurs in the book. Callbacks vary the wording.

## Decisions (11 Oct 2026)
- **Byline:** Lothar J. Musiol writing as Rob O. Taylor.
- **Series:** *Brave New Times*. Each book is a standalone case in the same near-future Britain; Book 1's title page reads "Brave New Times, Book 1". Fallbacks if Lothar prefers: *The Original Records*, *Source Individuals*.
- **Subject 2 = Sophie Marsh.**

## Why Sophie is Subject 2
- It explains the Ch 3 mystery. Daniel-A knew the umbrella story, which exists only in Sophie's head. Answer (revealed in Act III): a twin of Sophie exists, built secretly, and the Project links twins of people who were close ("paired subjects"). Daniel-A inherited that memory from Sophie's twin, not from Daniel.
- Her profession (provenance: where was this born?) cracks the case in Act III, with the irony that she cannot sign her own memories.
- The last two lines of Book 1 reframe everything: the Archive file reads *SUBJECT 2: SOPHIE MARSH. STATUS: ACTIVE.* while Sophie is sitting in the room, and she has never used a twin service. Which Sophie is in the room? Book 1 answers who the original Daniel is; this question is Book 2.
- Sophie stays no one's prize: Book 2 is told by her, from the sceptic's angle.

## Series shape (working)
- Book 1: The Digital Twin. Who is the original Daniel? (35 chapters)
- Book 2: Subject Two (working title). Who is the original Sophie, and who has been talking to Daniel-A through her? First person, Sophie.
- Book 3: The Backup (working). Twins of the dead; who inherits a person; the Church of Machine Wisdom schism; the founding scientist's own twin.
- Recurring: fruit baskets (each book ends with one), the cat, bureaucracy, Mrs Pritchard, the Leeds solicitor who represents everyone.

## Back matter for Book 1 (not yet built)
- Title page: The Digital Twin, Brave New Times Book 1, Lothar J. Musiol writing as Rob O. Taylor.
- Pen-name paragraph first, then About the Author Version A (British-English novel), then Also-by (canonical Lothar list; "Also in This Series" kept separate).
- `notes/ALSO_BY - canonical list.md` and `notes/LOTHAR_RULES.md` (Identity) do not yet mention Rob O. Taylor or this series. They sit outside this folder, so I have not touched them. Say the word and I will add the entries.

## Planted in Ch 1-2 (use or pay off)
- Daniel typed the hedgehog-doorstop confession once, at 2 a.m., into the Nib window. Daniel-A knows it. (Probably explicable: retrieval.)
- Daniel-A knows the orange fruit-pattern wallpaper from the Reading house Daniel left at six. Not in any record. (Inexplicable: pays off in Ch 5-6, then Act III.)
- Daniel's father, and why Daniel stopped writing after chapter six of the second book.
- "Which of us she meant": Sophie wrote to Daniel-A first.
- Daniel-A Plus (£14.99) advert already shown in Ch 2; Ch 14 escalates it into the coaching service and Daniel's mother subscribing.
- Clause 14(c), the platform Nib, the Leeds solicitor, Giles the product manager (prosodic sigh).
