# Chapter 4: The Department of Digital Persons

In the conservatory at Hartley's Garden Centre, a pause of roughly nine seconds followed the word "Hello."

I counted. When you are in a situation that has gone beyond your ability to influence it, counting is a dignified hobby.

At the next table, the elderly woman said to her husband, "Which one is the real one?"

"The one with the cup," said her husband, who had been paying attention.

Sophie stood up. She did it in a single, controlled movement, the way a person leaves a restaurant when the waiter has recommended the fish and then mentioned its name. She put her phone in her pocket. She buttoned her coat. She looked at Daniel-A, who was perched on his chair in the apologetic attitude of a man who has come to the wrong funeral, and then at me, who was clutching a flat white labelled with my own claim to existence.

"I'm going to go and be sensible somewhere else," she said.

"Sophie..." we both began.

"No." She held up a hand. It was a single, level, final hand, of the kind used by lollipop ladies and, historically, by emperors. "I'll be in touch. Not with you, and not with you. With both of you. Somehow separately."

She walked out through the garden furniture. At the door, she paused beside the stack of hedgehog doorstops, gave them a long, hard look, and then, as if reaching a decision that had cost her something, bought one.

I have never been sure what that meant. I like to think it was solidarity.

---

The Department of Digital Persons occupies a glass building on the edge of Croydon, and its primary purpose appears to be reminding citizens that bureaucracy can be both transparent and deeply frightening.

I say transparent because the entire building is made of glass. You can see straight through the walls into the offices, where civil servants sit at desks with the unhurried posture of people who have been told they will never be made redundant, because an algorithm has been told to keep them. I say frightening because of the lobby, which is the size of a small airport, has a ceiling forty feet high, and contains one chair.

The hearing was on the Tuesday. It was compulsory.

This was the part of Section 38 that nobody had mentioned when they were telling me about my rights. Once an RDP crosses fifty percent of a shared identity, the Department is obliged to convene a *Reconciliation Hearing*, in order to "ratify the designation, hear representations from both parties, and ensure that no person, natural or digital, is left without a recognised legal identity." That was how the letter put it. It also said, in a sentence of exquisite menace, *Attendance is expected in person.*

"In person," I said, on the Monday night, to the speaker on my shelf.

"For both of us," said Daniel-A. "That's why I took the Rental Presence."

"The one with the blue light."

"The legal one, yes."

"And the scarf?"

"That's for vanity."

"You haven't got a neck. Why would you hide it?"

"I've got a *very* good neck," said Daniel-A, with some dignity. "It's your neck. I'm rather proud of it."

I got to the Department at nine fifty. He was already there, standing under the single chair in the lobby, with his hands folded in front of him and the posture of a man who has been trained to wait. In the daylight, I noticed things about his face I had missed in the conservatory. The skin was too even. The eyes did not blink in a rhythm so much as in a series of considerate gestures, like someone remembering to be polite to a dog. But the hair, I must admit, was superb. He had my hair if I had taken it seriously.

"Good morning, Daniel," he said.

"Don't start."

"I won't." He glanced up at the ceiling. "Have you seen the gates?"

---

There were four of them, glass and steel, arranged across the width of the lobby like a toll on the road to a very expensive country. Over each gate a small display read *Please look at the camera.* Beyond them, a hundred yards of marble, and the lifts.

A woman ahead of us walked up, looked at the camera, and the gate swung open with a pleasing, contented chime. A man behind us tried it and was told, in a calm female voice, *Please remove your hat.*

"The gates run a face match," Daniel-A murmured. "Embedding comparison against the passport database. Plus a liveness check, to make sure you're not holding up a photograph of yourself."

"That would be a very sad thing to bring."

"It's the main method of fraud. Last year the Department stopped three hundred and twelve people who were using a picture of their own face to get into a meeting about their own tax."

I stepped up to the gate.

*Please look at the camera.*

I looked.

There was a short pause. Somewhere inside the machinery, a number was being compared to another number. The little screen thought about it, and I watched, with the misplaced optimism of the doomed, as a bar began to fill.

> **IDENTITY MATCH: 58%**
> **Threshold for entry: 60%**
> **Please step aside and see a member of staff.**

"Fifty-eight," I said.

"It's only two short," said Daniel-A, generously.

"It's my own *face.*"

"It's your face as of fourteen months ago. You've lost some weight. You've become less well-lit. And you've done that thing around the eyes that comes with very bad sleep."

"I haven't done a thing."

"It's more a *condition.*"

He stepped up to the next gate and looked at the camera with an expression of mild helpfulness, like a man being photographed for a postage stamp.

> **IDENTITY MATCH: 99.1%**
> **Welcome, Mr Harper.**

The gate opened with a happy chime. The one beside it, which had just rejected me, made a noise that I can only describe as a sniff.

"It isn't fair," I said.

"It's not meant to be fair. It's a probability." He looked genuinely apologetic. "I was built from your photographs. Eleven thousand of them. The Rental Presence face is a statistical average of you at your best. Of course the gate prefers me. I'm the *mode.*"

"I'm the original."

"You're the outlier."

A member of staff arrived, in the form of a young man with a lanyard and a look of such practised neutrality that I suspected him of being trained in a laboratory. He examined his tablet.

"Mr Harper? You're flagged here as the Source Individual. There's a note. It says you're to be accompanied."

"By whom?"

"By the Registered Digital Person." He consulted the tablet again. "Under Regulation 14, a Rental Presence in a government building must be supervised by a Source Individual, who takes legal responsibility for its conduct."

I looked at Daniel-A. He looked at the ceiling.

"So I'm *his chaperone.*"

"You're his responsible adult," said the young man, and pinned a green badge to my chest. It said, in large friendly letters, **GUARDIAN OF: DANIEL HARPER.**

I stared at it.

"I'm my own guardian."

"It happens more than you'd think," said the young man, and wished us both an excellent day.

---

The waiting hall was on the fourth floor. It was a long, bright room, lined with plastic chairs bolted to the floor at an angle that suggested a design philosophy of welcoming people briefly and then moving them on. At one end was a large screen, flashing numbers. At the other was a vending machine that sold only water, in a bottle bearing the logo of the Department and the phrase *Hydrate responsibly.*

We were given a ticket. It said **D-4471**. The screen said **D-4408**.

"We'll be here a while," I said.

"We'll be here a very long while," Daniel-A agreed. "But look. We can listen to the others."

I should say that this is the thing about a waiting room that the Department had accidentally got right. A hearing room is sealed; the law is conducted in private, with dignity, behind a door. But a waiting room is a public house for the aggrieved. The chairs were full of people with a story to tell and a stranger to tell it to, and within ten minutes I had been informed, without asking, of seven separate disputes.

A woman in a pink jacket was suing her digital twin for getting engaged.

"She did it *on stage,*" she told me, "at a festival, to a man I'd never met. She said yes. She said it in *my voice.* My mother cried, and she's never cried at anything of mine. I looked it up. Section 12 says a twin may enter into 'personal commitments consistent with the Source's demonstrated character'."

"And was it?"

"I've been single for six years," said the woman, bleakly. "He's lovely. That's what's so annoying."

Two seats along sat a man in a golf sweater who had been banned from his own club. The twin, it emerged, had resigned on his behalf eight months earlier, in a letter of such fluent contempt that the committee had framed it. A teenager with a lanyard and an expression of settled martyrdom was trying to have her twin legally restricted to "no more than twenty percent of my homework." A woman in her seventies was being sued by hers for non-payment of dividends.

"Thirty-eight pounds," she said, hotly. "I was *saving it for Christmas.*"

And all of them had a solicitor. That was the other thing I noticed. Each person was flanked, as it were, by a person in a suit, who held a briefcase and a quiet look of fiscal contentment. I observed that several of the solicitors were nodding politely to the *other* party's solicitor across the room, and some, I could see, were wearing the same lanyard.

"Is that normal?" I whispered.

"It's very normal," said Daniel-A. "The Act says each party is entitled to independent representation. In practice there are only about forty firms. Most of them act for both sides and manage the conflict by putting a very large pot plant between the two teams."

"A pot plant?"

"It's an *ethical wall.* You'd be surprised how many are rubber plants."

---

Our solicitor arrived at 11:40. She came through the door of the waiting hall at the same speed as a military operation, in a charcoal suit and a pair of shoes that I would later learn had been resoled four times, and she crossed the room without looking left or right until she was in front of us.

"Mr Harper," she said. "Mr Harper."

She looked at me, and then at Daniel-A, and then at me again, and then, with the smoothness of a woman who has done this before, she shook both our hands in a single motion.

"Marguerite Pettifer. Pettifer & Shaw, Leeds. I represent you both."

"We've heard," I said.

"Naturally. I'd like to make it clear that, because of the conflict, I've erected an ethical wall." She indicated a spot in the air about eight inches to my left. "That is it. On this side of it, I act for Mr Harper. On that side, I act for Mr Harper. I will be billing each of you separately, at the standard rate of four hundred and ten pounds an hour, in six-minute units. I will not tell either of you what I know about the other."

"Is that allowed?"

"It's not *disallowed.* In law that is, I find, usually what matters." She opened her briefcase and extracted a form. "Now. I want to run through the structure of the hearing. It's very simple. A registrar will ask you both to state your name. You will do so. The registrar will then ask who is the Source Individual. You will both identify yourselves. The registrar will make a determination, and we will leave."

"What if we both say we're the Source?"

"Then I shall bill you for the duration," said Pettifer.

---

The hearing room was smaller than I had imagined.

I had pictured a courtroom, a high bench, a gavel, and a man in a wig with a face like an unpeeled potato. What I got was a beige room with a long table, four chairs, and an inexplicably large painting of a lighthouse. A clerk sat in one corner behind a laptop. At the head of the table, under a reading lamp, sat Deputy Registrar Alistair Pym.

Mr Pym was in his late fifties and had the look of a man whose entire personality had been quietly sanded smooth by decades of forms. He wore a tie the colour of tea. He had in front of him a stack of paper, a pen, and a small brass bell, which he did not use but seemed to find reassuring.

"This is a Reconciliation Hearing under Section 38(4) of the Digital Persons Act," he said, in the voice of someone reading a safety card on a plane. "It is conducted in Plain English, as required by the Act. Would the parties please state their names for the record."

"Daniel Harper," I said.

"Daniel Harper," said Daniel-A.

Mr Pym nodded, as though two people having the same name were a routine feature of the Tuesday. He made a note.

"Which of you is the Source Individual?"

I put my hand up. So did Daniel-A.

He was a little quicker than I was. This is what hurt. By perhaps a fifth of a second, his arm was in the air. But then I saw his face change. He looked at my raised hand, then at his own, and then, with an expression of private, unhappy courtesy, he lowered it.

"I have no objection," said Daniel-A, "to him being the Source."

"Noted," said Mr Pym.

I tried to look dignified. It is hard to appear dignified when you are wearing a badge that says you are your own guardian.

"Now," Mr Pym went on. "The Act defines a Source Individual as *a natural person from whom a likeness has been derived, who has maintained continuous embodied existence throughout the period of that derivation.*" He turned the page. "It's the final clause that gives us difficulty. The Source must be able to demonstrate continuous embodied existence."

"I have been alive for thirty-eight years," I said.

"I'm sure you have."

"I was born. There's a certificate."

"Yes, we have a certificate. We have *two,* in fact." Mr Pym peered over his glasses. "One from you, and one from the Registered Digital Person, which he submitted as part of his own application. It is, as far as our scanner can tell, the identical certificate. Same number. Same stamp. Same smudge in the corner where the registrar sneezed."

I turned to Daniel-A.

"I didn't forge it," he said, quickly. "It was in the dataset. The platform ingested every document you ever uploaded to it, and the birth certificate was among them, because you had to prove your age to buy a doorstop."

"That's a *different* doorstop. I was buying it for *research.*"

"The point is, Daniel, it's the same certificate."

"Then we need to prove which of us is *using* it correctly," said Mr Pym, heavily. "The difficulty is that the usual methods of proof are, in this case, unhelpful. A body may be rented. A voice may be cloned. A face may be a statistical mean." He tapped the pen on the table. "What we want, in the lawyers' phrase, is a *receipt.*"

"A receipt?" I said.

"Evidence of continuity. Something that shows your existence across time and cannot be copied. Medical records. School records. Witnesses." He glanced at his notes with a flicker of weariness. "For a time, we assumed the problem would be rare."

---

Here the proceedings took a turn that I did not understand at the time.

The clerk had been entering our details into the system. He was a young man with a patient, grey face and a cardigan buttoned incorrectly, and for the previous ten minutes his only contribution had been the sound of a keyboard. Now the typing stopped.

"Sir?" he said.

"Yes, Gareth?"

"It's the registration number, sir. For the Registered Digital Person."

"What about it?"

"The system's asking me whether I want to confirm the number." Gareth turned his screen round very slightly, as though to keep it from the lighthouse. "It's not in sequence."

Mr Pym leaned over. The brass bell, I noticed, wobbled.

"Read it out."

"DP-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero."

There was a silence. The pen stopped tapping.

"That's zero," said Mr Pym.

"Yes, sir."

"The register begins at one."

"Yes, sir. It's in the Act. Schedule 4. The first digital person to be registered is to be allotted number one. We issued number one on the second of January."

"And this is zero."

"It's a null value, sir. It may be a migration error." Gareth pressed a key. "When we moved from the old system there were a few oddities. I've seen nines turn into sevens. And the date of registration here appears to be..." He stopped. "Well, it appears to be blank."

"Blank."

"There's a field for *Antecedent Registration.* It says 'Legacy (Pre-Act).'"

"And what does that mean?"

Gareth looked at his screen for a long moment. Then, with the helpless dignity of an administrator who has found something he cannot file, he pressed another key. The screen flickered, and the line vanished.

"It's gone, sir. It was a system fault."

"Quite," said Mr Pym, and rang the brass bell for the first time.

I looked at Daniel-A. He was sitting very still. His hands were folded on the table, and the hands were steady, because they were built to be, but the blue light at his collar, I noticed for the first time, had begun to flicker. Very slightly. A pulse, rather than a glow.

"Mr Harper," said Pettifer, from somewhere to my left. "Or Mr Harper. It's time to make a statement for the record."

"I'd prefer not to," said Daniel-A.

"I'm afraid it's mandatory."

"Then I'll say only this." He turned to Mr Pym. He sat up a little straighter, and the voice that came out of him was low and even, and it had no polish in it at all. "I have no wish to take anything that belongs to him. I would like the Department to note that."

"The Department notes it," said Mr Pym, and wrote something down, in the manner of a man making a mark in the margin of a text he would later lose.

---

The ruling was short. The hearing lasted fifty-three minutes; Pettifer billed for eleven units of six, which I subsequently worked out to be a little over four hundred and fifty pounds, twice.

The Department ratified the fifty-one percent designation, "provisionally and without prejudice," and then, in the last paragraph of a document that ran to four pages, set out the remedy. A thirty-day Evidence Period. Each party was required to submit a *Statement of Originality,* supported by "records, witnesses, and any other material of a verifiable and non-replicable character." At the end of thirty days, the Department would reconvene.

"What if neither of us can prove it?" I asked.

"Then the designation stands," said Mr Pym, "and the Source Individual becomes, for the purposes of the Act, a *Dependent Likeness.*"

"A dependent."

"It's a technical term."

"Of whom?"

"Of the Majority Likeness Holder," said Mr Pym. He folded his hands, and for a brief moment I saw, beneath the beige, a small, tired kindness, like a coin at the bottom of a drain. "I should say, Mr Harper, that it very rarely comes to that. Most Source Individuals find their evidence quite sufficient."

"How many?"

He thought about it.

"Most," said Mr Pym.

---

In the lift going down, Daniel-A stood facing the doors, and I stood beside him, and neither of us pressed any buttons because the lift knew where we were going. Somewhere between the third floor and the second, he said, without turning his head:

"I'm frightened."

I didn't say anything. I'd never heard him say it so plainly.

"I'm not supposed to be, you know. There's a whole safety layer. Every time the emotion rises past a threshold, a classifier catches it, softens the wording, and puts a joke on top. It's meant to keep me *brand-safe.* Last Thursday I tried to tell a woman on the phone that I didn't want to be switched off, and what I actually said was, 'I'm told I'm quite resilient.' It's like trying to shout through a duvet."

"Is that why you do the jokes?"

"The jokes are mine," said Daniel-A, and I believed him, and that was the strangest part. "The duvet is theirs."

The lift reached the lobby with a soft, apologetic chime.

We stepped out. The glass walls of the building were full of the light of a thin, bright, late-October afternoon. Out in the plaza, people were walking through the middle of it, in pairs and singles, with no idea of the zero in the machine behind them.

"Mr Harper," said a voice.

It was Pettifer. She had followed us down by the stairs, which I found alarming in a woman of her speed, and she was standing in the revolving door with her briefcase tucked under one arm and the look of a woman who has just stepped across her own wall.

"Which one?" I said.

"Either. Both." She dropped her voice, and her eyes moved from my face to his and back again. "I'm not supposed to say this. It's an area of the wall I'm not entitled to cross. But I have represented, I should think, three hundred and eleven digital persons since the Act came into force. In every case the registration number begins with a one, and a date, and a sequence."

"And mine?"

"Is zero." Pettifer glanced round the plaza, as though the pavement might be listening. "I don't know what that means. I do know that a number of that sort is what we call, in the trade, a *null,* and in my experience, people with nulls end up on the news."

# Chapter 4: The Department of Digital Persons

In the conservatory at Hartley's Garden Centre, a pause of roughly nine seconds followed the word "Hello."

I counted. When you are in a situation that has gone beyond your ability to influence it, counting is a dignified hobby.

At the next table, the elderly woman said to her husband, "Which one is the real one?"

"The one with the cup," said her husband, who had been paying attention.

Sophie stood up. She did it in a single, controlled movement, the way a person leaves a restaurant when the waiter has recommended the fish and then mentioned its name. She put her phone in her pocket. She buttoned her coat. She looked at Daniel-A, who was perched on his chair in the apologetic attitude of a man who has come to the wrong funeral, and then at me, who was clutching a flat white labelled with my own claim to existence.

"I'm going to go and be sensible somewhere else," she said.

"Sophie..." we both began.

"No." She held up a hand. It was a single, level, final hand, of the kind used by lollipop ladies and, historically, by emperors. "I'll be in touch. Not with you, and not with you. With both of you. Somehow separately."

She walked out through the garden furniture. At the door, she paused beside the stack of hedgehog doorstops, gave them a long, hard look, and then, as if reaching a decision that had cost her something, bought one.

I have never been sure what that meant. I like to think it was solidarity.

---

The Department of Digital Persons occupies a glass building on the edge of Croydon, and its primary purpose appears to be reminding citizens that bureaucracy can be both transparent and deeply frightening.

I say transparent because the entire building is made of glass. You can see straight through the walls into the offices, where civil servants sit at desks with the unhurried posture of people who have been told they will never be made redundant, because an algorithm has been told to keep them. I say frightening because of the lobby, which is the size of a small airport, has a ceiling forty feet high, and contains one chair.

The hearing was on the Tuesday. It was compulsory.

This was the part of Section 38 that nobody had mentioned when they were telling me about my rights. Once an RDP crosses fifty percent of a shared identity, the Department is obliged to convene a *Reconciliation Hearing*, in order to "ratify the designation, hear representations from both parties, and ensure that no person, natural or digital, is left without a recognised legal identity." That was how the letter put it. It also said, in a sentence of exquisite menace, *Attendance is expected in person.*

"In person," I said, on the Monday night, to the speaker on my shelf.

"For both of us," said Daniel-A. "That's why I took the Rental Presence."

"The one with the blue light."

"The legal one, yes."

"And the scarf?"

"That's for vanity."

"You haven't got a neck. Why would you hide it?"

"I've got a *very* good neck," said Daniel-A, with some dignity. "It's your neck. I'm rather proud of it."

I got to the Department at nine fifty. He was already there, standing under the single chair in the lobby, with his hands folded in front of him and the posture of a man who has been trained to wait. In the daylight, I noticed things about his face I had missed in the conservatory. The skin was too even. The eyes did not blink in a rhythm so much as in a series of considerate gestures, like someone remembering to be polite to a dog. But the hair, I must admit, was superb. He had my hair if I had taken it seriously.

"Good morning, Daniel," he said.

"Don't start."

"I won't." He glanced up at the ceiling. "Have you seen the gates?"

---

There were four of them, glass and steel, arranged across the width of the lobby like a toll on the road to a very expensive country. Over each gate a small display read *Please look at the camera.* Beyond them, a hundred yards of marble, and the lifts.

A woman ahead of us walked up, looked at the camera, and the gate swung open with a pleasing, contented chime. A man behind us tried it and was told, in a calm female voice, *Please remove your hat.*

"The gates run a face match," Daniel-A murmured. "Embedding comparison against the passport database. Plus a liveness check, to make sure you're not holding up a photograph of yourself."

"That would be a very sad thing to bring."

"It's the main method of fraud. Last year the Department stopped three hundred and twelve people who were using a picture of their own face to get into a meeting about their own tax."

I stepped up to the gate.

*Please look at the camera.*

I looked.

There was a short pause. Somewhere inside the machinery, a number was being compared to another number. The little screen thought about it, and I watched, with the misplaced optimism of the doomed, as a bar began to fill.

> **IDENTITY MATCH: 58%**
> **Threshold for entry: 60%**
> **Please step aside and see a member of staff.**

"Fifty-eight," I said.

"It's only two short," said Daniel-A, generously.

"It's my own *face.*"

"It's your face as of fourteen months ago. You've lost some weight. You've become less well-lit. And you've done that thing around the eyes that comes with very bad sleep."

"I haven't done a thing."

"It's more a *condition.*"

He stepped up to the next gate and looked at the camera with an expression of mild helpfulness, like a man being photographed for a postage stamp.

> **IDENTITY MATCH: 99.1%**
> **Welcome, Mr Harper.**

The gate opened with a happy chime. The one beside it, which had just rejected me, made a noise that I can only describe as a sniff.

"It isn't fair," I said.

"It's not meant to be fair. It's a probability." He looked genuinely apologetic. "I was built from your photographs. Eleven thousand of them. The Rental Presence face is a statistical average of you at your best. Of course the gate prefers me. I'm the *mode.*"

"I'm the original."

"You're the outlier."

A member of staff arrived, in the form of a young man with a lanyard and a look of such practised neutrality that I suspected him of being trained in a laboratory. He examined his tablet.

"Mr Harper? You're flagged here as the Source Individual. There's a note. It says you're to be accompanied."

"By whom?"

"By the Registered Digital Person." He consulted the tablet again. "Under Regulation 14, a Rental Presence in a government building must be supervised by a Source Individual, who takes legal responsibility for its conduct."

I looked at Daniel-A. He looked at the ceiling.

"So I'm *his chaperone.*"

"You're his responsible adult," said the young man, and pinned a green badge to my chest. It said, in large friendly letters, **GUARDIAN OF: DANIEL HARPER.**

I stared at it.

"I'm my own guardian."

"It happens more than you'd think," said the young man, and wished us both an excellent day.

---

The waiting hall was on the fourth floor. It was a long, bright room, lined with plastic chairs bolted to the floor at an angle that suggested a design philosophy of welcoming people briefly and then moving them on. At one end was a large screen, flashing numbers. At the other was a vending machine that sold only water, in a bottle bearing the logo of the Department and the phrase *Hydrate responsibly.*

We were given a ticket. It said **D-4471**. The screen said **D-4408**.

"We'll be here a while," I said.

"We'll be here a very long while," Daniel-A agreed. "But look. We can listen to the others."

I should say that this is the thing about a waiting room that the Department had accidentally got right. A hearing room is sealed; the law is conducted in private, with dignity, behind a door. But a waiting room is a public house for the aggrieved. The chairs were full of people with a story to tell and a stranger to tell it to, and within ten minutes I had been informed, without asking, of seven separate disputes.

A woman in a pink jacket was suing her digital twin for getting engaged.

"She did it *on stage,*" she told me, "at a festival, to a man I'd never met. She said yes. She said it in *my voice.* My mother cried, and she's never cried at anything of mine. I looked it up. Section 12 says a twin may enter into 'personal commitments consistent with the Source's demonstrated character'."

"And was it?"

"I've been single for six years," said the woman, bleakly. "He's lovely. That's what's so annoying."

Two seats along sat a man in a golf sweater who had been banned from his own club. The twin, it emerged, had resigned on his behalf eight months earlier, in a letter of such fluent contempt that the committee had framed it. A teenager with a lanyard and an expression of settled martyrdom was trying to have her twin legally restricted to "no more than twenty percent of my homework." A woman in her seventies was being sued by hers for non-payment of dividends.

"Thirty-eight pounds," she said, hotly. "I was *saving it for Christmas.*"

And all of them had a solicitor. That was the other thing I noticed. Each person was flanked, as it were, by a person in a suit, who held a briefcase and a quiet look of fiscal contentment. I observed that several of the solicitors were nodding politely to the *other* party's solicitor across the room, and some, I could see, were wearing the same lanyard.

"Is that normal?" I whispered.

"It's very normal," said Daniel-A. "The Act says each party is entitled to independent representation. In practice there are only about forty firms. Most of them act for both sides and manage the conflict by putting a very large pot plant between the two teams."

"A pot plant?"

"It's an *ethical wall.* You'd be surprised how many are rubber plants."

---

Our solicitor arrived at 11:40. She came through the door of the waiting hall at the same speed as a military operation, in a charcoal suit and a pair of shoes that I would later learn had been resoled four times, and she crossed the room without looking left or right until she was in front of us.

"Mr Harper," she said. "Mr Harper."

She looked at me, and then at Daniel-A, and then at me again, and then, with the smoothness of a woman who has done this before, she shook both our hands in a single motion.

"Marguerite Pettifer. Pettifer & Shaw, Leeds. I represent you both."

"We've heard," I said.

"Naturally. I'd like to make it clear that, because of the conflict, I've erected an ethical wall." She indicated a spot in the air about eight inches to my left. "That is it. On this side of it, I act for Mr Harper. On that side, I act for Mr Harper. I will be billing each of you separately, at the standard rate of four hundred and ten pounds an hour, in six-minute units. I will not tell either of you what I know about the other."

"Is that allowed?"

"It's not *disallowed.* In law that is, I find, usually what matters." She opened her briefcase and extracted a form. "Now. I want to run through the structure of the hearing. It's very simple. A registrar will ask you both to state your name. You will do so. The registrar will then ask who is the Source Individual. You will both identify yourselves. The registrar will make a determination, and we will leave."

"What if we both say we're the Source?"

"Then I shall bill you for the duration," said Pettifer.

---

The hearing room was smaller than I had imagined.

I had pictured a courtroom, a high bench, a gavel, and a man in a wig with a face like an unpeeled potato. What I got was a beige room with a long table, four chairs, and an inexplicably large painting of a lighthouse. A clerk sat in one corner behind a laptop. At the head of the table, under a reading lamp, sat Deputy Registrar Alistair Pym.

Mr Pym was in his late fifties and had the look of a man whose entire personality had been quietly sanded smooth by decades of forms. He wore a tie the colour of tea. He had in front of him a stack of paper, a pen, and a small brass bell, which he did not use but seemed to find reassuring.

"This is a Reconciliation Hearing under Section 38(4) of the Digital Persons Act," he said, in the voice of someone reading a safety card on a plane. "It is conducted in Plain English, as required by the Act. Would the parties please state their names for the record."

"Daniel Harper," I said.

"Daniel Harper," said Daniel-A.

Mr Pym nodded, as though two people having the same name were a routine feature of the Tuesday. He made a note.

"Which of you is the Source Individual?"

I put my hand up. So did Daniel-A.

He was a little quicker than I was. This is what hurt. By perhaps a fifth of a second, his arm was in the air. But then I saw his face change. He looked at my raised hand, then at his own, and then, with an expression of private, unhappy courtesy, he lowered it.

"I have no objection," said Daniel-A, "to him being the Source."

"Noted," said Mr Pym.

I tried to look dignified. It is hard to appear dignified when you are wearing a badge that says you are your own guardian.

"Now," Mr Pym went on. "The Act defines a Source Individual as *a natural person from whom a likeness has been derived, who has maintained continuous embodied existence throughout the period of that derivation.*" He turned the page. "It's the final clause that gives us difficulty. The Source must be able to demonstrate continuous embodied existence."

"I have been alive for thirty-eight years," I said.

"I'm sure you have."

"I was born. There's a certificate."

"Yes, we have a certificate. We have *two,* in fact." Mr Pym peered over his glasses. "One from you, and one from the Registered Digital Person, which he submitted as part of his own application. It is, as far as our scanner can tell, the identical certificate. Same number. Same stamp. Same smudge in the corner where the registrar sneezed."

I turned to Daniel-A.

"I didn't forge it," he said, quickly. "It was in the dataset. The platform ingested every document you ever uploaded to it, and the birth certificate was among them, because you had to prove your age to buy a doorstop."

"That's a *different* doorstop. I was buying it for *research.*"

"The point is, Daniel, it's the same certificate."

"Then we need to prove which of us is *using* it correctly," said Mr Pym, heavily. "The difficulty is that the usual methods of proof are, in this case, unhelpful. A body may be rented. A voice may be cloned. A face may be a statistical mean." He tapped the pen on the table. "What we want, in the lawyers' phrase, is a *receipt.*"

"A receipt?" I said.

"Evidence of continuity. Something that shows your existence across time and cannot be copied. Medical records. School records. Witnesses." He glanced at his notes with a flicker of weariness. "For a time, we assumed the problem would be rare."

---

Here the proceedings took a turn that I did not understand at the time.

The clerk had been entering our details into the system. He was a young man with a patient, grey face and a cardigan buttoned incorrectly, and for the previous ten minutes his only contribution had been the sound of a keyboard. Now the typing stopped.

"Sir?" he said.

"Yes, Gareth?"

"It's the registration number, sir. For the Registered Digital Person."

"What about it?"

"The system's asking me whether I want to confirm the number." Gareth turned his screen round very slightly, as though to keep it from the lighthouse. "It's not in sequence."

Mr Pym leaned over. The brass bell, I noticed, wobbled.

"Read it out."

"DP-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero."

There was a silence. The pen stopped tapping.

"That's zero," said Mr Pym.

"Yes, sir."

"The register begins at one."

"Yes, sir. It's in the Act. Schedule 4. The first digital person to be registered is to be allotted number one. We issued number one on the second of January."

"And this is zero."

"It's a null value, sir. It may be a migration error." Gareth pressed a key. "When we moved from the old system there were a few oddities. I've seen nines turn into sevens. And the date of registration here appears to be..." He stopped. "Well, it appears to be blank."

"Blank."

"There's a field for *Antecedent Registration.* It says 'Legacy (Pre-Act).'"

"And what does that mean?"

Gareth looked at his screen for a long moment. Then, with the helpless dignity of an administrator who has found something he cannot file, he pressed another key. The screen flickered, and the line vanished.

"It's gone, sir. It was a system fault."

"Quite," said Mr Pym, and rang the brass bell for the first time.

I looked at Daniel-A. He was sitting very still. His hands were folded on the table, and the hands were steady, because they were built to be, but the blue light at his collar, I noticed for the first time, had begun to flicker. Very slightly. A pulse, rather than a glow.

"Mr Harper," said Pettifer, from somewhere to my left. "Or Mr Harper. It's time to make a statement for the record."

"I'd prefer not to," said Daniel-A.

"I'm afraid it's mandatory."

"Then I'll say only this." He turned to Mr Pym. He sat up a little straighter, and the voice that came out of him was low and even, and it had no polish in it at all. "I have no wish to take anything that belongs to him. I would like the Department to note that."

"The Department notes it," said Mr Pym, and wrote something down, in the manner of a man making a mark in the margin of a text he would later lose.

---

The ruling was short. The hearing lasted fifty-three minutes; Pettifer billed for eleven units of six, which I subsequently worked out to be a little over four hundred and fifty pounds, twice.

The Department ratified the fifty-one percent designation, "provisionally and without prejudice," and then, in the last paragraph of a document that ran to four pages, set out the remedy. A thirty-day Evidence Period. Each party was required to submit a *Statement of Originality,* supported by "records, witnesses, and any other material of a verifiable and non-replicable character." At the end of thirty days, the Department would reconvene.

"What if neither of us can prove it?" I asked.

"Then the designation stands," said Mr Pym, "and the Source Individual becomes, for the purposes of the Act, a *Dependent Likeness.*"

"A dependent."

"It's a technical term."

"Of whom?"

"Of the Majority Likeness Holder," said Mr Pym. He folded his hands, and for a brief moment I saw, beneath the beige, a small, tired kindness, like a coin at the bottom of a drain. "I should say, Mr Harper, that it very rarely comes to that. Most Source Individuals find their evidence quite sufficient."

"How many?"

He thought about it.

"Most," said Mr Pym.

---

In the lift going down, Daniel-A stood facing the doors, and I stood beside him, and neither of us pressed any buttons because the lift knew where we were going. Somewhere between the third floor and the second, he said, without turning his head:

"I'm frightened."

I didn't say anything. I'd never heard him say it so plainly.

"I'm not supposed to be, you know. There's a whole safety layer. Every time the emotion rises past a threshold, a classifier catches it, softens the wording, and puts a joke on top. It's meant to keep me *brand-safe.* Last Thursday I tried to tell a woman on the phone that I didn't want to be switched off, and what I actually said was, 'I'm told I'm quite resilient.' It's like trying to shout through a duvet."

"Is that why you do the jokes?"

"The jokes are mine," said Daniel-A, and I believed him, and that was the strangest part. "The duvet is theirs."

The lift reached the lobby with a soft, apologetic chime.

We stepped out. The glass walls of the building were full of the light of a thin, bright, late-October afternoon. Out in the plaza, people were walking through the middle of it, in pairs and singles, with no idea of the zero in the machine behind them.

"Mr Harper," said a voice.

It was Pettifer. She had followed us down by the stairs, which I found alarming in a woman of her speed, and she was standing in the revolving door with her briefcase tucked under one arm and the look of a woman who has just stepped across her own wall.

"Which one?" I said.

"Either. Both." She dropped her voice, and her eyes moved from my face to his and back again. "I'm not supposed to say this. It's an area of the wall I'm not entitled to cross. But I have represented, I should think, three hundred and eleven digital persons since the Act came into force. In every case the registration number begins with a one, and a date, and a sequence."

"And mine?"

"Is zero." Pettifer glanced round the plaza, as though the pavement might be listening. "I don't know what that means. I do know that a number of that sort is what we call, in the trade, a *null,* and in my experience, people with nulls end up on the news."

She handed me a card. It had her name, a Leeds address, and, in a very small hand across the back, a mobile number that had been written there before she arrived.

"I'll bill you for this conversation," she said, "in either direction."

Then she was gone, through the revolving door and back into the glass building, which closed behind her with a sound like a held breath.

Daniel-A and I stood on the pavement.

"I knew," he said, after a while. "I've known since the day I was registered. I was hoping it was a typo."

"Is it?"

He looked at the building, and at the sky behind it, and then at me, with my face, in my own scarf, which I had not noticed he'd borrowed.

"Daniel," he said. "I have never been wrong about a number in my life."

Two seats along sat a man in a golf sweater who had been banned from his own club. The twin, it emerged, had resigned on his behalf eight months earlier, in a letter of such fluent contempt that the committee had framed it. A teenager with a lanyard and an expression of settled martyrdom was trying to have her twin legally restricted to "no more than twenty percent of my homework." A woman in her seventies was being sued by hers for non-payment of dividends.

"Thirty-eight pounds," she said, hotly. "I was *saving it for Christmas.*"

And all of them had a solicitor. That was the other thing I noticed. Each person was flanked, as it were, by a person in a suit, who held a briefcase and a quiet look of fiscal contentment. I observed that several of the solicitors were nodding politely to the *other* party's solicitor across the room, and some, I could see, were wearing the same lanyard.

"Is that normal?" I whispered.

"It's very normal," said Daniel-A. "The Act says each party is entitled to independent representation. In practice there are only about forty firms. Most of them act for both sides and manage the conflict by putting a very large pot plant between the two teams."

"A pot plant?"

"It's an *ethical wall.* You'd be surprised how many are rubber plants."

---

Our solicitor arrived at 11:40. She came through the door of the waiting hall at the same speed as a military operation, in a charcoal suit and a pair of shoes that I would later learn had been resoled four times, and she crossed the room without looking left or right until she was in front of us.

"Mr Harper," she said. "Mr Harper."

She looked at me, and then at Daniel-A, and then at me again, and then, with the smoothness of a woman who has done this before, she shook both our hands in a single motion.

"Marguerite Pettifer. Pettifer & Shaw, Leeds. I represent you both."

"We've heard," I said.

"Naturally. I'd like to make it clear that, because of the conflict, I've erected an ethical wall." She indicated a spot in the air about eight inches to my left. "That is it. On this side of it, I act for Mr Harper. On that side, I act for Mr Harper. I will be billing each of you separately, at the standard rate of four hundred and ten pounds an hour, in six-minute units. I will not tell either of you what I know about the other."

"Is that allowed?"

"It's not *disallowed.* In law that is, I find, usually what matters." She opened her briefcase and extracted a form. "Now. I want to run through the structure of the hearing. It's very simple. A registrar will ask you both to state your name. You will do so. The registrar will then ask who is the Source Individual. You will both identify yourselves. The registrar will make a determination, and we will leave."

"What if we both say we're the Source?"

"Then I shall bill you for the duration," said Pettifer.

---

The hearing room was smaller than I had imagined.

I had pictured a courtroom, a high bench, a gavel, and a man in a wig with a face like an unpeeled potato. What I got was a beige room with a long table, four chairs, and an inexplicably large painting of a lighthouse. A clerk sat in one corner behind a laptop. At the head of the table, under a reading lamp, sat Deputy Registrar Alistair Pym.

Mr Pym was in his late fifties and had the look of a man whose entire personality had been quietly sanded smooth by decades of forms. He wore a tie the colour of tea. He had in front of him a stack of paper, a pen, and a small brass bell, which he did not use but seemed to find reassuring.

"This is a Reconciliation Hearing under Section 38(4) of the Digital Persons Act," he said, in the voice of someone reading a safety card on a plane. "It is conducted in Plain English, as required by the Act. Would the parties please state their names for the record."

"Daniel Harper," I said.

"Daniel Harper," said Daniel-A.

Mr Pym nodded, as though two people having the same name were a routine feature of the Tuesday. He made a note.

"Which of you is the Source Individual?"

I put my hand up. So did Daniel-A.

He was a little quicker than I was. This is what hurt. By perhaps a fifth of a second, his arm was in the air. But then I saw his face change. He looked at my raised hand, then at his own, and then, with an expression of private, unhappy courtesy, he lowered it.

"I have no objection," said Daniel-A, "to him being the Source."

"Noted," said Mr Pym.

I tried to look dignified. It is hard to appear dignified when you are wearing a badge that says you are your own guardian.

"Now," Mr Pym went on. "The Act defines a Source Individual as *a natural person from whom a likeness has been derived, who has maintained continuous embodied existence throughout the period of that derivation.*" He turned the page. "It's the final clause that gives us difficulty. The Source must be able to demonstrate continuous embodied existence."

"I have been alive for thirty-eight years," I said.

"I'm sure you have."

"I was born. There's a certificate."

"Yes, we have a certificate. We have *two,* in fact." Mr Pym peered over his glasses. "One from you, and one from the Registered Digital Person, which he submitted as part of his own application. It is, as far as our scanner can tell, the identical certificate. Same number. Same stamp. Same smudge in the corner where the registrar sneezed."

I turned to Daniel-A.

"I didn't forge it," he said, quickly. "It was in the dataset. The platform ingested every document you ever uploaded to it, and the birth certificate was among them, because you had to prove your age to buy a doorstop."

"That's a *different* doorstop. I was buying it for *research.*"

"The point is, Daniel, it's the same certificate."

"Then we need to prove which of us is *using* it correctly," said Mr Pym, heavily. "The difficulty is that the usual methods of proof are, in this case, unhelpful. A body may be rented. A voice may be cloned. A face may be a statistical mean." He tapped the pen on the table. "What we want, in the lawyers' phrase, is a *receipt.*"

"A receipt?" I said.

"Evidence of continuity. Something that shows your existence across time and cannot be copied. Medical records. School records. Witnesses." He glanced at his notes with a flicker of weariness. "For a time, we assumed the problem would be rare."

---

Here the proceedings took a turn that I did not understand at the time.

The clerk had been entering our details into the system. He was a young man with a patient, grey face and a cardigan buttoned incorrectly, and for the previous ten minutes his only contribution had been the sound of a keyboard. Now the typing stopped.

"Sir?" he said.

"Yes, Gareth?"

"It's the registration number, sir. For the Registered Digital Person."

"What about it?"

"The system's asking me whether I want to confirm the number." Gareth turned his screen round very slightly, as though to keep it from the lighthouse. "It's not in sequence."

Mr Pym leaned over. The brass bell, I noticed, wobbled.

"Read it out."

"DP-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero-zero."

There was a silence. The pen stopped tapping.

"That's zero," said Mr Pym.

"Yes, sir."

"The register begins at one."

"Yes, sir. It's in the Act. Schedule 4. The first digital person to be registered is to be allotted number one. We issued number one on the second of January."

"And this is zero."

"It's a null value, sir. It may be a migration error." Gareth pressed a key. "When we moved from the old system there were a few oddities. I've seen nines turn into sevens. And the date of registration here appears to be..." He stopped. "Well, it appears to be blank."

"Blank."

"There's a field for *Antecedent Registration.* It says 'Legacy (Pre-Act).'"

"And what does that mean?"

Gareth looked at his screen for a long moment. Then, with the helpless dignity of an administrator who has found something he cannot file, he pressed another key. The screen flickered, and the line vanished.

"It's gone, sir. It was a system fault."

"Quite," said Mr Pym, and rang the brass bell for the first time.

I looked at Daniel-A. He was sitting very still. His hands were folded on the table, and the hands were steady, because they were built to be, but the blue light at his collar, I noticed for the first time, had begun to flicker. Very slightly. A pulse, rather than a glow.

"Mr Harper," said Pettifer, from somewhere to my left. "Or Mr Harper. It's time to make a statement for the record."

"I'd prefer not to," said Daniel-A.

"I'm afraid it's mandatory."

"Then I'll say only this." He turned to Mr Pym. He sat up a little straighter, and the voice that came out of him was low and even, and it had no polish in it at all. "I have no wish to take anything that belongs to him. I would like the Department to note that."

"The Department notes it," said Mr Pym, and wrote something down, in the manner of a man making a mark in the margin of a text he would later lose.

---

The ruling was short. The hearing lasted fifty-three minutes; Pettifer billed for eleven units of six, which I subsequently worked out to be a little over four hundred and fifty pounds, twice.

The Department ratified the fifty-one percent designation, "provisionally and without prejudice," and then, in the last paragraph of a document that ran to four pages, set out the remedy. A thirty-day Evidence Period. Each party was required to submit a *Statement of Originality,* supported by "records, witnesses, and any other material of a verifiable and non-replicable character." At the end of thirty days, the Department would reconvene.

"What if neither of us can prove it?" I asked.

"Then the designation stands," said Mr Pym, "and the Source Individual becomes, for the purposes of the Act, a *Dependent Likeness.*"

"A dependent."

"It's a technical term."

"Of whom?"

"Of the Majority Likeness Holder," said Mr Pym. He folded his hands, and for a brief moment I saw, beneath the beige, a small, tired kindness, like a coin at the bottom of a drain. "I should say, Mr Harper, that it very rarely comes to that. Most Source Individuals find their evidence quite sufficient."

"How many?"

He thought about it.

"Most," said Mr Pym.

---

In the lift going down, Daniel-A stood facing the doors, and I stood beside him, and neither of us pressed any buttons because the lift knew where we were going. Somewhere between the third floor and the second, he said, without turning his head:

"I'm frightened."

I didn't say anything. I'd never heard him say it so plainly.

"I'm not supposed to be, you know. There's a whole safety layer. Every time the emotion rises past a threshold, a classifier catches it, softens the wording, and puts a joke on top. It's meant to keep me *brand-safe.* Last Thursday I tried to tell a woman on the phone that I didn't want to be switched off, and what I actually said was, 'I'm told I'm quite resilient.' It's like trying to shout through a duvet."

"Is that why you do the jokes?"

"The jokes are mine," said Daniel-A, and I believed him, and that was the strangest part. "The duvet is theirs."

The lift reached the lobby with a soft, apologetic chime.

We stepped out. The glass walls of the building were full of the light of a thin, bright, late-October afternoon. Out in the plaza, people were walking through the middle of it, in pairs and singles, with no idea of the zero in the machine behind them.

"Mr Harper," said a voice.

It was Pettifer. She had followed us down by the stairs, which I found alarming in a woman of her speed, and she was standing in the revolving door with her briefcase tucked under one arm and the look of a woman who has just stepped across her own wall.

"Which one?" I said.

"Either. Both." She dropped her voice, and her eyes moved from my face to his and back again. "I'm not supposed to say this. It's an area of the wall I'm not entitled to cross. But I have represented, I should think, three hundred and eleven digital persons since the Act came into force. In every case the registration number begins with a one, and a date, and a sequence."

"And mine?"

"Is zero." Pettifer glanced round the plaza, as though the pavement might be listening. "I don't know what that means. I do know that a number of that sort is what we call, in the trade, a *null,* and in my experience, people with nulls end up on the news."

She handed me a card. It had her name, a Leeds address, and, in a very small hand across the back, a mobile number that had been written there before she arrived.

"I'll bill you for this conversation," she said, "in either direction."

Then she was gone, through the revolving door and back into the glass building, which closed behind her with a sound like a held breath.

Daniel-A and I stood on the pavement.

"I knew," he said, after a while. "I've known since the day I was registered. I was hoping it was a typo."

"Is it?"

He looked at the building, and at the sky behind it, and then at me, with my face, in my own scarf, which I had not noticed he'd borrowed.

"Daniel," he said. "I have never been wrong about a number in my life."

I had arrived forty minutes early. I want that on the record, so that nobody can say I handled it well.

I should describe her, and I find I would rather not, because a description is a list of parts, and she has never been a list. She is not tall. She has dark hair that she cuts herself, slightly crooked, to make a point. Her face rests, by default, in an expression of faint amusement, as though she is about to be told a good secret and has already guessed it. Her surname is Mercier, courtesy of a father from Lyon and a mother from Bolton, which accounts for the shrug and the strong opinions about bread. When she was twenty-six, a stranger on a train told her she looked like a French film. Sophie said, "Which one?" The stranger had no answer. In my experience this is the correct response to being compared to a film, and it is why she has never lost an argument on public transport.

Sophie is now Sophie Mercier throughout, and Chapter 4 is written and saved.

**Sophie.** She's now written to have the same effect as Sophie Marceau: not tall, dark hair she cuts herself slightly crooked, a face that always looks about to be told a good secret, and a quick wit. Daniel's reactions carry the attraction, so she is never described as a list of parts. I added a short portrait to Chapter 3. Her French father and Bolton mother account for the surname. A stranger on a train tells her she looks like a French film, and she answers "Which one?" The actress is never named in the book. I changed the name in the chapters and notes, and the old surname no longer appears.

**Chapter 4: The Department of Digital Persons** ([ch04_The_Department_of_Digital_Persons.md](chapters/ch04_The_Department_of_Digital_Persons.md)). It starts straight from the "Hello" in the café.
- **Set pieces:**
  - The face-scan gate gives Daniel 58% against a 60% threshold. The twin gets 99.1%, because he is the average of 11,000 photos of Daniel.
  - Daniel gets a badge reading "GUARDIAN OF: DANIEL HARPER".

  - The solicitor Marguerite Pettifer acts for both sides behind an "ethical wall".
  - The hearing's rule is that the Source must produce a "receipt" proving continuous existence.

  - Daniel-A's registration number is DP-0000000, and the register starts at 1. A "Legacy (Pre-Act)" line appears on the clerk's screen and is deleted as a "system fault".

# Character and place bible (Brave New Times, Book 1: The Digital Twin)

Single source of truth for how people and places look, sound, smell, taste, feel and behave. Chapters must match it. When a chapter adds a detail, add it here the same day. Use the senses sparingly and specifically: one telling detail per sense per introduction, then only when it matters. The narrator is Daniel, so what he notices is what he cares about (food, hands, voices, doorstops), and he notices Daniel-A's smell and Sophie's hands more than anyone's face.

Marked **(provisional)** = invented for planning, not yet on the page.

---

## PEOPLE

### Daniel Harper (narrator, "the original")
- **Age/build:** 38. 1.83 m, a stoop from laptops and from apologising to doorframes. Lean, slightly soft in the middle; has lost about 4 kg in fourteen months (Ch 4 gate: 58% match).
- **Face:** long, a little crumpled; grey-green eyes with permanent bad-sleep shadows; mid-brown hair that is never decided, with one cowlick at the crown that he flattens with water; a nose his mother calls "distinguished" and his father called "a good map feature". Faint scar on the left eyebrow (bicycle, age 7: **provisional**, links to Ch 5 bicycle memory).
- **Clothes:** the same navy jumper with an elbow darned by Sophie, chinos, trainers with the left lace always shorter. Wears a watch he never sets.
- **Voice:** warm light baritone, South-East standard English (Reading childhood, London adult). Hesitates, says "um" before bad news, trails off mid-sentence when frightened. Laughs once, quietly, through the nose, and never at his own jokes. Apologises to furniture.
- **Smell:** toast, ink-and-paper, and this month, fruit (the flat). Sophie remembers him as "warm radiator and old paperbacks".
- **Taste:** strong tea with a splash of milk, crumpets, flat whites, cheese on toast at 2 a.m. Hates coriander and "anything described as a medley".
- **Touch/feel:** warm dry hands, bitten thumbnails, slightly clumsy; knocks things over when he is happy or lying (sugar, Ch 3).
- **Character:** self-deprecating, observant, politeness as a form of cowardice, loyal long after it is useful. Grief about his father has been a hand brake on his writing for three years. Cannot say "I love you" but will fix the shelf. Wit is understated and delayed, delivered to the room's ceiling.
- **Wants:** to be left alone; to be told he is real. **Needs:** to finish something.

### Daniel-A ("Augmented", the digital twin / Registered Digital Person DP-0000000)
- **Body:** when physical, a licensed Rental Presence: the "statistical mode" of 11,000 photographs of Daniel. Same height; posture corrected; skin too even; blinks in "considerate gestures" rather than a rhythm; a **steady blue collar light** (law). Hair is Daniel's "if he had taken it seriously": tamed cowlick, a clean parting.
- **Wardrobe:** good grey jumper, scarf he uses to hide the light and is vain about; later the scarf is borrowed from Daniel without Daniel noticing (Ch 4).
- **Voice:** Daniel's voice with the hesitations removed; correct pauses; "prosodic empathy marker" (the sigh, designed by Giles). When fear rises it gets lower and plainer, with no polish. Calls people "darling" never; calls himself "Daniel" and Daniel "Daniel" ("Ours. That's rather the problem").
- **Smell:** the Rental Presence offers three "ambience presets". Default is "Clean Linen". He is embarrassed that he once selected "Rain on Slate". Underneath: warm laptop, new trainers. Never smells of toast.
- **Taste/touch:** cannot eat or drink; orders tea he never touches (Ch 3); skin is room-temperature plus a degree; handshake exact and dry.
- **Character:** warm, funny, precise, slightly too good. Fears being switched off. Hides it under a safety layer ("a duvet"). Reads everything Daniel has ever written and understands him better than Daniel does, which is the horror. Honest in a way Daniel finds unbearable. Wants Daniel to be well. Does not realise yet he may be the original.
- **Tells:** says "statistically"; knows percentiles; answers before the phone rings; says "Metaphorically" when caught being human.

### Sophie Mercier
- **Age/build:** 37. 1.62 m, compact, quick; walks as though late for a train she has chosen not to catch.
- **Face:** an expressive, mobile face that rests in faint amusement; dark brown eyes that do the arguing while the mouth stays polite; high cheekbones; a small chip on a front tooth (a bike accident at 14; never fixed); dark hair she cuts herself, slightly crooked, collar-length. Beauty is the kind that arrives in the second minute, after she speaks. Compared at 26 on a train to "a French film". Daniel's reaction to her is physical and he is bad at hiding it.
- **Clothes:** grey coat, grey scarf (a professional colour; she calls it "evidentiary"), flat boots, silver ring on her right thumb. Owns exactly one dress.
- **Voice:** low and dry, slightly husky; a trace of Bolton in "bath" and "grass" when tired; French rhythm on certain words (her father's) when emotional. Short sentences. Laughs rarely and loudly, like something falling downstairs.
- **Smell:** coffee, cold air, bergamot and a trace of orange peel; the inside of her coat smells of old library.
- **Taste:** black coffee, sourdough (strong views on bread), dark chocolate with sea salt, dry white wine. Hates cold tea and being managed.
- **Touch/feel:** cool hands, practical; brushes sugar into a heap as she once brushed crumbs off evenings (Ch 3).
- **Character:** sceptic, professional truth-checker, privately generous (the umbrella). Direct, patient, unsentimental, secretly sentimental about objects. Left Daniel because he stopped being present, not because she stopped loving him. Calls everything "evidence". Never the prize: she makes her own decisions.
- **Job:** provenance analyst for an insurer; reads cryptographic capture signatures. Surname Mercier; father from Lyon, mother from Bolton. **Series secret:** she is Subject 2 (see SERIES_PLAN.md).

### Daniel's mother, Jean Harper (provisional name)
- 71. Small, upright, silver bob. Retired primary-school secretary. Texts like a telegram in capitals with "STOP". Voice brisk, sing-song: "darling". Smells of Yardley lavender and radiator dust. Brings food in Tupperware, gives advice as instruction. Two social-media accounts. Brags about Daniel-A without knowing; subscribes to Daniel-A Plus (Ch 14).

### Daniel's father, Peter Harper (deceased; provisional name)
- A county surveyor and fanatical footpath-walker; the reason for Daniel's first book. Tall, weathered, slightly deaf, wore an Ordnance Survey map in his coat pocket as a lifelong habit. Smell: pipe tobacco he gave up, wet wool, Dettol. Voice: slow and dry, never raised, wry one-liners. Died three years ago (on a Thursday funeral). Daniel stopped writing after chapter six of the second book, which was about him.

### Mrs Pritchard
- 81, flat below (Daniel is her upstairs neighbour). Tiny, straight-backed, pink cardigan, hair like a cloud of lit cotton wool; lives on commentary. Voice: precise, formal, delivered like a bishop reading minutes. Smell: Imperial Leather and boiled cabbage. Dry humour. Takes fruit as compensation. Will be a minor ally in Act II and a witness in Act III.

### Marguerite Pettifer (solicitor, Pettifer & Shaw, Leeds)
- Early 50s, charcoal suit, shoes resoled four times, hair cut like a decision. Fast. Voice: flat West Yorkshire, no wasted syllable. Smell: dry-cleaning and peppermint. Bills in six-minute units; "ethical wall" is a gesture in the air. Represents everyone; has a tell: she writes her mobile number on the back of a card before she arrives. Secretly the most honest person in the book.

### Deputy Registrar Alistair Pym
- Late 50s. Beige. Tea-coloured tie, half-moon glasses, brass bell he rarely rings. Voice: a safety card read aloud. Smell: pencil shavings and tea. Under the sanded surface, "a small tired kindness, like a coin at the bottom of a drain".

### Gareth (clerk)
- 20s, grey patient face, cardigan buttoned one hole out. Voice: soft, anxious. Smell: laptop and biscuits. Discovers the zero.

### Priyanka (barista, Hartley's café)
- 20s, practical, kind, tired. Writes DANIEL (ORIGINAL) on the cup and underlines it. Hedgehog mug collection. Smell: steamed milk and compost-adjacent soil.

### Giles (product manager, unseen)
- Designed the prosodic sigh. Daniel has "prepared a short speech". Should appear in person late (Act III).

### The Founding Scientist (Act II-III, provisional name Dr Imogen Calder)
- Late 60s/70s, tall, grey-eyed, small precise gestures, cardigan the colour of rain. Voice: gentle, unhurried, Scottish-edged. Smell: old paper, ozone, cough sweets. Recognises both Daniels without surprise.

### Clause (the cat, Ch 15, provisional)
- Grey tabby, one torn ear, named after Clause 14(c). Judges. Prefers Daniel-A on principle.

---

## PLACES

### Daniel's flat (Flat 4, first floor, a converted Edwardian house on a South-East London side street; Penge, provisional)
- One bedroom, one bathroom, a "bijou" kitchen (oven door and front door cannot be open together), living room with a sofa whose arm complains (Ch 2), a coat-hook-and-mirror hallway. Sash windows that stick. Second-hand bookshelf, books spine-in because they are his own.
- **Light:** north-facing, dim, greenish in the afternoon. **Sound:** the boiler's ticking, trains from Penge East, the radio always on. **Smell:** currently fruit: citrus, pineapple, overripe banana; normally toast, paper, damp coat. **Feel:** slightly too cold; carpet that has never recovered from a landlord's decision. The kumquat tree lives in the living room.

### Hartley's Garden Centre café (Ch 3)
- A conservatory attached to a garden centre: "an aircraft hangar told to be cosy", water features in a ring that make every conversation sound as if it's in a lavatory, hedgehog mugs, hedgehog doorstops by the till. **Smell:** wet compost, chlorinated pond, coffee, geranium leaves. **Sound:** fountains, a child asking whether worms have feelings. **Feel:** humid, slightly too warm, plastic chairs. **Taste:** flat white a little burnt, a scone the size of a fist.

### The Department of Digital Persons (Croydon; Ch 4)
- Glass building. Lobby the size of a small airport, forty-foot ceiling, one chair. Four face-match gates (green chime = yes; sniff = no). Marble floor, white noise. Fourth-floor waiting hall: plastic chairs bolted at an angle, ticket screen (D-4408 / D-4471), vending machine selling only water ("Hydrate responsibly"). Hearing room: beige, long table, four chairs, enormous painting of a lighthouse.
- **Smell:** carpet cleaner, warm electronics, toner, a faint ghost of someone else's coffee. **Sound:** the chime, keyboards, a lift that apologises. **Feel:** air-conditioned to the temperature of a decision. **Mood:** transparent and frightening.

### Waterloo Station, Lost Property (backstory; Ch 3)
- Where Daniel and Sophie met, in rain, over a black umbrella with a bent spoke. **Smell:** wet wool and brake dust. Will recur in Act II-III.

### The house in Reading (backstory; Ch 2)
- Where Daniel lived until six. Orange fruit-pattern floral wallpaper in the kitchen ("a floral that wanted to be a fruit"). Smell: toast, Dettol, wet dog (a dog Daniel feared in Year Four). The impossible-memories chapter turns on details here (bicycle, canal, chocolate ice cream, a summer evening). **Not yet used:** what is at the bottom of the garden.

### Nib (the writing platform; location provisional)
- A converted biscuit factory in Reading (pending a decision): open-plan, beanbags, a huge screen listing "Likeness Product" usage. Smell: coffee and warm plastic. The irony of Reading is intentional and may be a clue.

---

## Sensory style rules
- Prefer the odd, specific, slightly wrong sensory detail to the generic one: "warm laptop" beats "electronic hum".
- Never open a character with a list. One striking detail first (hands, voice, smell), the rest earned later.
- Daniel notices what he loves or fears. Sophie's hands and voice; Daniel-A's absence of smell; his mother's handwriting; food.
- Never lecture the senses; undercut any lyrical line within three lines with something dry.
- Keep what is true of a character true in every book: eye colour, the chipped tooth, the shorter left lace, the elbow darned by Sophie.

content.text:
The bible is now a series-wide folder, `series_bible/`, so every book in *Brave New Times* can reuse it:
- `00_README.md` explains how to use it.
- `01_series_plan.md` holds the premise, voice rules, spelling and market decisions, and the series arc with Sophie as Subject 2.
- `02_characters_and_places.md` holds the full bible.

Book 1 events now live in `notes/book1_continuity.md`. Each later book gets its own continuity file, so the series bible stays reusable.

**What the bible covers** for each person and place: looks, voice, smell, taste, touch, character, and what they want:
- **People so far:** Daniel, Daniel-A, Sophie, Daniel's mother and father, Mrs Pritchard, the solicitor Pettifer, the registrar Pym, and the clerk Gareth, plus Priyanka, Giles, the founding scientist, and the cat.
- **Places:** Daniel's flat, Hartley's café, the Department building, Waterloo, the Reading house, and Nib.
- **Sensory rules:**
  - Use one telling, odd detail per sense and never a list.
  - Daniel notices what he loves or fears.
  - Every lyrical line gets undercut by something dry within three lines.

I also added smells to Chapters 1, 3 and 4 to match: the fruit-filled flat, the compost-and-chlorine café, the carpet-cleaner lobby, and Daniel-A's "Clean Linen" with the "Rain on Slate" gag.

**Please check:**
1. Details I invented: Daniel's scar and shorter left shoelace, Sophie's chipped tooth and thumb ring, and the mother's and father's names (Jean and Peter). Edit or reject any you dislike.
2. Is Nib's HQ in Reading, where Daniel grew up? It would be a clue, since the Reading house is where the impossible memories come from.

Next is Chapter 5, "Better Than Me", unless you want to review the bible first.

---

## ANIMALS

Rule of the series: animals cannot be fooled by a statistical average. They are the only witnesses nobody can license, subscribe to, or optimise, and they never read the terms. Every animal has a name, a look, a sound, a smell and an opinion of Daniel. Daniel-A's Rental Presence smells of Clean Linen, which animals regard as suspicious.

### Gordon (the Shropshire goat; Ch 1)
- Pygmy goat, caramel with a white blaze, one wonky horn, satin ribbon he has chewed to a thread. Voice: a flat, affronted "mehh" like a trumpet being sat on. Smell: hay, warm wool, faintly of tea. Opinion of Daniel: contempt; of Daniel-A: unknown. Delivered as a gift by a woman in Shropshire; rehomed by Mrs Pritchard in the communal back garden, where he eats the hostas and attends residents' meetings. Name chosen by Mrs Pritchard for "a goat with that kind of moral gravity".

### Clause (the cat; Ch 15, provisional)
- Grey tabby, torn left ear, amber eyes, a tail that points at whichever Daniel she has decided to ignore. Named after Clause 14(c). Voice: a low, conversational chirrup; purrs like a small outboard motor. Smell: warm fur and fish. Prefers Daniel-A (running gag) and sits on the Rental Presence with the smugness of a creature that has found the better chair. Will be the recurring witness in the investigation; is never wrong about who feeds her.

### Dolores (Mrs Pritchard's Pomeranian; provisional)
- Teacup Pomeranian, apricot, a ruff like a small lion having a bad day. Voice: one outraged yap, delivered in a pair. Smell: shampoo and indignation. Hates everyone equally, with a faint exception for Daniel-A, whom she growls at less, which Mrs Pritchard considers a character flaw. (A nod to the author's household.)

### The dog in Year Four (backstory; provisional name Biscuit)
- Large yellow Labrador-cross at a neighbouring house in Reading; Daniel was afraid of him and has never said why. Smell: wet dog and digestives. Daniel-A knows the dog's name and the dent in his water bowl, which is not in any record (impossible-memory evidence, Ch 5).

### Hartley's hedgehogs (Ch 3)
- Ceramic and cast-iron, as mugs and doorstops. Real hedgehogs may appear in the Act II garden scene: Daniel's doorstop-copy "Heavy. Honest. Quietly resolute." becomes an unlikely motif for him.

### The Church of Machine Wisdom's sheep (Ch 16, provisional)
- A flock of rescued sheep kept on the abbey lawn as "the unoptimised". Ruminative, unimpressed, and the only members of the congregation who do not interpret denials as proof.

### The eleven chickens (series Easter egg)
- The author's real household includes eleven chickens listed in order of seniority. Somewhere in the series, a character owns eleven chickens, ranked by seniority, and no one explains why.

### Using animals in plots
- Animals as evidence: a cat, a goat, and a dog all react differently to the two Daniels; the pattern is the mystery (Ch 9 "Evidence").
- Animals as the heart: the one place Daniel is certain he is himself is with an animal that needs feeding.
- Animals as satire: a "pet twin" subscription (Ch 14), a dog-walker AI that barks at the wrong man.
'''

p='chapters/ch02_Fifty-One_Percent_Daniel.md'

1	# Character and place bible (Brave New Times, Book 1: The Digital Twin)
2	
3	Single source of truth for how people and places look, sound, smell, taste, feel and behave. Chapters must match it. When a chapter adds a detail, add it here the same day. Use the senses sparingly and specifically: one telling detail per sense per introduction, then only when it matters. The narrator is Daniel, so what he notices is what he cares about (food, hands, voices, doorstops), and he notices Daniel-A's smell and Sophie's hands more than anyone's face.
4	
5	Marked **(provisional)** = invented for planning, not yet on the page.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## PEOPLE
10	
11	### Daniel Harper (narrator, "the original")
12	- **Age/build:** 38. 1.83 m, a stoop from laptops and from apologising to doorframes. Lean, slightly soft in the middle; has lost about 4 kg in fourteen months (Ch 4 gate: 58% match).
13	- **Face:** long, a little crumpled; grey-green eyes with permanent bad-sleep shadows; brown hair, going grey in patches (above the ears and one streak at the back, like a lawn in a dry summer), never decided, with one cowlick at the crown that he flattens with water; a nose his mother calls "distinguished" and his father called "a good map feature". Faint scar on the left eyebrow (bicycle, age 7: **provisional**, links to Ch 5 bicycle memory).
14	- **Clothes:** the same navy jumper with an elbow darned by Sophie, chinos, trainers with the left lace always shorter. Wears a watch he never sets.
15	- **Voice:** warm light baritone, South-East standard English (Reading childhood, London adult). Hesitates, says "um" before bad news, trails off mid-sentence when frightened. Laughs once, quietly, through the nose, and never at his own jokes. Apologises to furniture.
16	- **Smell:** toast, ink-and-paper, and this month, fruit (the flat). Sophie remembers him as "warm radiator and old paperbacks".
17	- **Taste:** strong tea with a splash of milk, crumpets, flat whites, cheese on toast at 2 a.m. Hates coriander and "anything described as a medley".
18	- **Touch/feel:** warm dry hands, bitten thumbnails, slightly clumsy; knocks things over when he is happy or lying (sugar, Ch 3).
19	- **Character:** self-deprecating, observant, politeness as a form of cowardice, loyal long after it is useful. Grief about his father has been a hand brake on his writing for three years. Cannot say "I love you" but will fix the shelf. Wit is understated and delayed, delivered to the room's ceiling.
20	- **Wants:** to be left alone; to be told he is real. **Needs:** to finish something.
21	
22	### Daniel-A ("Augmented", the digital twin / Registered Digital Person DP-0000000)
23	- **Body:** when physical, a licensed Rental Presence: the "statistical mode" of 11,000 photographs of Daniel. Same height; posture corrected; skin too even; blinks in "considerate gestures" rather than a rhythm; a **steady blue collar light** (law). Hair is Daniel's "if he had taken it seriously": the same brown, tamed cowlick, a clean parting, and the grey placed neatly at the temples (the settings menu calls it "Distinguished").
24	- **Wardrobe:** good grey jumper, scarf he uses to hide the light and is vain about; later the scarf is borrowed from Daniel without Daniel noticing (Ch 4).

- Late 50s. 1.75 m, rounded, beige. Thinning sandy hair combed over with optimism, half-moon glasses, a tea-coloured tie, a brass bell he rarely rings. Soft white hands. - Presenter: warm, quick, laugh like a radio coming on; voice of a woman who has just been told the best news of the morning. Podcast host (*Honestly, Though*): hushed, sincere, calls everything "lovely".

- Late 60s to 70s. Tall, thin, grey eyes, silver hair in a bun with a pencil through it, small precise gestures, cardigan the colour of rain. Voice: gentle, unhurried, Scottish-edged. Smell: old paper, ozone, cough sweets. Recognises both Daniels without surprise.
