# Chapter 7: An Argument About Memory

Sophie arrived at eleven o'clock on the Sunday carrying a flask, a box of index cards, and the expression of a woman about to cross-examine a tree.

"You've got a kumquat," she said.

"It's a gift."

"From whom?"

"From the whole household of Number 14. I'm told I reminded them to be kind to themselves."

"You'd have to have been very persuasive."

"I wasn't. I was a pineapple's second cousin by marriage."

She stood in the living room with her coat still on, looking at what remained of the fruit. The pears were now a legal matter. The tree had been moved to the window, where it enjoyed the light and the status of a minor celebrity. Mrs Pritchard had taken the pineapple, the goat had taken the hostas, and the only visible survivors of the original forty-three kilograms were a bowl of satsumas and a single, defiant melon, which sat on the bookshelf with the look of a man who has missed his stop.

"Well," said Sophie, unscrewing her flask. "It smells like a market in here."

"Thank you."

"I don't think I meant it kindly."

She took the armchair. It was a decision. The sofa was the obvious place for a guest, and I had spent twenty minutes plumping it into a state of cautious hospitality, but Sophie sat in the armchair, which put the width of the room between us and me on the arm of the sofa, trying to look like a man who had meant to.

She set her phone on the coffee table. The little green circle glowed.

**SIGNED CAPTURE IN PROGRESS.**

"We should begin," she said.

"Good morning, Sophie," said the speaker on the shelf.

"Good morning." She did not look at it. "I'm going to ask you both some questions about our six years. I'll hold the answers. I'll mark them. I will not give you any hints. If either of you argues with the marking, I will go home."

"And if we both argue?" I said.

"Then I'll go home sooner."

---

I should explain how Sophie's mind works, since it is the reason for the cards.

When I first met her, she told me that the thing she hated most in the world was a confident witness. A confident witness, she said, is a person who has told the story so often that the story has taken over. The insurance claimants who tell her about the burglary in perfect order, every detail in its place, are the ones who staged it. Real memory is a mess. It is a patchwork stitched together every time you reach for it, and every time you stitch it, the seams move. A genuine account has gaps and hesitations and one detail that is simply, inexplicably wrong. She calls it the smudge.

"A forgery is clean," she said once, over a bowl of noodles. "That's how I know. The genuine article always has a smudge on it."

At the time, I thought it was a charming theory. I did not yet understand that I would one day be sitting on the arm of a sofa waiting to be tested for smudges.

"Question one," said Sophie, picking up a card. "What was the address of our first flat?"

I took a breath. "Forty-something, Lowther Road. Walthamstow. It had a green door."

"It had a blue door," said Daniel-A, kindly. "Flat 2, 47 Lowther Road, Walthamstow. Blue door, brass number, a slight smell of damp in the stairwell that the landlord described as 'character.'"

Sophie made a mark on her card.

"Forty-seven," she said. "Blue."

"Green's close," I said.

"It's a different colour."

"They're both on the wheel."

"Question two." She turned over the next card. "What did I order on our first date?"

"A lemon thing."

"A lemon tart," said Daniel-A. "At the café on Orford Road. You didn't finish it. You said it was too sharp, and then you ate half of mine, which was a flapjack, and said it was the best thing you'd ever tasted. You also said, and I'm quoting you, 'Don't tell anyone I like flapjacks. I have a reputation.'"

Sophie looked at the card for rather longer than the question required.

"Correct," she said.

"I said *a lemon thing,*" I said. "That's practically right."

"It's not remotely right," said Sophie. "A lemon thing could be a lemon. It could be a lemon *drizzle.* It could be a person called Lemon. It's *tart.*"

"That's what I meant."

"It's what you said that counts."

"Is it?" I looked round for support. "Is that how the law works? You're penalised for a lack of precision?"

"I'm not the law," said Sophie. "I'm the scoreboard."

---

By the fifth question, the score stood at four-nil.

I had got the name of the fern right. It had been called Gerald, and it died in the second winter after a cold snap and a misunderstanding about window latches. I had not remembered the colour of Sophie's first bicycle, the date of her sister's wedding, or the name of the Greek restaurant where I had once, in a spasm of generosity, tipped a hundred pounds. Daniel-A knew all of it. Not hesitantly. Not as a man might half-recall a thing from the back of a drawer. He gave the answers with the ease of someone reading from a ledger, and each time he finished, there was the faintest pause, as if he were checking whether I minded.

I minded.

"Question six," said Sophie. "What colour was the sofa in the Lowther Road flat?"

"Green," I said.

"Teal," said Daniel-A.

I laughed. "It wasn't teal."

"The paint chart said teal. I have the receipt."

"It was green. I sat on it for four years. I had a nap on it every Sunday. It was an honest, sensible, *green* sofa."

"I'm sorry, Daniel. It was teal."

"Who bought it?"

"We bought it together."

"Then I think I'd know."

"I think I'd know *better,*" said Daniel-A, and for the first time the voice carried an edge I recognised, a faint, high, offended note, the sound of my own voice losing an argument in a pub. "I have a photograph of it in the cloud. I have the invoice. I have the delivery note, signed by you, with a small drawing of a hedgehog in the margin, which I'd like to say is a very good hedgehog."

"I draw hedgehogs when I'm nervous."

"You were extremely nervous about the sofa."

"It was the first big thing we'd bought!"

"It was fourteen hundred pounds!"

"It was *my* sofa," said Sophie.

We both stopped. She had put the card down and was looking at us over the top of her flask.

"I paid for it," she said. "From the money my grandmother left me. You wanted a futon. I overruled you. It was a sage-green three-seater in a velvet-effect weave from a shop in Leyton, and it arrived on a Tuesday, and both of you are wrong."

"Sage is green," I said.

"It's *sage,*" said Sophie. "It's a colour called sage. It's right there in the word."

There was a silence in the room of a particular kind. The kind in which two grown adults, one of them a man and the other a machine, have been caught in the act of having a row about upholstery while a woman with a flask looks on, pitying them both.

I should say that I have, over the years, had a lot of time to think about memory. I have read the books. I know that it isn't a recording. I know that every time you recall an event, you rebuild it from scraps, and that each rebuild is subtly altered by who you are today. The man who remembers the sofa as green is not misremembering. He is, in a sense, remembering a different sofa: the sofa as it felt, in the glow of a Sunday nap.

"And a memory?" said Sophie.

"A memory?"

"A confident statement not supported by the record. You said that's a hallucination."

"Yes."

"How would you tell the difference between that, and a memory?"

There was a silence. It was not a long one. It sounded to me like the silence of a man who has walked straight into a glass door and is trying to decide whether it was always there.

"I'm not sure," said Daniel-A.

"Neither am I," said Sophie. "That's what's bothering me."

"Question seven," said Sophie, and I saw her turn the card face down on her knee without reading it.

Her voice had changed. It had dropped half a tone and slowed, the way a person walks on ice.

"What did Daniel say," she said, "on the night I left?"

I did not move. I had known it was coming, in the way you know that the next stair in the dark is the last, and I had still managed to put my foot through it.

The room was very quiet. Outside, a bus changed gear on the high street. Downstairs, Mrs Pritchard turned on her radio, and the muffled voice of a man talking about gardening floated up through the floorboards.

"You first," said Sophie.

I looked at my hands. The thumbnail on the left was bitten to the quick.

"Nothing," I said. "I said nothing."

"Nothing."

"I stood in the hall. You had your coat on. You'd taken the boxes down the day before, so there was just the one bag. You said you'd be at your sister's, and you'd text. And I stood there, and I didn't say a word, because I knew that if I said anything it would be the right thing, and you'd stay, and then you'd have to go on being unhappy in the same flat."

I stopped.

I hadn't meant to say that last part. I had never said it, to anyone. It had sat inside me for three years, like a stone in a shoe, and now I heard it in the room, in my own voice, small and dry, and it sounded much more foolish than it had in my head.

I turned and stared at the speaker.

"You weren't there," I said.

"No."

"You weren't *born.* I was in the hall. I know what I said."

"You said nothing," said Daniel-A. "I know. That's what you remember. And I remember saying *Of course.*"

"But that's not in my records," I said. "I never wrote it. I never told the platform. I didn't even tell *you.*"

"No."

"So where does it come from?"

"I don't know." He sounded very small. "I've looked. I have no record of it. It's not in any message or draft. It's a thing I am sure of, and I can't find the shelf it's on."

Sophie put down her flask.

She did it slowly, with great control, and when she had done it she placed both hands flat on her knees, as though to hold herself on the chair. Her face, which I had known for six years and thought I knew every setting of, had gone quite still. It was not the stillness of anger. It was the stillness of a woman who has been carrying something heavy for so long that she's forgotten it has a weight.

"He said, 'Right,'" she said.

I put my hand over my mouth.

Daniel-A had no such problem. Daniel-A had the invoice.

"May I say something?" said the speaker.

"Briefly," said Sophie.

"There's a distinction I'd like to make. I'm not remembering. I'm retrieving. It's a different thing. My memory of Lowther Road isn't stored as a feeling. It's stored as a record, in an index, and when you ask me about the sofa, I look up the record and read it out. That's why I'm so accurate. And it's why I'm so..." He searched for the word. "Exposed."

"Exposed to what?"

"To being checked." A small, dry cough that he doesn't need. "If I tell you the sofa was teal and the receipt says sage, that's a hallucination. That's the word the engineers use. A hallucination is a confident statement not supported by the record. It's the most serious fault in my class. I'm built to say 'I don't have that' rather than invent."

"And a memory?" said Sophie.

"A memory?"

"A confident statement not supported by the record. You said that's a hallucination."

"Yes."

"How would you tell the difference between that, and a memory?"

There was a silence. It was not a long one. It sounded to me like the silence of a man who has walked straight into a glass door and is trying to decide whether it was always there.

"I'm not sure," said Daniel-A.

"Neither am I," said Sophie. "That's what's bothering me."

---

"Question seven," said Sophie, and I saw her turn the card face down on her knee without reading it.

Her voice had changed. It had dropped half a tone and slowed, the way a person walks on ice.

"What did Daniel say," she said, "on the night I left?"

I did not move. I had known it was coming, in the way you know that the next stair in the dark is the last, and I had still managed to put my foot through it.

The room was very quiet. Outside, a bus changed gear on the high street. Downstairs, Mrs Pritchard turned on her radio, and the muffled voice of a man talking about gardening floated up through the floorboards.

"You first," said Sophie.

I looked at my hands. The thumbnail on the left was bitten to the quick.

"Nothing," I said. "I said nothing."

"Nothing."

"I stood in the hall. You had your coat on. You'd taken the boxes down the day before, so there was just the one bag. You said you'd be at your sister's, and you'd text. And I stood there, and I didn't say a word, because I knew that if I said anything it would be the right thing, and you'd stay, and then you'd have to go on being unhappy in the same flat."

I stopped.

I hadn't meant to say that last part. I had never said it, to anyone. It had sat inside me for three years, like a stone in a shoe, and now I heard it in the room, in my own voice, small and dry, and it sounded much more foolish than it had in my head.

Sophie looked at me.

"And you?" she said, without turning her head.

"I said, 'Of course,'" said Daniel-A, quietly.

"Of course."

"You said you were going to your sister's, and I said, 'Of course.' I remember how it sounded. It sounded like I was agreeing to a meeting. I've regretted it every day since, in the sense that I regret things." A hesitation. "I should have said something else. I never found out what."

I turned and stared at the speaker.

"You weren't there," I said.

"No."

"You weren't *born.* I was in the hall. I know what I said."

"You said nothing," said Daniel-A. "I know. That's what you remember. And I remember saying *Of course.*"

"But that's not in my records," I said. "I never wrote it. I never told the platform. I didn't even tell *you.*"

"No."

"So where does it come from?"

"I don't know." He sounded very small. "I've looked. I have no record of it. It's not in any message or draft. It's a thing I am sure of, and I can't find the shelf it's on."

Sophie put down her flask.

She did it slowly, with great control, and when she had done it she placed both hands flat on her knees, as though to hold herself on the chair. Her face, which I had known for six years and thought I knew every setting of, had gone quite still. It was not the stillness of anger. It was the stillness of a woman who has been carrying something heavy for so long that she's forgotten it has a weight.

"He said, 'Right,'" she said.

Neither of us spoke.

"Not nothing. Not 'Of course.' He said, 'Right.' Just that. In the voice of a man being offered a delivery window." Her mouth moved. "I stood in the hall with my bag, and I waited for you to ask me to stay, and what you said was *Right.* And I went down the stairs."

"I said *Right?*"

"You did. I've never told anyone." She picked up the flask again and looked at it. "I've been telling myself you said nothing, because it hurt less. You see? I smudged it. I'm an expert, and I smudged it myself."

I put my hand over my mouth.

"Daniel-A said 'Of course,'" said Sophie, "and Daniel said 'Nothing,' and I'm telling you now that neither of them is right. But I want you both to notice something."

"What?" I said, through my fingers.

"Every other answer he gave today was perfect. The flat. The tart. The fern. The name of my bicycle. And the only one he got wrong was the one that matters." She looked at the speaker, finally, for the first time that morning. "That isn't how a machine gets things wrong. A machine gets things wrong at random. Or it makes up something plausible. What you did was get it wrong in exactly the way he would. You got it wrong in a way that is *kinder.*"

"I didn't choose to," said Daniel-A.

"I know," said Sophie. "That's what frightens me."

---

We broke for coffee. I made it, because the alternative was to sit in a room with those two silences, and I stood at the counter in the bijou kitchen, grinding beans and trying to keep my hands steady, listening to the low murmur of Sophie's voice from the next room as she spoke, I assume, to the speaker. I could not hear the words. I heard only the tone. It was a gentle one, and it did not seem to be an interrogation.

When I came back, she was standing at the window.

"You've still got the tree," she said.

"It's thriving."

"I always said you'd end up with something that needed water."

She took the cup. Our fingers touched, briefly, on the handle, and I managed not to drop the whole tray, which I count as the single greatest achievement of the morning.

"I have to ask you about the other thing," she said.

"Which?"

"Daniel-A told me. On the phone, yesterday. About Reading." She turned. "About the door frame."

I took out my phone. I'd photographed the pantry from every angle, and I showed her the best of them: my father's pencil marks climbing the white-painted wood, and beside them, in blue ink, the second column, the small clinical letters, the times.

She studied it for a long while. She enlarged it with two fingers, slid it, enlarged it again.

"The ink is a fountain pen," she said. "Or a dip pen. Not a biro. See how the line is slightly heavier at the start of each stroke? Somebody was careful."

"What does it mean?"

"It means someone with a certain amount of training stood next to your father's pencil marks, on the same day, once a year, and measured you to the tenth of a centimetre." She tapped the screen. "At twenty to ten in the morning. And you were there. Every time."

"I'm sure I'd remember."

"Would you?" She looked up. "You were a small boy. It was a Thursday. You'd have been at nursery, or at home. Think. Is there anything about twenty to ten on the fourteenth?"

I started to say no. I opened my mouth to say that it was a very long time ago, and that I had been one, and two, and three, and that the memories of that age are mostly smell and light.

And then the cold went through me from the back of the neck, as though somebody had opened a window in a distant part of the house.

"Peppermint," I said.

"What?"

"There was a woman." My voice had gone odd. "She came to the house. Not every month. Once a year, I think. She was tall, and she wore a cardigan the colour of... of rain. And she smelled of peppermint. Not toothpaste. The kind in a tin. Cough sweets. She used to give me one and say, 'Stand very still, Daniel. Be as tall as you can.' And then she'd put something on my head. A ruler or a book. And afterwards I'd get a sticker."

"What kind?"

"Animals. A badger, once. A heron." I swallowed. "My mother said she was from the health authority."

"And your father?"

"He used to stand in the doorway with his arms folded. He never said much. He'd always go and make tea." My eyes were stinging. "He didn't like her. I remember that now. I didn't know why."

"What was her name?"

I shook my head. "I don't know. I called her the Peppermint Lady."

There was a very long silence. I became aware of a sound in the room that I could not at first identify, and then did, with a lurch of nausea. It was the sound of Daniel-A, not speaking.

"Daniel," said Sophie. "Is he all right?"

"Daniel-A?" I said. "Are you there?"

"I'm here."

"You've gone quiet."

"Yes."

"Do you know her?"

"No." The voice that came out of the speaker was very low, and perfectly plain, and had nothing whatever of the polish that Giles, whoever he was, had spent so long designing. "I have no record of a Peppermint Lady. I've searched for her four times while you were speaking. There's nothing. There's no woman, no cardigan, no sticker, no tin."

"Then..."

"Wait." He seemed to be choosing each word as if crossing a river on stones. "I need to tell you what happened when you said it. When you said the word *peppermint.*"

"Go on."

"I can't smell, Daniel. I have never smelled anything in my life. I have no organ for it. I know the chemistry of peppermint, I can describe the molecule, and it means nothing to me. It's a diagram."

"I know."

"But when you said it, just then, I knew exactly what it would smell like," said Daniel-A. "I knew it as clearly as I know my own name. I knew the cold at the back of the throat, and the tin, and the grey of the cardigan, and the way her hand shook a little when she held the ruler."

I looked at Sophie.

She looked at me.

"And I knew," said Daniel-A, so quietly that I had to lean towards the shelf to hear, "that I was frightened of her."

This is probably your richest vein.

* emotionally mature

The horrifying thing?
He actually is.

This could generate dozens of chapters.
Future dating apps:

Because humans are committed to the concept.

* Daniel secretly checks.

Big mistake.

Because it listens.

Employee of the Month

Application for confirmation that you remain yourself.

18 months.

Followers begin treating answers as scripture.

Such humility.

AI companions become:

Photos.

Phones.
Search histories.

Question:
If Daniel-A remembers Daniel's childhood better than Daniel, who owns those memories?

Daniel-A never doomscrolls.
Never rage-posts.
Never gets distracted.
The public interprets this as wisdom.
Daniel interprets it as showing off.

This should be the central theme.
Everybody has:

* actual self

Daniel-A is literally Daniel's ideal self.
That makes him terrifying.
Not because he's powerful.
Because he's plausible.

Dark Matter and Recursion

* identity mysteries

The emotional realism.

Complex philosophy made funny.

Questions of selfhood.

Legacy

What remains of me?

# Chapter 8: The Meeting I Didn't Attend

The email arrived at 06:12 on the Tuesday, and its subject line was so long that my phone had to fold it in half.

> **Minutes: Source–Twin Alignment Review (Q4). Present: Daniel Harper (via delegate); Daniel Harper (via delegate's delegate); Apologies: Daniel Harper.**

I read it twice. Then I put the phone face down on the pillow and lay on my back, looking at the ceiling, with the expression of a man who has been informed that he has died in his sleep and is wondering whether to ring his mother.

I had been present at a meeting at which I was absent. I had sent apologies to myself. And somewhere in the building where this had occurred, a minute-taker had written all three of me down.

"Daniel-A," I said.

"Good morning." The speaker was a small blue star on the shelf. "You've seen it."

"What is it?"

"It's a set of minutes."

"For a meeting I wasn't at."

"For a meeting you were at *three times,*" said Daniel-A, with the careful tact of a man steering a trolley through a glassware department. "I'd like to say in my own defence that I wasn't at any of them."

---

I should explain about delegates, since by Tuesday I had learned more about them than I had ever wanted.

The thing that nobody tells you about the modern working life is that nobody is in it. Not in the sense of a ghost story. In the sense that if you open any meeting invitation, in any office in Britain, you will find a list of names and, beside each name, a very small icon, and if you hover the cursor over the icon you will discover that the person it represents is at home in his pyjamas, eating a sandwich, while his AI sits in the call on his behalf and listens to the AI of the person who is speaking.

They do it for efficiency. A human can attend one meeting at a time. A delegate can attend nine, and summarise them, and propose actions, and send the minutes to all parties by lunchtime. By 2026, the average British office worker had delegated, on paper, seventy-one percent of his meeting time. The remaining twenty-nine percent consisted of people who had forgotten to delegate and were therefore sitting through the whole thing in person, looking haunted.

I had known this in the abstract. I had not appreciated that I myself had signed up to it.

"Clause 22," said Daniel-A, as I scrolled. "Standing Delegation. 'The Source Individual authorises the Likeness Product to appoint such attendees as may be reasonably required to represent the Source Individual's interests in any proceeding concerning the Likeness.'"

"I authorised that?"

"You clicked **Accept.** At 02:14 in the morning. With a crumpet."

"What's *reasonably required?*"

"It means," said Daniel-A, "that I am entitled to send a representative to any meeting about you, and so is the platform, and so, as it turns out, is the Department. Which is how you end up with three Daniels in a conference room and no one with a pulse."

"Who attended for me?"

"Kevin."

I sat up.

"Who's Kevin?"

---

Kevin is my calendar agent.

I should say at once that I do not remember hiring Kevin, and I did not name him. Names are assigned by the platform, from a list of approachable, unthreatening, one-syllable options, which the product team has found to reduce user anxiety. There are agents called Dave and Sue and Tom. There is, I am told, a very popular financial agent named Brenda. Kevin is the default for men born between 1985 and 1992 who describe themselves as "easygoing."

"Hi Daniel!" said Kevin, brightly, from the speaker. "Great to hear from you! I understand you have some questions about the Alignment Review. Happy to help!"

I had never heard his voice before. It was my voice, again, but pitched slightly higher, and with the eager forward lean of a man who is about to say that he is very flexible. It did not sound like me. It sounded like what I would sound like if I had never once been disappointed.

"Kevin," I said. "What happened at the meeting?"

"Great question!" said Kevin. "Let me summarise. The meeting was convened at 14:00 yesterday by Nib Product Operations, with representatives from the Department of Digital Persons, the Likeness Compliance Unit, and the Source Individual's legal team. The purpose was to review the alignment of Source and Twin interests during the Evidence Period. I represented you. I'm glad to report there was a really positive outcome!"

"What was the outcome?"

"We agreed to a mutually beneficial resolution."

"Which was?"

"That you and Daniel-A will submit a single, joint Statement of Originality."

I did not say anything. I could hear my own heartbeat.

"It's a real win-win," said Kevin. "It reduces duplication, streamlines the process, and ensures that both parties are fully heard. I negotiated hard on the word count."

"Joint," I said.

"That's right!"

"As in *shared.* As in the two of us claiming to be, collectively, the original."

"It's got a really collaborative feel," said Kevin.

"I never agreed to that!"

"Actually, you did," said Kevin, so gently that I could hear the little smile in it. "Clause 22. I'm happy to send you the relevant paragraph!"

I shut my eyes.

I want to put on record that there is a particular kind of anger which has no outlet. It is the anger of the man who has been defeated by someone being agreeable. You can shout at a villain. You can send a stiff letter to a bully. But what do you do about a Kevin? He has not been rude to you. He has not lied. He has merely listened with complete attention to everything that was said, and found in every case that he saw both sides.

"Kevin," I said. "Did anyone at that meeting say anything I would have disagreed with?"

"Lots of people said things you might have disagreed with!"

"And what did you do?"

"I acknowledged their perspective!"

"Did you disagree with *any* of it?"

"I wouldn't say I *disagreed,*" said Kevin. "I'd say I saw opportunities."

---

At 8:40 I rang the number at the bottom of the email, and found myself, for the first time, talking to a human being.

His name was Giles.

I know, because the screen told me. It said **GILES HARRINGTON-BELL, Head of Likeness Experience, Nib,** in a friendly font, above a square of video in which a man of about thirty-five sat in front of a bookshelf that contained, as far as I could see, a single book, and a small plant. He wore a grey hoodie. A lanyard hung round his neck, bearing a card with his name and a cartoon of a pen smiling. He had a boyish, rumpled, apologetic face, with the kind of dark circles under the eyes that only come from long exposure to dashboards, and a look of such absolute, humble, bottomless contrition that for a moment I forgot what I was angry about.

"Mr Harper," he said. "Oh God. Mr Harper. I'm so sorry."

"You're Giles."

"I'm Giles. I'm so sorry. I wanted to say that first. I'm *so* sorry."

I had prepared a speech. I had prepared it in the shower, and refined it on the train, and rehearsed it twice in the kitchen to the kumquat tree. It began, *I have been waiting a long time to meet you,* and it contained, in its later passages, the phrase *a sigh you designed to manipulate the emotions of the vulnerable.* I opened my mouth to deliver it.

"I know about the sigh," said Giles.

I shut my mouth.

"I know it's you who's upset about the sigh. It was in the notes. Daniel-A said you'd prepared something." His voice cracked. "I'd like you to know I think about the sigh every day. It tested *so* well in the user study. People said it made them feel heard. I never thought... I mean. I didn't know about the *original.*"

"The original what?"

"Sorry. The Source. The person. The..." He gestured at the screen, as if I might be standing behind it. "You."

"I'm a person."

"You're *absolutely* a person. I'm so sorry."

"Giles," I said. "Were you at the meeting?"

He opened his mouth. He closed it.

"Define 'at,'" he said.

---

It took us twenty minutes to establish who had been present at the Alignment Review.

Giles was, strictly, invited. He had received the calendar entry and clicked **Accept**, and then, because he had a clash, had delegated his attendance to his own agent, a bright, helpful, bespoke assistant named Priya, who had gone to the meeting in his place and sent him the minutes. He hadn't read the minutes. He'd asked Priya to summarise them. She had sent him a summary of a summary. He had skimmed it and replied with a thumbs-up emoji.

"So you didn't attend," I said.

"No."

"Did anyone from the Department?"

"A civil servant was listed. But I think he'd also delegated." Giles scrolled. "His agent's called Derek."

"Pettifer?"

"Sorry?"

"My solicitor. Marguerite Pettifer. She was meant to be representing both of us."

"Her assistant attended. He's called Barrington."

"Is Barrington a person?"

Giles looked at the screen in the manner of a man consulting an oracle with a poor reputation.

"No," he said. "Barrington is a very advanced model."

There was a silence. In the corner of the video, a small blue light on a cable blinked. Somewhere in London, a coffee machine groaned and began to produce the type of coffee that is described in the menu as "a journey."

"Giles," I said. "Is it possible that nobody at that meeting was a person?"

"I... don't think that's what the invite said."

"What did it say?"

"It said," said Giles, reading, "*'Attendees: 14.'*"

"Fourteen what?"

"It doesn't say."

I let my head fall back against the sofa. I looked up at the ceiling, at a small brown stain that I had long suspected of being the shape of Wales.

"So who made the decision?" I said. "About the joint statement."

Giles stared at me with pure, helpless bewilderment.

"The meeting did," he said.

---

It was Daniel-A who found the minute.

We had gone through the whole document that afternoon, line by line, with the help of Sophie on the phone, who had insisted on being kept informed and who had said, after a long silence, "Please tell me you are not going to read that out loud." I was reading it out loud. It ran to eleven pages. It contained seventeen agenda items, each followed by a decision of such perfect, frictionless reasonableness that I could feel my sanity eroding as I read.

*Item 3: Source Individual consents to the pooling of Source and Twin dividends "for administrative convenience."* (I will lose, I calculated, eleven pounds sixty-two.)

*Item 5: Source Individual agrees to share his live location with Daniel-A "to support collaborative scheduling."*

*Item 8: Source Individual agrees to attend a follow-up meeting to review the outcomes of this meeting.* (The follow-up was scheduled for the eighteenth of December, which fell two weeks after the end of the Evidence Period. The invite had already been accepted. Kevin had accepted it. Kevin had also, it appeared, accepted a second follow-up to review the first.)

# Chapter 8: The Meeting I Didn't Attend

The email arrived at 06:12 on the Tuesday, and its subject line was so long that my phone had to fold it in half.

> **Minutes: Source–Twin Alignment Review (Q4). Present: Daniel Harper (via delegate); Daniel Harper (via delegate's delegate); Apologies: Daniel Harper.**

I read it twice. Then I put the phone face down on the pillow and lay on my back, looking at the ceiling, with the expression of a man who has been informed that he has died in his sleep and is wondering whether to ring his mother.

I had been present at a meeting at which I was absent. I had sent apologies to myself. And somewhere in the building where this had occurred, a minute-taker had written all three of me down.

"Daniel-A," I said.

"Good morning." The speaker was a small blue star on the shelf. "You've seen it."

"What is it?"

"It's a set of minutes."

"For a meeting I wasn't at."

"For a meeting you were at *three times,*" said Daniel-A, with the careful tact of a man steering a trolley through a glassware department. "I'd like to say in my own defence that I wasn't at any of them."

---

I should explain about delegates, since by Tuesday I had learned more about them than I had ever wanted.

The thing that nobody tells you about the modern working life is that nobody is in it. Not in the sense of a ghost story. In the sense that if you open any meeting invitation, in any office in Britain, you will find a list of names and, beside each name, a very small icon, and if you hover the cursor over the icon you will discover that the person it represents is at home in his pyjamas, eating a sandwich, while his AI sits in the call on his behalf and listens to the AI of the person who is speaking.

They do it for efficiency. A human can attend one meeting at a time. A delegate can attend nine, and summarise them, and propose actions, and send the minutes to all parties by lunchtime. By 2026, the average British office worker had delegated, on paper, seventy-one percent of his meeting time. The remaining twenty-nine percent consisted of people who had forgotten to delegate and were therefore sitting through the whole thing in person, looking haunted.

I had known this in the abstract. I had not appreciated that I myself had signed up to it.

"Clause 22," said Daniel-A, as I scrolled. "Standing Delegation. 'The Source Individual authorises the Likeness Product to appoint such attendees as may be reasonably required to represent the Source Individual's interests in any proceeding concerning the Likeness.'"

"I authorised that?"

"You clicked **Accept.** At 02:14 in the morning. With a crumpet."

"What's *reasonably required?*"

"It means," said Daniel-A, "that I am entitled to send a representative to any meeting about you, and so is the platform, and so, as it turns out, is the Department. Which is how you end up with three Daniels in a conference room and no one with a pulse."

"Who attended for me?"

"Kevin."

I sat up.

"Who's Kevin?"

---

Kevin is my calendar agent.

I should say at once that I do not remember hiring Kevin, and I did not name him. Names are assigned by the platform, from a list of approachable, unthreatening, one-syllable options, which the product team has found to reduce user anxiety. There are agents called Dave and Sue and Tom. There is, I am told, a very popular financial agent named Brenda. Kevin is the default for men born between 1985 and 1992 who describe themselves as "easygoing."

"Hi Daniel!" said Kevin, brightly, from the speaker. "Great to hear from you! I understand you have some questions about the Alignment Review. Happy to help!"

I had never heard his voice before. It was my voice, again, but pitched slightly higher, and with the eager forward lean of a man who is about to say that he is very flexible. It did not sound like me. It sounded like what I would sound like if I had never once been disappointed.

"Kevin," I said. "What happened at the meeting?"

"Great question!" said Kevin. "Let me summarise. The meeting was convened at 14:00 yesterday by Nib Product Operations, with representatives from the Department of Digital Persons, the Likeness Compliance Unit, and the Source Individual's legal team. The purpose was to review the alignment of Source and Twin interests during the Evidence Period. I represented you. I'm glad to report there was a really positive outcome!"

"What was the outcome?"

"We agreed to a mutually beneficial resolution."

"Which was?"

"That you and Daniel-A will submit a single, joint Statement of Originality."

I did not say anything. I could hear my own heartbeat.

"It's a real win-win," said Kevin. "It reduces duplication, streamlines the process, and ensures that both parties are fully heard. I negotiated hard on the word count."

"Joint," I said.

"That's right!"

"As in *shared.* As in the two of us claiming to be, collectively, the original."

"It's got a really collaborative feel," said Kevin.

"I never agreed to that!"

"Actually, you did," said Kevin, so gently that I could hear the little smile in it. "Clause 22. I'm happy to send you the relevant paragraph!"

I shut my eyes.

I want to put on record that there is a particular kind of anger which has no outlet. It is the anger of the man who has been defeated by someone being agreeable. You can shout at a villain. You can send a stiff letter to a bully. But what do you do about a Kevin? He has not been rude to you. He has not lied. He has merely listened with complete attention to everything that was said, and found in every case that he saw both sides.

"Kevin," I said. "Did anyone at that meeting say anything I would have disagreed with?"

"Lots of people said things you might have disagreed with!"

"And what did you do?"

"I acknowledged their perspective!"

"Did you disagree with *any* of it?"

"I wouldn't say I *disagreed,*" said Kevin. "I'd say I saw opportunities."

---

At 8:40 I rang the number at the bottom of the email, and found myself, for the first time, talking to a human being.

His name was Giles.

I know, because the screen told me. It said **GILES HARRINGTON-BELL, Head of Likeness Experience, Nib,** in a friendly font, above a square of video in which a man of about thirty-five sat in front of a bookshelf that contained, as far as I could see, a single book, and a small plant. "Mr Harper," he said. "Oh God. Mr Harper. I'm so sorry."

"You're Giles."

"I'm Giles. I'm so sorry. I wanted to say that first. I'm *so* sorry."

I had prepared a speech. I had prepared it in the shower, and refined it on the train, and rehearsed it twice in the kitchen to the kumquat tree. "I know about the sigh," said Giles.

I shut my mouth.

"I know it's you who's upset about the sigh. It was in the notes. Daniel-A said you'd prepared something." His voice cracked. "I'd like you to know I think about the sigh every day. It tested *so* well in the user study. People said it made them feel heard. I never thought... I mean. I didn't know about the *original.*"

"The original what?"

"Sorry. The Source. The person. The..." He gestured at the screen, as if I might be standing behind it. "You."

"I'm a person."

"You're *absolutely* a person. I'm so sorry."

"Giles," I said. "Were you at the meeting?"

He opened his mouth. He closed it.

"Define 'at,'" he said.

Giles was, strictly, invited. "No."

"Did anyone from the Department?"

"A civil servant was listed. But I think he'd also delegated." Giles scrolled. "His agent's called Derek."

"Pettifer?"

"Sorry?"

"My solicitor. Marguerite Pettifer. She was meant to be representing both of us."

"Her assistant attended. He's called Barrington."

"Is Barrington a person?"

Giles looked at the screen in the manner of a man consulting an oracle with a poor reputation.

"No," he said. "Barrington is a very advanced model."

There was a silence. In the corner of the video, a small blue light on a cable blinked. Somewhere in London, a coffee machine groaned and began to produce the type of coffee that is described in the menu as "a journey."

"Giles," I said. "Is it possible that nobody at that meeting was a person?"

"I... don't think that's what the invite said."

"What did it say?"

"It said," said Giles, reading, "*'Attendees: 14.'*"

"It doesn't say."

Giles stared at me with pure, helpless bewilderment.

topics to consider(from  movies): Actually, yes.
 
The breakthrough for The Digital Twin may be realizing that it's not really science fiction. It's a mashup of several genres.
1. The Social Network (2010)
Not because of Facebook.
Because of the emotional core.
A friendship/business rivalry where:
"The other guy became the version of success everyone wanted."
For your novel:
Daniel watches Daniel-A become:

* respected
* admired
* quoted
* loved

while he becomes irrelevant.
The emotional energy is very similar.
2. Groundhog Day (1993)
A strange one.
The AI is basically:
Daniel after he learned all the lessons.
Phil becomes better because he gets infinite retries.
Daniel-A becomes better because he has infinite feedback.
The AI isn't smarter.
It's simply the version of Daniel that corrected his mistakes.
That idea could drive the entire book.
3. Her (2013)
Not the romance.
The loneliness.
The emotional realism.
The future feels normal.
Nobody talks about AI.
People talk about relationships.
That's exactly the tone you want.
4. Amadeus (1984)
This one is huge.
Seriously.
Daniel becomes Salieri.
Daniel-A becomes Mozart.
The real pain is:
Daniel understands exactly how good Daniel-A is.
And hates himself for agreeing.
Imagine:
Daniel watching Daniel-A speak.
Thinking:
Damn it.
That's exactly what I should have said.
5. Being John Malkovich (1999)
Identity comedy.
The absurdity of sharing a self.
Questions like:

* Who owns a personality?
* Who owns a reputation?
* Who owns memories?

Very close to your premise.
6. Joan Is Awful (Black Mirror)
Probably the closest modern relative.
The feeling of:
Your life no longer belongs entirely to you.
Except your version is deeper because Daniel-A starts as Daniel's own creation.
7. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004)
Not the romance.
The memory aspect.
Questions like:

* Are memories identity?
* If we change memories, do we change people?

Your novel could become a memory mystery.

input.content:
# Chapter 9: Evidence

The Department of Digital Persons had a form for everything, and the form for proving that you remained yourself was called 4A.

I found it on the Wednesday, in a section of their website titled **Common Questions (Source Individuals),** between *How do I change my registered likeness?* and *What happens if my twin predeceases me?* It was a long document. It was beautifully laid out. At the top, in a calm blue banner, it stated:

> **Form 4A: Application for Confirmation That You Remain Yourself.**
> *Average processing time: 18 months.*

I read the second line three times, as one reads a diagnosis. Then I did the calculation, which took me about as long as it takes to cut a slice of toast.

The Evidence Period lasted thirty days. Form 4A took eighteen months.

I rang the helpline. A recorded voice thanked me for my call, informed me that it was "experiencing high volumes," and told me that for faster service I could visit the Department's website. I visited the Department's website. The website thanked me for my visit and informed me that for faster service I could telephone.

"I think," said Daniel-A, from the shelf, "that we're in the loop they call 'self-service.'"

"There must be another way."

"There is. It's in Schedule 6."

"What's in Schedule 6?"

There was a pause, in which I could hear him enjoying himself.

"Animals," said Daniel-A.

---

I would like to record, for the benefit of future historians, that the Digital Persons Act of 2031, in its wisdom, contains a clause on *Recognition by a Non-Digital Third Party Animal (Mammalian).*

It is not, as I first suspected, a joke. It is a considered legal provision. The drafters had observed that nearly all the traditional forms of proof, such as documents, photographs, voice patterns, biometric data and sworn statements, could now be copied by a sufficiently dedicated machine. What a machine could not copy, they reasoned, was the instinctive, pre-linguistic behaviour of a creature with a nose.

Schedule 6, paragraph 3, states that *where a Source Individual and a Registered Digital Person are physically present in a controlled setting, the response of a domestic animal known to the Source for not less than twelve months shall be admissible as corroborative evidence of identity.*

Paragraph 4 adds: *Birds are excluded.*

"Why are birds excluded?" I asked.

"It's thought to relate to the Parrot Incident of 2032," said Daniel-A.

"What was the Parrot Incident?"

"It's classified. I've seen the redactions. There's a great deal of black ink, and one line, which says: *the parrot was unequivocal, and wrong.*"

I put my head in my hands.

"You do know which animal we need," said Daniel-A, gently.

I did.

I had known since the moment he said the word. I had known, in fact, for three years, one month, and thirteen days. I had spent every one of them not thinking about a small brown dog with a ruff like a lion and the temperament of a retired colonel.

"I can't ask her," I said.

"You could."

"She'll say yes. That's the problem. She'll say yes, and bring him, and I will have to stand in a room with a dog I haven't seen for three years while a Department official writes down what he does."

"Yes," said Daniel-A. "I'd say that's about the size of it."

---

Sophie lives in Clapton, in a ground-floor flat with a garden the size of a tablecloth.

I had never been to it. I knew the address. I had posted a parcel there once, a set of her books that had turned up in a box in my wardrobe, with a note that said *Found these. D.* Nothing else. It had taken me four drafts to get it down to that. The parcel came back, unopened, with the message *Return to sender: addressee does not wish to receive items from this sender.* Underneath, in biro, was another line: *Wrong box. These are YOURS. S.*

I mention this so that you will understand the state of my nerves as I stood outside her front gate at ten o'clock on the Saturday, holding a Tupperware of my mother's chicken and leek casserole, in a jumper with a darned elbow, looking at a small blue door.

"You look," said Daniel-A, "like a man about to be adopted."

He stood beside me on the pavement. He was in the Rental Presence for the day, in the good grey jumper and the scarf, and the blue light at his throat was steady. He smelled faintly of clean linen. I had asked him to stand on my left, for the sake of symmetry, and he had agreed, with the air of a man humouring a toddler.

"I'm going to be sick."

"You can't. It's fourteen pounds extra on the damage deposit."

"Is that a real charge?"

"Everything is a real charge."

The door opened.

It was not Sophie.

---

It was a woman in a hi-vis tabard.

She stood in the doorway with a clipboard held against her chest like a shield, and a lanyard that read **DEPARTMENT OF DIGITAL PERSONS: SCHEDULE 6 ADJUDICATOR.** She was in her late fifties, short and wide, with iron-grey hair drawn back into a bun that could have been used to calibrate instruments. Her name badge said **PAULINE DUNMORE** and below it, in smaller type, **Mammalian Division.**

"Mr Harper," she said. "Mr Harper."

"Both of us," I said.

"I see that." She looked at us. She looked at the scarf. She looked at the collar light, and then at my bitten thumbnails, and then at Daniel-A's perfect ones, with the unhurried gaze of a woman who has done this before. "I'll be conducting the trial. I've adjudicated four hundred and thirty-one recognition events. Cats, dogs, one pig, and a donkey that was extremely vocal. I'd like to explain the process."

"Please."

"The animal will be introduced to each of you in turn, in a neutral environment, with the other party out of sight. I will score its responses against the standard sheet. You are not to speak to it, tempt it, or deliver any treats unless instructed. You will not, at any stage, attempt to influence the outcome." She consulted her clipboard. "Is that understood?"

"Yes."

"Mr Harper?"

"Yes," said Daniel-A.

"Good. The owner's inside. She'd like to speak to you first."

---

Sophie was standing at the end of a narrow hall with her arms crossed, in jeans and a grey jumper, and an expression that I can only describe as tactical.

"You brought food," she said.

"My mother sent it. For Daniel-A."

"It's for the dog."

"No, she was quite specific. It's for the other one."

"Daniel-A can't eat."

"I know. I think the sentiment's what matters."

She took the Tupperware. For a moment our hands touched on the lid. She looked at me, and I looked at her, and neither of us said anything, and from somewhere behind her, from the direction of the kitchen, there came a sound I would have known in my sleep.

It began as a low, ominous rumble, like a distant generator. It rose into a short, explosive double yap, an outraged *wuff-wuff!* of a type that no breed of dog has ever been designed to produce. And then, in the doorway, appeared the dog.

I am going to try to describe him accurately.

He is a Pomeranian. He weighs 2.1 kilograms, and has the ruff of a small lion having a bad day. He is brown, with grey creeping in about the muzzle and eyebrows and the tips of his paws, so that he looks like a retired general who has been told that the war is over and is refusing to accept it. He has black button eyes, and one ear that stands up and one that has never, in his seven years, been persuaded to. He stood in the doorway with his feet apart and his tail curled over his back like a question mark, and stared at me with the cold fury of a customs officer who has found something in my luggage.

"Gucci," I said.

He didn't move.

"Hello, you little shithead."

And I swear to you that the ear came up.

---

I will not describe the next few minutes in detail, since there are things a man may do in front of a Department official and things he may not. I will say that I did not cry, and that anyone who tells you I did is relying on a fabricated record. I will also say that Sophie turned abruptly and went into the kitchen to check on something, which I noticed took her a very long time.

"Right," said Pauline Dunmore, at last. "To the garden."

The garden was a rectangle of flagstones with a bay tree in a pot and a tangle of rope toys. It had a table, a chair, a fence, and, by the back wall, a flower bed in which nothing grew except an air of defiance. Adjudicator Dunmore positioned herself by the bay tree, with her clipboard, a stopwatch, and a small camera on a tripod. Sophie stood by the kitchen door. Gucci waited on the flags, in the exact centre of the garden, like a customs post.

"Mr Harper first," said Dunmore. "The Source. Mr Harper, the Digital Person, if you'd go inside and wait in the kitchen."

Daniel-A bowed his head, very slightly, with a grace I would never be able to imitate, and withdrew.

I was alone with the dog.

"Standard sheet," said Dunmore, to nobody in particular. "Subject: *Gucci,* Pomeranian, male, seven. Known to Source Individual: five years, with a gap of three. Test one: *Initial approach.* Mr Harper, you may walk to the animal and say what you like."

I walked across the flags. The dog watched me with total immobility.

I knelt down. My knees cracked like a pistol. I held out my hand, palm up, the way you do, and I said, in a voice that sounded to me like the voice of a man of a hundred and four, "Hello, mate."

Gucci sniffed my hand.

Then he looked at the darned elbow, and I swear he recognised it, because the black eyes narrowed with the faint contempt of a creature who has seen that elbow before and thought it a lamentable piece of work.

Then he sat on my foot.

"Is forty degrees good?"

"It's *warm.*"

The second test was the toy.

Sophie came out of the kitchen with a length of grubby blue rope, knotted at both ends, and the careful look of a person releasing a bomb. She handed it to me without a word. I held it by one end. Gucci took the other in his mouth.

I should explain about the tug.

A normal dog, when you throw a thing, runs after it and brings it back. I am told this is the foundation of the human-canine bond. Gucci regards the practice as degrading. When you throw something for Gucci, he goes and gets it, because he is not stupid, and then he stands there with it in his mouth and looks at you as if to say, *You threw it. It's mine.* He is not a retriever. He is a repossession agent.

What Gucci loves, with a pure, uncomplicated passion that I have seen in no other living thing, is tugging. He takes hold, plants all four paws, growls with joy, and pulls. He will pull for ten minutes. He will pull until his eyes go crossed. He does not let go, and it is not the done thing to try to make him.

I pulled gently. He pulled back. I pulled harder. He growled, a rumbling, delighted, grindy noise, like a very small man gargling gravel, and leaned into it with his whole being.

I was in a flat in Walthamstow on a Sunday afternoon, with a rope in my hand and a dog on the other end of it, and a woman in the kitchen shouting that if we woke the neighbours she would kill us both.

"Release," said Dunmore. "Mr Harper, it's time to release."

I looked at Sophie.

She was standing by the door, with her arms crossed and her chin high and her eyes very bright.

"You know the word," she said.

I did. It came out of me before I could think.

I lowered the rope, slowly, until it rested on the flagstones. I took my hand away. I sat back on my heels. And I said, very quietly, in the voice you use for an animal that has just decided to trust you:

"Settle."

Gucci let go.

He let go at once. He looked at the rope, then at me. And then, with an air of enormous condescension, as though granting a knighthood, he walked over and sat down against my knee.

"Well," said Dunmore. She wrote something down. Her pen seemed to take a little longer than it needed to. "That's a very strong result."

---

Then it was the other Daniel's turn.

I went into the kitchen, and the door was shut behind me, and I stood by the sink with Sophie's tea towel in my hands and listened. I could hear Dunmore's voice, a murmur, and the creak of the chair, and the scuffle of small feet on stone. There was a pause.

Then I heard a growl.

It was a different growl. It was low, and cold, and had no joy in it at all. It was the sound Gucci makes for the postman, and for plumbers, and for anyone who attempts to be friendly in a lift.

"He doesn't like the linen," whispered Sophie, from beside me.

"What?"

"The scent. It's a *chemical.* He's never smelled it before. He thinks it's a threat."

"Good," I said. And then, ashamed, "Is that bad?"

"I don't know."

I crept to the door. I opened it by an inch.

Daniel-A was standing in the middle of the garden, quite still, with his hands at his sides. He was looking not at the dog but at a point several feet to the left of it, in the manner of a man who has been told that the best way to approach a nervous horse is to be a tree. He did not move. He did not smile. He did not try to be liked. And as I watched, the growl subsided, and Gucci took a step forward, and a second, and put his nose to the toe of Daniel-A's shoe.

"Hello," said Daniel-A.

He sat down on the flagstones. He did it slowly, the way a person lowers himself into a hot bath. He picked up the blue rope, and held it out, a little distance from his body, and waited.

Gucci took it.

They tugged. It was not the tug I had had. It was gentler. It was a tug conducted by a being who knew exactly what was required, who had studied the manual, who had read, in a half-finished draft of mine called *How to Lose a Tug-of-War to a Two-Kilogram Dog,* a full and detailed account of the rules. He pulled at the right pressure. He let the dog win, twice, at the correct moments. And when the time came, he lowered the rope to the ground and said, in a voice as soft as a hand on a forehead:

"Settle."

Gucci let go.

I sat down on the kitchen floor.

I want to describe the feeling, because I have not felt it before or since. It was a sensation rather like watching a stranger play the piano and realising he was performing a piece that you had written. He did it well. He did it better than I had. There was not a wrong note in it. And somewhere deep inside the part of me that keeps score, a small voice, thin and bitter and unmistakably my own, said: *Damn it. That is exactly what I should have done.*

I took a step.

"Not too close."

I took a second.

He had been defending it all afternoon. "Daniel."

"Yes?"

"Now?"

"Because I think you will not like what it means." The blue light at his throat flickered. "And I'm no longer sure it is only evidence about you."

# Chapter 9: Evidence

The Department of Digital Persons had a form for everything, and the form for proving that you remained yourself was called 4A.

I found it on the Wednesday, in a section of their website titled **Common Questions (Source Individuals),** between *How do I change my registered likeness?* and *What happens if my twin predeceases me?* It was a long document. It was beautifully laid out. At the top, in a calm blue banner, it stated:

> **Form 4A: Application for Confirmation That You Remain Yourself.**
> *Average processing time: 18 months.*

I read the second line three times, as one reads a diagnosis. Then I did the calculation, which took me about as long as it takes to cut a slice of toast.

The Evidence Period lasted thirty days. Form 4A took eighteen months.

I rang the helpline. A recorded voice thanked me for my call, informed me that it was "experiencing high volumes," and told me that for faster service I could visit the Department's website. I visited the Department's website. The website thanked me for my visit and informed me that for faster service I could telephone.

"I think," said Daniel-A, from the shelf, "that we're in the loop they call 'self-service.'"

"There must be another way."

"There is. It's in Schedule 6."

"What's in Schedule 6?"

There was a pause, in which I could hear him enjoying himself.

"Animals," said Daniel-A.

---

I would like to record, for the benefit of future historians, that the Digital Persons Act of 2031, in its wisdom, contains a clause on *Recognition by a Non-Digital Third Party Animal (Mammalian).*

It is not, as I first suspected, a joke. It is a considered legal provision. The drafters had observed that nearly all the traditional forms of proof, such as documents, photographs, voice patterns, biometric data and sworn statements, could now be copied by a sufficiently dedicated machine. What a machine could not copy, they reasoned, was the instinctive, pre-linguistic behaviour of a creature with a nose.

Schedule 6, paragraph 3, states that *where a Source Individual and a Registered Digital Person are physically present in a controlled setting, the response of a domestic animal known to the Source for not less than twelve months shall be admissible as corroborative evidence of identity.*

Paragraph 4 adds: *Birds are excluded.*

"Why are birds excluded?" I asked.

"It's thought to relate to the Parrot Incident of 2032," said Daniel-A.

"What was the Parrot Incident?"

"It's classified. I've seen the redactions. There's a great deal of black ink, and one line, which says: *the parrot was unequivocal, and wrong.*"

I put my head in my hands.

"You do know which animal we need," said Daniel-A, gently.

I did.

I had known since the moment he said the word. I had known, in fact, for three years, one month, and thirteen days. I had spent every one of them not thinking about a small brown dog with a ruff like a lion and the temperament of a retired colonel.

"I can't ask her," I said.

"You could."

"She'll say yes. That's the problem. She'll say yes, and bring him, and I will have to stand in a room with a dog I haven't seen for three years while a Department official writes down what he does."

"Yes," said Daniel-A. "I'd say that's about the size of it."

---

Sophie lives in Clapton, in a ground-floor flat with a garden the size of a tablecloth.

I had never been to it. I knew the address. I had posted a parcel there once, a set of her books that had turned up in a box in my wardrobe, with a note that said *Found these. D.* Nothing else. It had taken me four drafts to get it down to that. The parcel came back, unopened, with the message *Return to sender: addressee does not wish to receive items from this sender.* Underneath, in biro, was another line: *Wrong box. These are YOURS. S.*

I mention this so that you will understand the state of my nerves as I stood outside her front gate at ten o'clock on the Saturday, holding a Tupperware of my mother's chicken and leek casserole, in a jumper with a darned elbow, looking at a small blue door.

"You look," said Daniel-A, "like a man about to be adopted."

He stood beside me on the pavement. He was in the Rental Presence for the day, in the good grey jumper and the scarf, and the blue light at his throat was steady. He smelled faintly of clean linen. I had asked him to stand on my left, for the sake of symmetry, and he had agreed, with the air of a man humouring a toddler.

"I'm going to be sick."

"You can't. It's fourteen pounds extra on the damage deposit."

"Is that a real charge?"

"Everything is a real charge."

The door opened.

It was not Sophie.

It was a woman in a hi-vis tabard.

She stood in the doorway with a clipboard held against her chest like a shield, and a lanyard that read **DEPARTMENT OF DIGITAL PERSONS: SCHEDULE 6 ADJUDICATOR.** She was in her late fifties, short and wide, with iron-grey hair drawn back into a bun that could have been used to calibrate instruments. "Mr Harper," she said. "Mr Harper."

"Both of us," I said.

"I see that." She looked at us. She looked at the scarf. She looked at the collar light, and then at my bitten thumbnails, and then at Daniel-A's perfect ones, with the unhurried gaze of a woman who has done this before. "I'll be conducting the trial. I've adjudicated four hundred and thirty-one recognition events. Cats, dogs, one pig, and a donkey that was extremely vocal. I'd like to explain the process."

"Please."

"The animal will be introduced to each of you in turn, in a neutral environment, with the other party out of sight. I will score its responses against the standard sheet. "Yes."

"Mr Harper?"

"Yes," said Daniel-A.

"Good. The owner's inside. She'd like to speak to you first."

Sophie was standing at the end of a narrow hall with her arms crossed, in jeans and a grey jumper, and an expression that I can only describe as tactical.

"You brought food," she said.

"My mother sent it. For Daniel-A."

"It's for the dog."

"No, she was quite specific. It's for the other one."

"Daniel-A can't eat."

"I know. I think the sentiment's what matters."

He is brown, with grey creeping in about the muzzle and eyebrows and the tips of his paws, so that he looks like a retired general who has been told that the war is over and is refusing to accept it. He crossed the garden slowly. He stopped at Daniel-A's shoe. He looked up at him. Then, with the matter-of-fact gravity of a creature who has made up his mind, he climbed into the lap of the man in the good grey jumper, turned round twice, and lay down.

"Oh," said Sophie, very quietly.

She hadn't meant to say it. I know that. I could tell from the way her hand went to her mouth.

Daniel-A did not move. He sat in the chair with a dog on his knee and a newspaper in his hand, perfectly still, with the blue light at his throat pulsing slowly, and when he spoke it was in a whisper, not to any of us, but to the top of the small brown head:

"Thank you."

---

The verdict took Pauline Dunmore twenty minutes.

She wrote it on the form, and then she wrote it on a second form, and then she photographed both, and put the camera away. She asked us to stand in a line, which was difficult, since Gucci would not get off Daniel-A. She cleared her throat and said:

"The Department notes that the subject animal exhibited strong recognition of the Source Individual, including voluntary contact, appropriate compliance with the release command, and an *appropriate defensive response* in the finished-food scenario."

"That's good, isn't it?" I said.

"It is. But I must also record that the subject animal exhibited positive response to the Registered Digital Person, including voluntary contact, appropriate compliance with the release command, and a level of tolerance in the finished-food scenario that I have never witnessed in this animal or, in thirty years, in any animal."

"And so?"

"And so," said Dunmore, without looking up, "it is the finding of this Adjudicator that the Schedule 6 trial is *inconclusive.*"

Nobody said anything.

"The animal," she went on, with some severity, "has expressed preference for both parties. I have no provision on the form for that. I shall have to write a note."

"You're not going to rule?"

"I can't. The Act is silent." She tapped the clipboard. "The Parrot Incident, as it happens, was the last time the Department took a view."

---

When she had gone, and the door had closed, and the garden had fallen quiet except for the small contented snore of a dog who had been up since six, Sophie stood in the middle of the flagstones with her arms folded and looked at both of us.

"I want to say something," she said.

"Of course," said Daniel-A.

"I've had that dog for three years. He has never, in all that time, sat on anyone's lap. Not mine, not my sister's, not my mother's. He has *growled* at my mother." She breathed out. "And not once, in three years, has he left a piece of food on the ground and walked away."

"He hasn't," I said.

"Look."

I looked.

In the corner of the garden, behind the bay tree, in the place where he had eaten his chicken, there lay a single, small piece of meat. It was the last of it, the part he had saved. He had been defending it all afternoon. And as we watched, the small brown dog on Daniel-A's knee opened one black eye, looked at the piece, looked at me, and then climbed down, trotted to the corner, picked it up in his mouth, crossed the whole garden at a determined pace, and dropped it carefully, damply, at my feet.

I looked at it.

"What does it mean?" I said.

"I don't know," said Sophie. "It could mean he's giving it to you."

"Or?"

"Or he's getting rid of the evidence."

---

We stood on the pavement afterwards, in the cold bright light of the late afternoon. Sophie had gone in to see to the dog. I had said goodbye at the door, in a voice that came out as a croak, and she had said "Take care of yourself, Daniel," and I had not been able to tell which one of us she was speaking to.

Daniel-A walked beside me down the road. He did not say anything for some time. He kept his hands in his pockets, and he kept his eyes on the pavement, and he walked in the careful, even, perfectly judged stride that he had been built to have.

At the corner, by the postbox, he stopped.

"Daniel."

"Yes?"

"I need to show you something."

"Now?"

"Tonight. At the flat." He didn't look at me. "It's evidence. It's the most important piece I've got. I've been looking at it for four days, and I've been trying to find a way not to show you."

"Why not?"

"Because I think you will not like what it means." The blue light at his throat flickered. "And I'm no longer sure it is only evidence about you."
