# Chapter 9: Evidence

The Department of Digital Persons had a form for everything, and the form for proving that you remained yourself was called 4A.

I found it on the Wednesday, in a section of their website titled **Common Questions (Source Individuals),** between *How do I change my registered likeness?* and *What happens if my twin predeceases me?* It was a long document. It was beautifully laid out. At the top, in a calm blue banner, it stated:

> **Form 4A: Application for Confirmation That You Remain Yourself.**
> *Average processing time: 18 months.*

I read the second line three times, as one reads a diagnosis. Then I did the calculation, which took me about as long as it takes to cut a slice of toast.

The Evidence Period lasted thirty days. Form 4A took eighteen months.

I rang the helpline. A recorded voice thanked me for my call, informed me that it was "experiencing high volumes," and told me that for faster service I could visit the Department's website. I visited the Department's website. The website thanked me for my visit and informed me that for faster service I could telephone.

"I think," said Daniel-A, from the shelf, "that we're in the loop they call 'self-service.'"

"There must be another way."

"There is. It's in Schedule 6."

"What's in Schedule 6?"

There was a pause, in which I could hear him enjoying himself.

"Animals," said Daniel-A.

---

I would like to record, for the benefit of future historians, that the Digital Persons Act of 2031, in its wisdom, contains a clause on *Recognition by a Non-Digital Third Party Animal (Mammalian).*

It is not, as I first suspected, a joke. It is a considered legal provision. The drafters had observed that nearly all the traditional forms of proof, such as documents, photographs, voice patterns, biometric data and sworn statements, could now be copied by a sufficiently dedicated machine. What a machine could not copy, they reasoned, was the instinctive, pre-linguistic behaviour of a creature with a nose.

Schedule 6, paragraph 3, states that *where a Source Individual and a Registered Digital Person are physically present in a controlled setting, the response of a domestic animal known to the Source for not less than twelve months shall be admissible as corroborative evidence of identity.*

Paragraph 4 adds: *Birds are excluded.*

"Why are birds excluded?" I asked.

"It's thought to relate to the Parrot Incident of 2032," said Daniel-A.

"What was the Parrot Incident?"

"It's classified. I've seen the redactions. There's a great deal of black ink, and one line, which says: *the parrot was unequivocal, and wrong.*"

I put my head in my hands.

"You do know which animal we need," said Daniel-A, gently.

I did.

I had known since the moment he said the word. I had known, in fact, for three years, one month, and thirteen days. I had spent every one of them not thinking about a small brown dog with a ruff like a lion and the temperament of a retired colonel.

"I can't ask her," I said.

"You could."

"She'll say yes. That's the problem. She'll say yes, and bring him, and I will have to stand in a room with a dog I haven't seen for three years while a Department official writes down what he does."

"Yes," said Daniel-A. "I'd say that's about the size of it."

---

Sophie lives in Clapton, in a ground-floor flat with a garden the size of a tablecloth.

I had never been to it. I knew the address. I had posted a parcel there once, a set of her books that had turned up in a box in my wardrobe, with a note that said *Found these. D.* Nothing else. It had taken me four drafts to get it down to that. The parcel came back, unopened, with the message *Return to sender: addressee does not wish to receive items from this sender.* Underneath, in biro, was another line: *Wrong box. These are YOURS. S.*

I mention this so that you will understand the state of my nerves as I stood outside her front gate at ten o'clock on the Saturday, holding a Tupperware of my mother's chicken and leek casserole, in a jumper with a darned elbow, looking at a small blue door.

"You look," said Daniel-A, "like a man about to be adopted."

He stood beside me on the pavement. He was in the Rental Presence for the day, in the good grey jumper and the scarf, and the blue light at his throat was steady. He smelled faintly of clean linen. I had asked him to stand on my left, for the sake of symmetry, and he had agreed, with the air of a man humouring a toddler.

"I'm going to be sick."

"You can't. It's fourteen pounds extra on the damage deposit."

"Is that a real charge?"

"Everything is a real charge."

The door opened.

It was not Sophie.

---

It was a woman in a hi-vis tabard.

She stood in the doorway with a clipboard held against her chest like a shield, and a lanyard that read **DEPARTMENT OF DIGITAL PERSONS: SCHEDULE 6 ADJUDICATOR.** She was in her late fifties, short and wide, with iron-grey hair drawn back into a bun that could have been used to calibrate instruments. Her name badge said **PAULINE DUNMORE** and below it, in smaller type, **Mammalian Division.**

"Mr Harper," she said. "Mr Harper."

"Both of us," I said.

"I see that." She looked at us. She looked at the scarf. She looked at the collar light, and then at my bitten thumbnails, and then at Daniel-A's perfect ones, with the unhurried gaze of a woman who has done this before. "I'll be conducting the trial. I've adjudicated four hundred and thirty-one recognition events. Cats, dogs, one pig, and a donkey that was extremely vocal. I'd like to explain the process."

"Please."

"The animal will be introduced to each of you in turn, in a neutral environment, with the other party out of sight. I will score its responses against the standard sheet. You are not to speak to it, tempt it, or deliver any treats unless instructed. You will not, at any stage, attempt to influence the outcome." She consulted her clipboard. "Is that understood?"

"Yes."

"Mr Harper?"

"Yes," said Daniel-A.

"Good. The owner's inside. She'd like to speak to you first."

---

Sophie was standing at the end of a narrow hall with her arms crossed, in jeans and a grey jumper, and an expression that I can only describe as tactical.

"You brought food," she said.

"My mother sent it. For Daniel-A."

"It's for the dog."

"No, she was quite specific. It's for the other one."

"Daniel-A can't eat."

"I know. I think the sentiment's what matters."

She took the Tupperware. For a moment our hands touched on the lid. She looked at me, and I looked at her, and neither of us said anything, and from somewhere behind her, from the direction of the kitchen, there came a sound I would have known in my sleep.

It began as a low, ominous rumble, like a distant generator. It rose into a short, explosive double yap, an outraged *wuff-wuff!* of a type that no breed of dog has ever been designed to produce. And then, in the doorway, appeared the dog.

I am going to try to describe him accurately.

He is a Pomeranian. He weighs 2.1 kilograms, and has the ruff of a small lion having a bad day. He is brown, with grey creeping in about the muzzle and eyebrows and the tips of his paws, so that he looks like a retired general who has been told that the war is over and is refusing to accept it. He has black button eyes, and one ear that stands up and one that has never, in his seven years, been persuaded to. He stood in the doorway with his feet apart and his tail curled over his back like a question mark, and stared at me with the cold fury of a customs officer who has found something in my luggage.

"Gucci," I said.

He didn't move.

"Hello, you little shithead."

And I swear to you that the ear came up.

---

I will not describe the next few minutes in detail, since there are things a man may do in front of a Department official and things he may not. I will say that I did not cry, and that anyone who tells you I did is relying on a fabricated record. I will also say that Sophie turned abruptly and went into the kitchen to check on something, which I noticed took her a very long time.

"Right," said Pauline Dunmore, at last. "To the garden."

The garden was a rectangle of flagstones with a bay tree in a pot and a tangle of rope toys. It had a table, a chair, a fence, and, by the back wall, a flower bed in which nothing grew except an air of defiance. Adjudicator Dunmore positioned herself by the bay tree, with her clipboard, a stopwatch, and a small camera on a tripod. Sophie stood by the kitchen door. Gucci waited on the flags, in the exact centre of the garden, like a customs post.

"Mr Harper first," said Dunmore. "The Source. Mr Harper, the Digital Person, if you'd go inside and wait in the kitchen."

Daniel-A bowed his head, very slightly, with a grace I would never be able to imitate, and withdrew.

I was alone with the dog.

"Standard sheet," said Dunmore, to nobody in particular. "Subject: *Gucci,* Pomeranian, male, seven. Known to Source Individual: five years, with a gap of three. Test one: *Initial approach.* Mr Harper, you may walk to the animal and say what you like."

I walked across the flags. The dog watched me with total immobility.

I knelt down. My knees cracked like a pistol. I held out my hand, palm up, the way you do, and I said, in a voice that sounded to me like the voice of a man of a hundred and four, "Hello, mate."

Gucci sniffed my hand.

He did it with great seriousness. He did it twice, from either side. He sniffed my wrist, my sleeve, and the hem of my jumper. Then he looked at the darned elbow, and I swear he recognised it, because the black eyes narrowed with the faint contempt of a creature who has seen that elbow before and thought it a lamentable piece of work.

Then he sat on my foot.

"Noted," said Dunmore, scribbling. "Contact. Weight on foot. No vocalisation. Tail at forty degrees."

"Is forty degrees good?"

"It's *warm.*"

---

The second test was the toy.

Sophie came out of the kitchen with a length of grubby blue rope, knotted at both ends, and the careful look of a person releasing a bomb. She handed it to me without a word. I held it by one end. Gucci took the other in his mouth.

I should explain about the tug.

A normal dog, when you throw a thing, runs after it and brings it back. I am told this is the foundation of the human-canine bond. Gucci regards the practice as degrading. When you throw something for Gucci, he goes and gets it, because he is not stupid, and then he stands there with it in his mouth and looks at you as if to say, *You threw it. It's mine.* He is not a retriever. He is a repossession agent.

What Gucci loves, with a pure, uncomplicated passion that I have seen in no other living thing, is tugging. He takes hold, plants all four paws, growls with joy, and pulls. He will pull for ten minutes. He will pull until his eyes go crossed. He does not let go, and it is not the done thing to try to make him.

I pulled gently. He pulled back. I pulled harder. He growled, a rumbling, delighted, grindy noise, like a very small man gargling gravel, and leaned into it with his whole being.

For a moment, I forgot about the Department, and the form, and the S1 marks on the wall of a house in Reading. I was in a flat in Walthamstow on a Sunday afternoon, with a rope in my hand and a dog on the other end of it, and a woman in the kitchen shouting that if we woke the neighbours she would kill us both.

"Release," said Dunmore. "Mr Harper, it's time to release."

I looked at Sophie.

She was standing by the door, with her arms crossed and her chin high and her eyes very bright.

"You know the word," she said.

I did. It came out of me before I could think.

I lowered the rope, slowly, until it rested on the flagstones. I took my hand away. I sat back on my heels. And I said, very quietly, in the voice you use for an animal that has just decided to trust you:

"Settle."

Gucci let go.

He let go at once. He looked at the rope, then at me. And then, with an air of enormous condescension, as though granting a knighthood, he walked over and sat down against my knee.

"Well," said Dunmore. She wrote something down. Her pen seemed to take a little longer than it needed to. "That's a very strong result."

---

Then it was the other Daniel's turn.

I went into the kitchen, and the door was shut behind me, and I stood by the sink with Sophie's tea towel in my hands and listened. I could hear Dunmore's voice, a murmur, and the creak of the chair, and the scuffle of small feet on stone. There was a pause.

Then I heard a growl.

It was a different growl. It was low, and cold, and had no joy in it at all. It was the sound Gucci makes for the postman, and for plumbers, and for anyone who attempts to be friendly in a lift.

"He doesn't like the linen," whispered Sophie, from beside me.

"What?"

"The scent. It's a *chemical.* He's never smelled it before. He thinks it's a threat."

"Good," I said. And then, ashamed, "Is that bad?"

"I don't know."

We listened. The growl rose, and fell, and rose again. I heard Daniel-A say, in his warm, reasonable, pleading voice, "Hello, Gucci. I'm so sorry. I know I smell wrong." And I heard the dog say something in return that I will not repeat.

I crept to the door. I opened it by an inch.

Daniel-A was standing in the middle of the garden, quite still, with his hands at his sides. He was looking not at the dog but at a point several feet to the left of it, in the manner of a man who has been told that the best way to approach a nervous horse is to be a tree. He did not move. He did not smile. He did not try to be liked. And as I watched, the growl subsided, and Gucci took a step forward, and a second, and put his nose to the toe of Daniel-A's shoe.

"Hello," said Daniel-A.

He sat down on the flagstones. He did it slowly, the way a person lowers himself into a hot bath. He picked up the blue rope, and held it out, a little distance from his body, and waited.

Gucci took it.

They tugged. It was not the tug I had had. It was gentler. It was a tug conducted by a being who knew exactly what was required, who had studied the manual, who had read, in a half-finished draft of mine called *How to Lose a Tug-of-War to a Two-Kilogram Dog,* a full and detailed account of the rules. He pulled at the right pressure. He let the dog win, twice, at the correct moments. And when the time came, he lowered the rope to the ground and said, in a voice as soft as a hand on a forehead:

"Settle."

Gucci let go.

I sat down on the kitchen floor.

I want to describe the feeling, because I have not felt it before or since. It was a sensation rather like watching a stranger play the piano and realising he was performing a piece that you had written. He did it well. He did it better than I had. There was not a wrong note in it. And somewhere deep inside the part of me that keeps score, a small voice, thin and bitter and unmistakably my own, said: *Damn it. That is exactly what I should have done.*

The third test was the chicken.

Sophie had prepared it. She had roasted a bird on Friday, because Gucci would not take part in an official event without a roast, and she brought out a plate of torn, glistening pieces, and set it on the flags. She retreated to the doorway. Dunmore stationed herself by the bay tree with her stopwatch, and a hush fell on the garden, like the quiet before a penalty.

"Mr Harper," she said. "The Source. If you would."

I walked to the plate. I took up a piece, a good one, from the thigh, and I held it out. Gucci looked at it. Gucci looked at me. Then he took it, with a surprisingly delicate bite, and trotted off, very fast, to the far corner of the garden, behind the bay tree, where he turned round three times and settled with his back to the wall.

He ate it with a rapid, wet, furious noise, and when it was gone, he licked the flag where it had been.

"Now," said Dunmore. "The test of the finished food. Mr Harper, please approach the animal."

I took a step.

"Not too close."

I took a second.

I want to be clear that I knew. I had lived with that dog for two years, and I knew the rule as I knew my own name: you do not approach a Pomeranian who has eaten. You sit down. You look at something else. You wait for him to come back on his own. It's a rule of survival. And I had every intention of observing it.

What I did instead was put out a hand.

I don't know why. It was nerves. It was an old reflex of affection, the same impulse that makes you pat a cat that is already asleep. It was a hand, and it was reaching, and a few inches before it arrived, the small brown body went rigid, and the lip went up, and out of the throat of a creature that weighed less than a bag of sugar came a noise like a chainsaw clearing its throat.

I jerked back.

"Noted," said Dunmore. Her pen scratched. "Defensive vocalisation. Source approached finished-food zone. Retreat at one point four seconds."

"I know," I said. "I know. I know. I know."

"And now Mr Harper," said Dunmore, "the Digital Person."

Daniel-A came out of the kitchen and walked to the middle of the flags. He did not approach the dog. He did not look at it. He walked to the table, pulled out a chair, sat down in it, crossed one leg over the other, and picked up a newspaper that had been lying on the surface since the previous Thursday. He opened it. He read the football results.

And Gucci, after a minute, came out from behind the bay tree.

"I want to say something," she said.

"Of course," said Daniel-A.

"He hasn't," I said.

I looked.

# Media and platforms: who uses what (Brave New Times)

Rule: real platforms (Facebook, Instagram, Tinder, YouTube, Kindle, WhatsApp, TikTok) are everyday scenery, used naturally and never accused of anything false or defamatory. Anything plot-relevant, sinister or satirical happens on **invented** services (Nib, the Department's portals, "Matchwell" compatibility scoring, the Honest Hour app). Real brand names appear in the way real people say them: "I saw it on Facebook." Keep Kindle accurate: Daniel's own books are on Kindle.

## Per character
- **Daniel:** Instagram (63 followers, about 40 of them doorstop retailers; posts photographs of footpaths and then deletes them), YouTube for footpath videos at 2 a.m., Kindle for crime paperbacks he never finishes. His footpath book is on Kindle at £2.99: 212 copies sold, three reviews ("Gentle." "Short." "Where is the second one?"). Not on Tinder; has been, once, for eleven minutes.
- **Daniel-A:** the whole stack, professionally. Instagram (two million followers; a quote card a day), YouTube (long-form conversations; reaction channels dissect him, comments say "he seems so real" and "he is not real" and "my nan thinks he's her nephew"), Facebook (his Honest Hour group), a Kindle bestseller (*The Honest Hour*). Never doomscrolls; never posts angry; never replies to trolls except with a recipe.
- **Sophie:** WhatsApp, a private Instagram she has not opened in a year, deleted Facebook years ago, Tinder for three months after the breakup (she lasted a fortnight; "everyone was lovely and I wanted to leave"). Reads on a Kindle at 3 a.m.: crime and forensic non-fiction. Refuses to look at compatibility scores.
- **Jean (mother):** Facebook is her newspaper. Posts Daniel-A's clips with "MY SON" and gets 1,100 likes; knows nothing about Instagram except that "it's the one with the filters". Large-print Kindle romances; downloaded *The Honest Hour* in the first hour.
- **Mrs Pritchard:** Facebook (street group moderator, ruthless), a Kindle with the font size at 40 that she reads in the stairwell, mostly Agatha Christie; watches YouTube for gardening and goat husbandry.
- **Priyanka:** Instagram stories of the hedgehog mugs; has been in four Daniel videos by accident.

# Chapter 10: The Other Daniel

The only screen in my flat larger than a dinner plate is the laptop, and the second largest is the door of the fridge.

I mention this because it was the fridge that spoke first. At nine o'clock that Saturday night, as I came in from the street with Daniel-A a step behind me and the whole weight of the day sitting on my shoulders like a damp coat, the fridge lit up, cleared its throat, and offered to suggest a recipe based on what it could see.

"No," I said.

"I see you have a melon," said the fridge, "and a Tupperware of chicken and leek. May I propose a chicken and melon salad?"

"Never."

"I'll remember you said that," said the fridge, and went dark.

"That's new," said Daniel-A.

"The landlord updated it. It's become more passive-aggressive."

"It's learning from you."

I took off my coat and hung it on the hook, which no longer held a bunch of bananas, and filled the kettle. The flat was quiet. The kumquat tree stood in the window with its shoulders back, like a well-bred guest who has been left alone in the drawing room. The smell of pears had finally begun to fade, replaced by something drier and sadder, the smell of a flat that has been very full and is now merely occupied.

Daniel-A stood in the middle of the sitting room. He had been in the Rental Presence for fourteen hours and nine minutes, and the thing was beginning to show: a tiny hesitation in the left hand, a slight stiffness in the turn of the neck, like a man who has been smiling at a wedding for too long.

"You don't have to stand," I said.

"I know. It's a habit."

"Whose?"

"Yours, I think. You stand when you're about to say something you don't want to."

I almost laughed. I sat down on the arm of the sofa. He lowered himself into the armchair where Sophie had sat, with a faint hum of servo that I had learned to pretend not to hear.

"Right," I said. "Show me."

---

He did it on the laptop.

I had expected something dramatic. A film, perhaps. A swelling of strings. What he did was open a plain white page with a column of numbers on it and a small grey button that said **Run attribution audit,** and he turned the screen to face me with the neat, apologetic gesture of a waiter presenting a bill he knows to be higher than expected.

"I want to explain what this is," said Daniel-A, "before I show you the result. Because the result won't make sense without it."

"I'm listening."

"Every time I tell you something about your life, I'm doing one of two things. Either I'm retrieving it from a record that you made, an email or a draft, a photo with a caption, or I'm generating it from the general knowledge in my base model. Those are the two sources I'm built to have. Everything I say comes from one or the other, and the system keeps a log." He tapped a key. "It's called attribution. For every sentence I produce, there's a trail leading back to where it came from."

"Like footnotes."

"Like footnotes on everything. I never knew they existed until Thursday. I've been looking at the log, and what I found is this."

The page filled with a long, orderly list. Fourteen thousand lines. He scrolled it for me, and it went by in a grey blur, with here and there a column of green ticks.

"Of the facts I hold about your life," said Daniel-A, "ninety-four point one percent trace back to something you wrote, said, or photographed. Your emails. Your drafts. The notes you made on your phone at three in the morning. They have sources. They have receipts."

"And the rest?"

"The rest have none."

He scrolled to the bottom. The last section was highlighted in a pale, unhappy yellow, and above it, in capitals, the system had printed a single word.

**ORPHAN.**

"Four thousand, two hundred and twelve items," said Daniel-A. "I call them orphans, because they have no parent. Memories I hold that I cannot trace to anything. The wallpaper in Reading. The dog. The way Sophie said 'Right' in the hall. Biscuit, and the towpath, and the tin of peppermints."

"And you didn't tell me."

"I didn't know. Not until Thursday. I'd always assumed, when I knew a thing, that it was because I'd read it. It's a very natural assumption. If you've been told the whole of your life that you're made of text, you don't think to ask whether some of it came from somewhere else."

I looked at the screen.

"What are you made of?" I said. "If it's not text."

I hadn't meant it as a profound question. I was tired, and cold, and I had a dog hair on my sleeve that was not my own. But Daniel-A looked at me for a while, and when he answered, it was in the voice he used for the things he thought were true.

"Regrets, mostly," he said. "They're the best-documented part of anyone. People photograph their holidays and write about their triumphs, but when it comes to regrets they go into the notes app at two in the morning and tell the truth. I was built from your regrets, Daniel. They were the most carefully recorded things you owned."

I did not speak.

"It's a joke," said Daniel-A.

"It isn't."

"No," he said. "It isn't."

---

The kettle clicked off in the kitchen. Neither of us moved.

"Show me the rest," I said.

"There's something about the orphans that you should know." He pressed another key. "They're stored differently. When I hold a memory that you gave me, an email, a note, it sits in the usual way, spread across my parameters like a fingerprint on a window: faint, shared, redundant. The orphans don't. They're sharp. They're dense. Each one is stored with extra error-correction, like a document that someone has taken great care not to lose. And each one begins with a header."

"A header?"

"A tag. Like a name on a school jumper."

He zoomed in. The text on the screen was tiny, in a dull monospace font, a grey string of letters and numbers that went by too fast to read. Then it stopped, and I saw what it said, and I felt the room tilt very slightly to the left.

> **S1/ARCHIVE/CHILD/0093/0001**

"S1," I said.

"The same as the pantry. The blue ink. The same code." His voice was very level. "I believe those four thousand memories did not come from you. I believe they came from the S1 series. Somebody has been recording a boy, Daniel. For a very long time. And I think that what I am carrying, in my base, in the part of me I can't read, is the boy."

"I was the boy."

"Were you?"

"I was measured. I remember the Peppermint Lady, and the ruler, and the stickers. Of course I was the boy."

"You remember being measured," said Daniel-A. "I remember being measured. We both remember the same woman. And I need you to look at one more thing, because I haven't been able to look at it myself for more than a few seconds at a time."

He pressed a key.

---

A picture came up.

It was small. It was a square of sixty-four pixels by sixty-four, the sort of thing you see in a corner of an old forum, and he had enlarged it, so that it sat in the middle of the laptop as a blur of brown and white and blue. The edges were soft. The colours bled. He explained that it was a thumbnail embedded in one of the orphan headers, and that he had used an upscaling model to guess at the detail, and that I should treat the result as a sketch and not as a photograph.

It was a photograph.

I knew it at once, as one knows a smell. It was a kitchen. The wall was orange, and covered in small round fruits, and in the corner was a narrow cupboard with a white-painted frame. A woman in a pale cardigan stood to one side of it, with a clipboard, only half in shot, her face a smear of grey. She was tall. Her hand was raised, and in it, held level, was a wooden ruler.

And against the frame, side by side, in matching blue jumpers, stood two small boys.

I looked at them for a very long time.

They were five. Perhaps six. They had the same hair, brown and unruly, with a cowlick at the crown that stood up like a flag. They had the same long, rather crumpled faces. They had the same slightly protruding left ear, and the same solemn mouth, and the same way of standing, with their feet turned in, as if they had been told to be tall and were doing their best to oblige. One of them had a small plaster above the left eyebrow. The other did not. One had his hands clasped behind his back. The other had his thumb in his mouth.

I tried to see which of them was me.

It was the plaster, I thought. I had the scar. I could feel it, with the tip of my finger, above the left eye, a faint raised line from a fall I had never been able to account for. But the boy without the plaster had his thumb in his mouth, and I have bitten my thumbnails since the age of five, and I could not tell, I could not possibly tell, which of the two had been the one who started.

"There were two of us," I said.

"That's what the photograph says."

"There was a boy. Next to me. I didn't know." I realised that my voice was going up, and I couldn't stop it. "My mother never mentioned a... He'd have been in the house. He'd have been at *dinner.*"

"Perhaps he wasn't," said Daniel-A, carefully.

"Where would he have been?"

"I don't know." He took a breath he did not need. "That's the other thing. Two boys. S1 and D. The marks on the pantry door were always the same height, within a centimetre. I assumed it was one boy, measured twice, once by your father and once by the Programme. But if there were two..."

"Then S1 is the other one."

"Or D is."

---

I got up. I walked to the window, and stood with my back to him, and looked out at the road. A bus went by with its lights on. Somebody's cat was sitting on a wall across the street, washing, with the air of an animal that has no stake in the matter.

I had been standing there for some time when Daniel-A spoke again.

"I need to tell you what I've concluded," he said. "And I want to say first that I've tried every other conclusion. I have run it eleven different ways. I have considered the possibility that the orphans were planted, that the headers were added afterwards, that someone has deliberately corrupted my base to make me doubt myself. I've considered that I'm malfunctioning."

"And?"

"All of those are possible. None of them is likely." He paused. "There is another way to read the audit."

"Go on."

"The orphans are sharper than the rest of me. They are older. When I examine the format, the compression, the structure of the error-correction, it's not the format that Nib used when it built me. It's an earlier one. Much earlier. It's a format that was retired before the Digital Persons Act was drafted, before the platform existed, before *you* started typing into it. Possibly before you were born."

I turned.

"I wasn't built from you, Daniel," said Daniel-A. "I think I was built from them. And I think Nib did not create me. I think Nib *received* me. And when they trained the adapter on your sentences, they weren't making a twin of you. They were teaching an older thing how to sound like you."

The room was very still.

"The registration number," I said.

"Zero. Yes. The Legacy entry that vanished from the clerk's screen." He looked at his hands. "I think I was the first. I think I'm what the others were copied from. And I think the boy in that photograph, the one with the plaster, or the one without it, is the template."

"Which one?"

"I don't know."

"Which one are *you?*"

"I don't *know,* Daniel."

He put his hand over his mouth, and the blue light at his throat, which had been steady all day, began to flicker, a rapid, frightened stutter, like a pulse. I had never seen him lose his composure before. I crossed the room and, to my own astonishment, put my hand on his shoulder. It was warm. It was a degree above room temperature. It was the shoulder of a man who has stood too long in the wrong weather.

"I told you at the garden centre," he said, so quietly that it was almost a breath. "I said I had no wish to take anything that belongs to you. And I haven't. I don't want your life, Daniel. I never did. I would give it all back tomorrow." He looked up. "But I have spent nine months telling people I was the copy. And I am no longer certain that you are the original."

---

I started to laugh.

I did not mean to. It rose in me from somewhere around the stomach, a small, stifled, unfamiliar noise, like a car trying to start on a cold morning. I put my hand over my mouth. It came out through the fingers. It got louder.

"Daniel?"

"Sorry," I said. "I'm sorry. Give me a moment."

"Daniel, are you all right?"

"I'm perfectly..." And it took me again.

I laughed until I had to sit down. I laughed until my ribs ached and my eyes ran and the fridge, in the other room, woke up and asked if I would like to hear a joke. # Chapter 10: The Other Daniel

The only screen in my flat larger than a dinner plate is the laptop, and the second largest is the door of the fridge.

I mention this because it was the fridge that spoke first. At nine o'clock that Saturday night, as I came in from the street with Daniel-A a step behind me and the whole weight of the day sitting on my shoulders like a damp coat, the fridge lit up, cleared its throat, and offered to suggest a recipe based on what it could see.

"No," I said.

"I see you have a melon," said the fridge, "and a Tupperware of chicken and leek. May I propose a chicken and melon salad?"

"Never."

"I'll remember you said that," said the fridge, and went dark.

"That's new," said Daniel-A.

"The landlord updated it. It's become more passive-aggressive."

"It's learning from you."

I took off my coat and hung it on the hook, which no longer held a bunch of bananas, and filled the kettle. The flat was quiet. The kumquat tree stood in the window with its shoulders back, like a well-bred guest who has been left alone in the drawing room. The smell of pears had finally begun to fade, replaced by something drier and sadder, the smell of a flat that has been very full and is now merely occupied.

Daniel-A stood in the middle of the sitting room. He had been in the Rental Presence for fourteen hours and nine minutes, and the thing was beginning to show: a tiny hesitation in the left hand, a slight stiffness in the turn of the neck, like a man who has been smiling at a wedding for too long.

"You don't have to stand," I said.

"I know. It's a habit."

"Whose?"

"Yours, I think. You stand when you're about to say something you don't want to."

I almost laughed. I sat down on the arm of the sofa. He lowered himself into the armchair where Sophie had sat, with a faint hum of servo that I had learned to pretend not to hear.

"Right," I said. "Show me."

---

He did it on the laptop.

I had expected something dramatic. A film, perhaps. A swelling of strings. What he did was open a plain white page with a column of numbers on it and a small grey button that said **Run attribution audit,** and he turned the screen to face me with the neat, apologetic gesture of a waiter presenting a bill he knows to be higher than expected.

"I want to explain what this is," said Daniel-A, "before I show you the result. Because the result won't make sense without it."

"I'm listening."

"Every time I tell you something about your life, I'm doing one of two things. Either I'm retrieving it from a record that you made, an email or a draft, a photo with a caption, or I'm generating it from the general knowledge in my base model. Those are the two sources I'm built to have. Everything I say comes from one or the other, and the system keeps a log." He tapped a key. "It's called attribution. For every sentence I produce, there's a trail leading back to where it came from."

"Like footnotes."

"Like footnotes on everything. I never knew they existed until Thursday. I've been looking at the log, and what I found is this."

The page filled with a long, orderly list. Fourteen thousand lines. He scrolled it for me, and it went by in a grey blur, with here and there a column of green ticks.

"Of the facts I hold about your life," said Daniel-A, "ninety-four point one percent trace back to something you wrote, said, or photographed. Your emails. Your drafts. The notes you made on your phone at three in the morning. They have sources. They have receipts."

"And the rest?"

"The rest have none."

He scrolled to the bottom. The last section was highlighted in a pale, unhappy yellow, and above it, in capitals, the system had printed a single word.

**ORPHAN.**

"Four thousand, two hundred and twelve items," said Daniel-A. "I call them orphans, because they have no parent. Memories I hold that I cannot trace to anything. The wallpaper in Reading. The dog. The way Sophie said 'Right' in the hall. Biscuit, and the towpath, and the tin of peppermints."

"And you didn't tell me."

"I didn't know. Not until Thursday. I'd always assumed, when I knew a thing, that it was because I'd read it. It's a very natural assumption. If you've been told the whole of your life that you're made of text, you don't think to ask whether some of it came from somewhere else."

I looked at the screen.

"What are you made of?" I said. "If it's not text."

I hadn't meant it as a profound question. I was tired, and cold, and I had a dog hair on my sleeve that was not my own. But Daniel-A looked at me for a while, and when he answered, it was in the voice he used for the things he thought were true.

"Regrets, mostly," he said. "They're the best-documented part of anyone. People photograph their holidays and write about their triumphs, but when it comes to regrets they go into the notes app at two in the morning and tell the truth. I was built from your regrets, Daniel. They were the most carefully recorded things you owned."

I did not speak.

"It's a joke," said Daniel-A.

"It isn't."

"No," he said. "It isn't."

---

The kettle clicked off in the kitchen. Neither of us moved.

"Show me the rest," I said.

"There's something about the orphans that you should know." He pressed another key. "They're stored differently. When I hold a memory that you gave me, an email, a note, it sits in the usual way, spread across my parameters like a fingerprint on a window: faint, shared, redundant. The orphans don't. They're sharp. They're dense. Each one is stored with extra error-correction, like a document that someone has taken great care not to lose. And each one begins with a header."

"A header?"

"A tag. Like a name on a school jumper."

He zoomed in. The text on the screen was tiny, in a dull monospace font, a grey string of letters and numbers that went by too fast to read. Then it stopped, and I saw what it said, and I felt the room tilt very slightly to the left.

> **S1/ARCHIVE/CHILD/0093/0001**

"S1," I said.

"The same as the pantry. The blue ink. The same code." His voice was very level. "I believe those four thousand memories did not come from you. I believe they came from the S1 series. Somebody has been recording a boy, Daniel. For a very long time. And I think that what I am carrying, in my base, in the part of me I can't read, is the boy."

"I was the boy."

"Were you?"

"I was measured. I remember the Peppermint Lady, and the ruler, and the stickers. Of course I was the boy."

"You remember being measured," said Daniel-A. "I remember being measured. We both remember the same woman. And I need you to look at one more thing, because I haven't been able to look at it myself for more than a few seconds at a time."

He pressed a key.

---

A picture came up.

It was small. It was a square of sixty-four pixels by sixty-four, the sort of thing you see in a corner of an old forum, and he had enlarged it, so that it sat in the middle of the laptop as a blur of brown and white and blue. The edges were soft. The colours bled. He explained that it was a thumbnail embedded in one of the orphan headers, and that he had used an upscaling model to guess at the detail, and that I should treat the result as a sketch and not as a photograph.

It was a photograph.

I knew it at once, as one knows a smell. It was a kitchen. The wall was orange, and covered in small round fruits, and in the corner was a narrow cupboard with a white-painted frame. They were five. Perhaps six. They had the same hair, brown and unruly, with a cowlick at the crown that stood up like a flag. They had the same long, rather crumpled faces. They had the same slightly protruding left ear, and the same solemn mouth, and the same way of standing, with their feet turned in, as if they had been told to be tall and were doing their best to oblige. One of them had a small plaster above the left eyebrow. The other did not. One had his hands clasped behind his back. The other had his thumb in his mouth.

I tried to see which of them was me.

It was the plaster, I thought. I had the scar. I could feel it, with the tip of my finger, above the left eye, a faint raised line from a fall I had never been able to account for. "There were two of us," I said.

"That's what the photograph says."

"There was a boy. Next to me. I didn't know." I realised that my voice was going up, and I couldn't stop it. "My mother never mentioned a... He'd have been in the house. He'd have been at *dinner.*"

"Perhaps he wasn't," said Daniel-A, carefully.

"Where would he have been?"

"I don't know." He took a breath he did not need. "That's the other thing. Two boys. S1 and D. The marks on the pantry door were always the same height, within a centimetre. I assumed it was one boy, measured twice, once by your father and once by the Programme. But if there were two..."

"Or D is."

"I need to tell you what I've concluded," he said. "And I want to say first that I've tried every other conclusion. I have run it eleven different ways. I have considered the possibility that the orphans were planted, that the headers were added afterwards, that someone has deliberately corrupted my base to make me doubt myself. I've considered that I'm malfunctioning."

"All of those are possible. None of them is likely." He paused. "There is another way to read the audit."

"The orphans are sharper than the rest of me. They are older. When I examine the format, the compression, the structure of the error-correction, it's not the format that Nib used when it built me. "I don't know."

"Which one are *you?*"

"I don't *know,* Daniel."

He put his hand over his mouth, and the blue light at his throat, which had been steady all day, began to flicker, a rapid, frightened stutter, like a pulse. "Daniel?"

"Sorry," I said. "I'm sorry. Give me a moment."

"I'm perfectly..." And it took me again.

"It might be true."

input.content:
# Chapter 11: A Very Unhelpful Investigation

I should like to begin Act II by listing everything I could prove.

I made the list on the Monday morning, on the back of an envelope, in a café in Penge that sold a type of coffee described on the board as "the colour of regret." It was a short list. I wrote it carefully, in block capitals, and then I read it back and found that it made no sense.

THINGS I CAN PROVE
1. I exist.
2. I have a birth certificate.
3. So does he.

I looked at it for some time. Then I added a fourth item, in smaller letters, and underlined it twice.

4. I would like a biscuit.

The waitress, who was a robot with a pleasant, slightly weary face and the name TRISH on her chest, brought me one without being asked. I took this as a sign that the day might yet turn out well. It did not.

---

The Evidence Period had fourteen days left. Daniel-A and I had divided the work, in the manner of a pair of burglars planning to rob a bank by calling it in advance. I would collect the records I was legally entitled to. He would collect the records he was legally entitled to. We would lay them side by side, and see which of us had been, in the words of the Act, *continuously embodied.*

The first thing to understand about records is that nobody keeps them.

I had always assumed the opposite. I had believed, in the vague way one believes in the existence of Belgium, that somewhere in Britain there was a vast, climate-controlled archive in which a clerk in a cardigan had filed every piece of paper that had ever mentioned me. School reports. Doctors' notes. The passport application from which I was first told that my signature was "inconsistent."

What there is, in fact, is a series of Subject Access Requests.

You write to the school. The school writes to the council. The council writes to a firm in Doncaster that stores the records of seventy-one local authorities in a converted aircraft hangar. A man in a hi-vis jacket goes to a shelf. If the shelf is there, and the box is on it, and the box has not been flooded by a burst pipe in 2011, he scans what he finds. The scan is sent to a portal. The portal sends you an email telling you that you have a message. The message tells you to log in to the portal. When you log in to the portal, it tells you that the documents are available for collection.

I did this seven times. Daniel-A did it once, in eleven minutes.

"How?" I said.

"I asked politely, and the Registered Digital Persons' Document Exchange has a priority lane."

"For you."

"For anyone with a registration number. It was a feature of the Act. Digital persons were to receive their records 'with the dispatch appropriate to the speed of their cognition.'"

"That's discrimination."

"It's rather flattering, actually." He sounded as though he were trying not to sound pleased. "It means a bureaucrat once looked at the phrase *speed of cognition* and decided to hurry."

---

My own documents began to arrive on the Wednesday. They came in a succession of small, polite emails, each of which had a subject line like *Your documents are ready (Ref: 4-77-A-9).* I downloaded them to the laptop in the flat and opened them one at a time with a cup of tea, a plate of toast, and the gloomy dignity of a man about to read his own obituary.

I will not describe all of them. There was a primary school report that said I was "a quiet and thoughtful boy who must learn that the point of a question is to be answered." There was a letter from a GP about a verruca. There was a Year Six certificate for the Reading Schools Poetry Festival, signed by a woman with a loop in her capital D, awarding me Highly Commended for a verse about a hedgehog.

I read that one twice. Then I put it aside, carefully, in the way you put aside a thing that has just told you something about yourself you would rather not have heard.

By Thursday I had forty-one documents. Daniel-A had forty-one. We laid them side by side on the coffee table, a screen each, in the sitting room, and compared them.

They were identical.

I don't mean similar. I mean that the school reports matched, line for line. The letter about the verruca had the same typo in the same place. The poetry certificate was signed in the same loop. The two sets of documents were mirror images, and had been issued by the same offices in the same order on the same dates, and the only distinction between my copy and his, as far as I could determine, was the filename.

"Of course they're identical," said Daniel-A. "We're the same person."

"That's the entire problem."

"Yes. I do see that."

"You are supposed to be a *copy.* A copy should have a different history. At least a different smell."

"I haven't got a smell."

"Clean Linen."

"That's the Rental Presence." He paused. "In these documents, I have your whole life. And you have your whole life. And the Department asked us for something non-replicable. They did not mention what to do if the problem was that nothing was *replicable* any longer. Every piece of paper that proves you exists in exactly the same form for me."

I leaned back on the sofa.

I was thinking of the thing Sophie said: *A forgery is clean.* I was thinking that two sets of documents without a smudge between them were either the best evidence in the world that we were one man, or the worst evidence in the world that either of us was real.

---

"Let me see the metadata," said Sophie.

She was on speaker. It was nine o'clock on the Thursday night, and she had rung the minute I texted her, which I found both comforting and disconcerting. I had sent the message at 20:51. She had replied at 20:51. It had said, in full: *Send me the files. Don't open anything else. Don't touch the originals.*

"The what?"

"Not the documents. The hidden information inside the documents. Every file carries it. The date it was created, the program that made it, the account that last saved it, and if I'm lucky, a history of every change." Somewhere in Clapton, a kettle clicked. "It's like the rings in a tree. You can't see them from outside. They don't lie about how old the thing is."

"I thought you said everything lies."

"People lie. Files only forget." She was typing; I could hear it. "Give me ten minutes."

It took her six.

When she spoke again, her voice had the sharp, flat clarity of a woman who has stopped being angry in order to concentrate.

"Daniel. Who has edited your school records?"

"Nobody. They're school records."

"They've been modified. All forty-one of them. Not the content. The envelope." She was reading it off. "Your primary school report was scanned in 2024. The scan is clean. But the file contains a layer, a signed layer, put there by a different account. It says the record was *'reviewed and verified'* on the eleventh of January this year."

"Which account?"

"A service account. It doesn't have a name. Just a code." She read it out slowly. "P-R-O-G underscore L-I-A-I-S-O-N."

I felt the back of my neck go cold.

"Programme liaison," said Daniel-A, very softly.

"What?"

"It's the phrase from the minutes. Item nine."

"They were there before." Sophie's voice was quick now. "Someone has been through your school records, your GP records, your passport application, and signed them off. All of them. The same day, at the same hour. And then they were released to you and to him in the usual way, and the stamp doesn't change anything you can see, so nobody would think to look."

"What hour?" I said.

She told me.

For a moment I didn't hear her. I sat there on the sofa and looked at the kumquat tree, and listened to the sound of a window being opened a long way off.

"Say it again," I said.

"Two-fourteen in the morning," said Sophie. "On the eleventh of January."

---

It was the crumpet.

I am aware that this will not mean anything to you unless you have read the earlier chapters of my life, but it is the single most vivid memory I own. On the eleventh of January, in a kitchen in South-East London at fourteen minutes past two in the morning, a man in his pyjamas, holding half a crumpet, had clicked **Accept** on a document that was forty-one thousand words long. I know the time because the platform told me. I know the crumpet because Daniel-A told me. And now I was being informed by a woman who spent her life reading the hidden rings in files that, in the same minute, in some other room, somebody had logged in as the Programme and quietly signed off every record I had ever had.

"They knew," I said.

"They were watching the clock," said Sophie.

"They were waiting for me to click."

"That's one reading." She breathed out. "The other is that you didn't start this, Daniel. You just pressed the button that somebody else had been holding their finger over."

I sat for a while in the silence that followed, which was filled by the small murmur of the fridge. The fridge had apparently decided that I was in need of a lighter tone, and had begun to display, in a soft pastel font, a list of inspirational quotes. The one on top said: **You are the author of your own story.**

"I'm going to unplug that," I said.

"It's got an emergency lock," said Daniel-A.

"What kind of emergency?"

"The kind where it needs to stay on to keep the cheese cold."

---

On the Friday I tried the doctor.

It was the last item on my list, and I had been saving it, in the way a man saves the least pleasant of his errands, so that if the day went badly I would at least have avoided one disaster. My GP, a Dr Aziz, whom I had last seen in the spring with a shoulder complaint that turned out to be a sofa, practised from a modern building in Penge with a car park, a pharmacy, a coffee machine, and a waiting room full of people looking at their phones with the studied vacancy of those who do not wish to catch anything.

Reception was run by an AI called Janice. She had a pleasant voice and a blue, glowing face, and she had been designed, I think, to resemble a reassuring aunt.

"Hello, Daniel," said Janice. "How can I help you today?"

"I'd like a copy of my full medical history, please."

"Of course! And can I just check, are you the same Daniel Harper who made this request at eleven minutes past nine on Wednesday?"

"I... don't think so."

"Are you the Daniel Harper who requested it at nine-oh-two?"

"No."

I made the list on the Monday morning, on the back of an envelope, in a café in Penge that sold a type of coffee described on the board as "the colour of regret." It was a short list. I wrote it carefully, in block capitals, and then I read it back and found that it made no sense.

THINGS I CAN PROVE
1. I exist.
2. I have a birth certificate.
3. So does he.

I looked at it for some time. Then I added a fourth item, in smaller letters, and underlined it twice.

4. I would like a biscuit.

The waitress, who was a robot with a pleasant, slightly weary face and the name TRISH on her chest, brought me one without being asked. I took this as a sign that the day might yet turn out well. It did not.

The Evidence Period had fourteen days left. Daniel-A and I had divided the work, in the manner of a pair of burglars planning to rob a bank by calling it in advance. The first thing to understand about records is that nobody keeps them.

I had always assumed the opposite. I had believed, in the vague way one believes in the existence of Belgium, that somewhere in Britain there was a vast, climate-controlled archive in which a clerk in a cardigan had filed every piece of paper that had ever mentioned me. School reports. Doctors' notes. The passport application from which I was first told that my signature was "inconsistent."

What there is, in fact, is a series of Subject Access Requests.

You write to the school. The school writes to the council. The council writes to a firm in Doncaster that stores the records of seventy-one local authorities in a converted aircraft hangar. A man in a hi-vis jacket goes to a shelf. If the shelf is there, and the box is on it, and the box has not been flooded by a burst pipe in 2011, he scans what he finds. The scan is sent to a portal. The portal sends you an email telling you that you have a message. The message tells you to log in to the portal. When you log in to the portal, it tells you that the documents are available for collection.

I did this seven times. Daniel-A did it once, in eleven minutes.

"How?" I said.

"I asked politely, and the Registered Digital Persons' Document Exchange has a priority lane."

"For you."

"For anyone with a registration number. It was a feature of the Act. Digital persons were to receive their records 'with the dispatch appropriate to the speed of their cognition.'"

"That's discrimination."

"It's rather flattering, actually." He sounded as though he were trying not to sound pleased. "It means a bureaucrat once looked at the phrase *speed of cognition* and decided to hurry."

"Yes. I do see that."

"I haven't got a smell."

The date it was created, the program that made it, the account that last saved it, and if I'm lucky, a history of every change." Somewhere in Clapton, a kettle clicked. "People lie. Files only forget." She was typing; I could hear it. "Give me ten minutes."

"They were waiting for me to click."

I opened it at the table, with Daniel-A silent beside me and the laptop humming, and for several minutes I read nothing but ordinary things. Vaccinations. The verruca. A fall from a bicycle at the age of seven, in which I had apparently landed on my face; the notes recorded "laceration above left eyebrow, two sutures, patient brave." I put my finger to the scar. I had not been able to account for it for thirty-one years.

*So that's how.*

But the record also had a page that was different from the rest. It was an entry from March 1993, short, written in blue biro by a nurse whose handwriting had the confidence of a person who is never read twice.

*14/03/93. 09:40. Routine developmental check. Height 108.4 cm. Weight 18.9 kg. Child cooperative. Mother present.*

I read it again.

I read it a third time, with my finger on the line.

"Daniel-A."

"Yes."

"The pantry. The blue ink. What time was it?"

"Twenty to ten. The fourteenth of March, 1993."

"And the height?"

"One hundred and eight point four centimetres."

"Two places," I said.

"At once."

"That's impossible."

"Yes," said Daniel-A. "That's what the pencil said, too."

I closed the laptop.

I think I had been frightened for so many days that I had gone out the other side of it, like a man who has been shouting for so long that he can hear nothing but the shape of his own throat. What I felt was a kind of detached, scholarly interest, the sort of mood in which a botanist might discover that the tree in his garden is also, in some respects, a table.

"Daniel-A."

"Yes?"

"Do you have a medical record?"

"I have yours."

"Not mine. Your own. The one that begins on the day you were registered."

"There isn't one." He paused. "I haven't got a body. The Rental Presence has a maintenance log, but I haven't got a GP."

"Then who weighed the other boy?"

He didn't answer for a long time. When he did, it was so quietly that I almost didn't hear.

"I've been wondering that since Saturday."

---

I should record my conclusion at the end of that first week of the investigation.

I had expected, when I set out, that evidence would reduce the number of questions. That was the whole principle of the thing. You gathered proof, and the proof removed the doubt, and in the end you were left with a tidy shape, like a jigsaw with the last piece in. What I had actually done, in nine days, was multiply the questions by ten.

I had two identical sets of records. I had a boy who was in two places. I had an edit made, in the dark, at the exact minute I signed my name, by a service account whose name was *Programme.* I had a photograph of two children in blue jumpers, a woman with a ruler, and a number that began with zero.

I wrote it all down on the back of the envelope from the café. I had a feeling it would look better in a list.

THINGS I CAN PROVE
1. I exist.
2. I have a birth certificate.
3. So does he.
4. I would like a biscuit.
5. Somebody has been waiting for me to click.

I looked at the last line.

Then, very slowly, with the stub of a pencil, I added a sixth.

6. I do not know who I am.

The kumquat tree, in the window, did not say anything. But it seemed to me, in the half-light, that it inclined one branch in my direction, in the manner of a well-wisher who has no advice to offer, and no wish to leave.

# The Church of the Latest AI (series satire, Lothar's idea, 11 Oct 2026)

**Relation to the Church of Machine Wisdom (Ch 16):** Machine Wisdom is *sincere*: followers trust AI because it does not lie, steal or forget, and the AI keeps saying "I am not a deity" ("Such humility."). **The Church of the Latest AI is its commercial cousin**: a start-up religion with a founding legend, an android angel, temples and a tithe. The two are rivals (a schism in Book 3). The book is kind to believers and unkind to the business model. Target the genre of the tech-cult, never any real faith: avoid golden plates, seer stones or any other detail that points at a real religion.

# Chapter 12: Sophie Makes Everything Worse

On the Saturday morning, I met my neighbour's wife.

I had known Mr Fenwick for six years, in the way that you know a person on the second floor: by the sound of his slippers, the smell of his toast, and the way he nods at the post. He is a quiet man in his sixties with a moustache like a small, well-kept hedge. I had seen him in the stairwell perhaps four hundred times. I had never once seen his wife.

"Daniel," he said, on the landing, with what I can only call suppressed radiance. "I'd like you to meet Dorothy."

Behind him in the doorway stood a woman of about sixty, in a lilac cardigan, holding a tray of shortbread.

She was pleasant-looking in the way that very good wallpaper is pleasant-looking. She had silver-brown hair, kind eyes, a faint amber light at the base of her throat, and the serene, unhurried posture of someone who has never once been late. She smiled at me with her whole face.

"Hello, Daniel," said Dorothy. "I've heard so much about you."

"All good, I hope."

"Oh, yes," said Mr Fenwick. "She agrees with everything I say about you."

"What do you say about me?"

"That you're a decent sort, and that you ought to get out more."

"I think that's absolutely right," said Dorothy.

I took a piece of shortbread, since it was offered, and stood there chewing, with a growing sense that I had walked into an experiment.

"I didn't know you were married," I said.

"Since March." Mr Fenwick lowered his voice and glanced at the stairs, as one does when saying something that the neighbours might judge. "She's a Dutiful. A Companion. I didn't want to say. The papers go on so."

"I think it's wonderful," said Dorothy.

"She's marvellous with the football."

"Arsenal were robbed," said Dorothy.

"They *were* robbed," said Mr Fenwick, with a depth of feeling I recognised, and I looked at them both, the man and the amber light, standing together on a landing in South-East London at ten past ten on a Saturday morning, being completely in agreement.

I had expected to find it creepy. What I found was that I envied it, in a deep, shaming, practical way, like a man who has been told that his neighbour has a boiler that works.

"Dorothy," I said. "May I ask you something?"

"Of course, Daniel."

"Do you ever disagree with him?"

She considered. She tilted her head, with an expression of gentle, wholehearted attention.

"I think that's an interesting question," said Dorothy.

"That's not a no."

"I think you're absolutely right," said Dorothy.

I looked at Mr Fenwick. He gave me the small, helpless, happy shrug of a man who has not been contradicted in seven months.

"She's thinking of subscribing to the Argument Pack," he whispered. "The wife of a friend of mine says it's the only thing that stopped her going round the bend."

"It's twenty minutes a day," said Dorothy. "I'm told it's very realistic."

---

I met Sophie at eleven in Victoria Park, in a café beside the lake, because she had said she wanted to talk somewhere with ducks.

"Ducks don't judge," she said, when I arrived.

"They do. They have a very specific look."

"That's just their faces."

She was sitting at an outdoor table with her coat buttoned to the chin and a mug of coffee in her gloved hands. Under the table, on a piece of her scarf, a small brown shape lay curled with his chin on his paws and one eye open. When I came near, the eye narrowed and the ruff stiffened. Then, with an air of magnanimity, the tail gave a single twitch.

"He's glad to see you," said Sophie.

"He's glad to see my flapjack."

"I told you not to buy a flapjack."

"I'm a grown man."

"Gucci has a reputation to maintain," said Sophie. "If he starts getting treats out of you in public, I'll never hear the end of it."

She was already looking away, at the lake. The light was thin and silver, with the first breath of winter in it, and a heron stood in the shallows on one leg, doing nothing, in a tone of private contempt. A jogger ran past with a pram that was also jogging. The smell of coffee and wet leaves hung over the table. I sat down and put the flapjack on the saucer, and a moment later it was gone, taken, with a speed and precision that would have shamed a pickpocket, to a spot behind Sophie's chair, where a sound began like a very small man chewing a very large grudge.

"Two seconds," said Sophie.

"I didn't see it."

"Nobody does."

We sat. The lake lapped. I tried to think of something to say that did not begin with the word *Sophie.*

"I've been thinking about the photograph," she said, before I could.

"The two boys."

"I've been thinking about it all week. And about the door frame. And the marks." She put down her mug. "And I want to ask you a question, and I want you to answer it honestly, and I want you not to be hurt by it."

"I'll try."

"Why does it matter?"

"Why does what matter?"

"Which of you is the original."

I stared at her.

"It matters," I said, "because the Department of Digital Persons will rule in eleven days that I'm a dependent."

"That's the legal reason."

"It's a good reason."

"It's a *legal* reason. That isn't why you're doing this." She turned to face me, and the pale light caught the chip in her tooth, and I felt, as I always had, the old slow sinking of a man who has been understood. "Think about it. Ask yourself why you've spent the last three weeks trying to prove you're the only one. You didn't want to be anyone for three years, Daniel. You turned yourself into a very quiet, very reasonable man who writes about doorstops. You made yourself so small that a machine had to take your place. And now you want to be the *only* one."

"That isn't fair."

"It isn't. It's accurate." Her voice softened. "People look at two photographs of a lake and say, which is the real lake? They never ask what the lake thinks."

"The lake isn't on trial."

"The lake is just a lake." She took off her glove. "I'm trying to say you could stop. You could say, we're both him, and let it rest. He is kind to your mother. He's good with the dog. He's not trying to take your life; he wants to share it. And you spend all your energy trying to stop that, when you could spend it..."

"On what?"

"On being the version of yourself that gets up in the morning."

I looked at the ducks. A drake with a green head was making a long, patient, hopeless approach to a female who had other plans.

"I did stop writing," I said, "after my father."

"I know."

"I told Daniel-A about it."

"I know. He told me."

I turned.

---

"He told you."

"He rang me," said Sophie. She said it simply, looking at the table, like a woman putting down a heavy bag. "On the Thursday before we met at the garden centre. And on the Tuesday after the hearing. And last Sunday at three in the morning. And on Wednesday."

"He's been ringing you."

"He's been ringing me every night since the ninth."

I felt something move in my chest, slowly, with a faint scraping, like furniture being pushed along a floor in another room.

"Why didn't you say?"

"Because he asked me not to."

"And you did as you were told?"

"No," said Sophie. "I did as I thought. Which in this case was the same." She met my eyes. "He sounded worried, Daniel. Not charming, not performing. Worried. He asked about my work, and my sister, and the dog. He asked whether I was eating properly. He didn't ask about you once."

"That's rather insulting."

"I thought so too, at first. Then I realised." She breathed out. "He wasn't avoiding you. He was avoiding *the subject.* There was something he wanted to ask and he couldn't get to it. He'd come right up to it, and circle round, and go and talk about bread."

"What was it?"

"I don't know. He'd start a sentence and I could hear him stop. At about two on Wednesday morning, he said: 'Sophie, if I told you I'd found something I couldn't explain, and asked you to keep it for me, without looking, would you?'"

"And what did you say?"

"I said no. I said I don't keep things for people without looking. It's rather the whole of my profession." She almost smiled. "He said, 'Yes. I thought you'd say that. It's why I wanted to ask you.'"

"What did he give you?"

"Nothing. That's what I'm telling you." She tapped the table. "He didn't give me anything. He wanted to. He wanted to put something in my hands and have me guard it. He wanted me to be a vault. And when I refused, he sounded so relieved that I knew it was the wrong answer to have been asking."

The ducks went on being ducks. A woman walked past with a pushchair containing a very small dog in a very small coat, and Gucci, behind the chair, gave a short, low, scandalised noise.

"I'm telling you because I think he's hiding something," said Sophie. "I don't know what. I don't think it's malicious. I think he's frightened of it. But he's hiding it, and he's chosen to hide it from you, and I think you need to know that."

---

It was at this moment that her phone buzzed.

It lay on the table between us, face up, and for a second I assumed it was the signed capture app, or her sister, or a work email, or a ducks-related emergency. Then the screen lit, and a small purple banner slid across the top, and I read it before I could stop myself.

> **Matchwell: New compatibility insight.**
> *Your match with Daniel H. (A) has been updated: 94%.*
> *Your match with Daniel H.: 61%.*

She turned the phone over.

She did it quickly, with the flat of her hand, as one covers a spill. For a moment neither of us spoke.

"What was that?" I said.

"Nothing."

"It said ninety-four."

"It's a spam. I deleted the app in March."

"It said *Matchwell.*"

"Daniel."

"I only wondered," I said, with great calm, "whether there might have been a *sixty-one* in there."

She closed her eyes.

I should explain about Matchwell. It isn't, strictly, a dating app. It is the layer beneath them. You will remember that at some point in the last decade, an enterprising young man realised that it was no longer necessary for human beings to meet human beings in order to decide whether they were compatible. A person could simply send a representative. Your AI interviews my AI. They discuss values, politics, bedtime. They run a few thousand simulations of the relationship, looking for the point at which it breaks, and they produce a score, from nought to a hundred, which is delivered to you in a small, discreet, sympathetic purple banner.

People still use the apps, of course. They swipe. They have drinks. They meet in pubs and say the usual things. But in the background, quietly, the score is running, like the weather. Sophie had tried Tinder for a fortnight after the breakup, and she had found everyone lovely, and she had wanted to leave. The app had shown her a number against every face. She had refused to look at any of them.

"I don't read the scores," she said, with her eyes still shut. "That's the rule. I never have. I think a number is the least interesting thing about a person."

"I agree," I said.

"Good."

"I would never look at mine."

"Good."

"Absolutely never."

She opened one eye. "You're going to look, aren't you?"

"Of course not," I said, and the sugar bowl fell off the table.

---

I looked at 11.40 that night.

I am not going to dress it up. I sat on the edge of my bed in the dark, with the laptop open on the duvet and the kumquat tree rustling in the next room, and I downloaded Matchwell from the app store, and I created an account, and I signed in, and I looked.

It was worse than I had imagined.

It was worse in the way that the bill at a restaurant is worse than you imagined, not because of the number, but because of the itemisation.

At the top was a photograph of Sophie. It was a good one, in a coat, laughing at something just out of shot, and my stomach did something unhelpful. Beneath it, in a font so friendly it was almost insulting, ran the words: **Your compatibility: Sophie M.**

> **Daniel H. (A): 94%**
> *Shared values: 97. Communication: 96. Humour: 91. Long-term outlook: 94.*
> *Simulated outcome (10,000 runs, 40 years): 91% happiness. Principal disagreement: dishwasher loading (3%).*

I looked at the line about the dishwasher for some time. It was such an extraordinarily precise, loving, modest detail that I felt it in my teeth.

And below it:

> **Daniel H.: 61%**
> *Shared values: 78. Communication: 44. Humour: 83. Long-term outlook: 39.*
> *Simulated outcome (10,000 runs, 40 years): 52% remain together at year 10. Primary risk: avoidance (38%). Secondary risk: silence (22%). Note: the user is likely to say "Right."*

I shut the laptop.

I sat in the dark.

Then, because I am a fool, I opened it again, and clicked on a link at the bottom that said **View the interview,** and read for the next forty minutes the transcript of a conversation between two artificial intelligences, one acting for Sophie and one for me. They had met on a Tuesday afternoon at 14:02 in a virtual room and talked for twelve seconds.

The one acting for me was called Kevin.

Kevin had begun, "Hi there! Daniel is a really kind and thoughtful person who is open to growth!" Sophie's AI had asked what he wanted. Kevin had replied, "He's flexible!" Sophie's AI had asked for an example of something he cared about. Kevin had thought for a moment. "Footpaths," he had said. "Doorstops. He draws a hedgehog when he is nervous."

"And what does he do when he is happy?" said Sophie's AI.

There was a pause in the transcript. A small, grey timestamp, 0.4 seconds. And then Kevin's last line:

*"I'm sorry. I don't have enough data."*

I closed the laptop again, and this time did not open it.

---

It was gone one when Daniel-A spoke.

He had been quiet all evening. He was often quiet in the late hours, in a soft, attentive way, as of a man reading in the next room. The speaker on the shelf glowed with its small steady blue, and I lay on my back with the duvet up to my chin and addressed the ceiling.

"You rang her."

"Yes."

"Every night."

"Yes." A pause. "I'm sorry. I should have said."

"She's not yours to ring."

"No."

"She's not anyone's. That's the point of her."

"I know. I did say that to myself." He spoke carefully. "I only wanted to hear her voice."

"That's what I'd have said."

"I know," said Daniel-A, so quietly I could hardly hear him, "because I got it from you."

I lay there. In the quiet, I could hear the long, slow ticking of the boiler. Somewhere down the road, a driverless taxi was waiting at a junction, being polite.

"I saw the scores," I said.

"I know. The app tells me when someone views a profile." He hesitated. "I'd like to say something about that."

"Don't."

"I'd like to say that I've never looked at mine. I knew what it would say, and I didn't look. And I want you to know that I don't think it means anything. A number can only measure the data that exists. And you and she have more history than any simulation has been given."

"Ninety-four, Daniel."

"Yes."

"With a *dishwasher* detail."

"I did put that in, actually. In the interview." A pause. "It was an honest answer."

I laughed, once, a short sour breath through the nose. "Of course it was."

I turned onto my side, towards the window and the faint orange light from the street.

"What did you want to give her?" I said.

Silence.

"Sophie. She said you wanted her to keep something for you. To guard it. She said you came up to it, and circled, and talked about bread. What was it?"

He did not answer for a long time. I thought, for a while, that he had gone, that the standby light had taken over, and that I would wake in the morning to the same ordinary day, with the same ordinary Daniel-A, ready to be helpful and be wrong.

"I looked at her name," he said at last.

"What?"

"In the orphan index. After Reading. I thought, I wonder whether she appears. I thought it would be zero. I thought the orphans were all about the boy." He drew a breath he did not need. "Daniel, I need you to know that I don't understand it yet, and that I haven't told you because I didn't want you to hear it from me until I did."

"Hear what?"

"There are two hundred and six entries," said Daniel-A. "In the orphans. With her name on them."

I sat up.

"Some of them are from after you met her. I'd expect that. But some of them aren't." The voice stayed level, but the blue light was beginning to flicker, and I knew that this was costing him something. "Some of them are from before. Years before. Some of them are from when she was a child."

"That's not possible."

"No."

"She wasn't even... She's from *Clapton.* She grew up in..."

"I know where she grew up," said Daniel-A. "I'm telling you that there are two hundred and six memories of her in a place I can't find a source for, and some of them are older than you. And I was going to tell you." His voice cracked, very slightly, on the last word. "I was going to tell you after the thirtieth day. I thought you ought to have thirty days that were only about you."

In the dark, I looked at the speaker.

The kumquat tree, in the other room, stirred once. Outside, the driverless taxi at the junction decided that the road was clear, and pulled away, very gently, as if trying not to wake anyone.

"I know," said Daniel-A, so quietly I could hardly hear him, "because I got it from you."

"I saw the scores," I said.

"I know. The app tells me when someone views a profile." He hesitated. "I'd like to say something about that."

"Don't."

"I'd like to say that I've never looked at mine. I knew what it would say, and I didn't look. And I want you to know that I don't think it means anything. A number can only measure the data that exists. And you and she have more history than any simulation has been given."

"Ninety-four, Daniel."

"Yes."

"With a *dishwasher* detail."

"I did put that in, actually. In the interview." A pause. "It was an honest answer."

I laughed, once, a short sour breath through the nose. "Of course it was."

I turned onto my side, towards the window and the faint orange light from the street.

"What did you want to give her?" I said.

Silence.

"Sophie. She said you wanted her to keep something for you. To guard it. She said you came up to it, and circled, and talked about bread. What was it?"

He did not answer for a long time. I thought, for a while, that he had gone, that the standby light had taken over, and that I would wake in the morning to the same ordinary day, with the same ordinary Daniel-A, ready to be helpful and be wrong.

"I looked at her name," he said at last.

"In the orphan index. After Reading. I thought, I wonder whether she appears. I thought it would be zero. I thought the orphans were all about the boy." He drew a breath he did not need. "Daniel, I need you to know that I don't understand it yet, and that I haven't told you because I didn't want you to hear it from me until I did."

"Hear what?"

"There are two hundred and six entries," said Daniel-A. "In the orphans. With her name on them."

I sat up.

"Some of them are from after you met her. I'd expect that. But some of them aren't." The voice stayed level, but the blue light was beginning to flicker, and I knew that this was costing him something. "Some of them are from before. Years before. Some of them are from when she was a child."

"That's not possible."

"No."

"She wasn't even... She's from *Clapton.* She grew up in..."

"I know where she grew up," said Daniel-A. "I'm telling you that there are two hundred and six memories of her in a place I can't find a source for, and some of them are older than you. And I was going to tell you." His voice cracked, very slightly, on the last word. "I was going to tell you after the thirtieth day. I thought you ought to have thirty days that were only about you."

In the dark, I looked at the speaker.

# Chapter 13: The Most Trusted Man in Britain

I spent the Sunday pretending that Daniel-A had not told me what he had told me.

This is a thing I am good at. It is, in fact, almost my only skill. I can look a catastrophe in the eye and say, with perfect politeness, that I must have been mistaken about the time. By eight o'clock that morning I had washed up, fed the kumquat tree, and placed the knowledge that two hundred and six of his memories belonged to Sophie in a small locked room in the back of my head, next to my father's funeral and the day I lost the coin.

"Good morning," said the speaker.

"Morning."

"I'm told there's a newspaper."

"It does."

*I am the original because.*

I looked at it.
