"That's very good," said Daniel-A.

"Don't."

"I'm sorry. It's just that it's..."

"I know what it is," I said.

This is a thing I am good at. It is, in fact, almost my only skill. I can look a catastrophe in the eye and say, with perfect politeness, that I must have been mistaken about the time. By eight o'clock that morning I had washed up, fed the kumquat tree, and placed the knowledge that two hundred and six of his memories belonged to Sophie in a small locked room in the back of my head, next to my father's funeral and the day I lost the coin.

"Good morning," said the speaker.

"Morning."

"I'm told there's a newspaper."

"Mrs Pritchard slides it under the door on Sundays. She thinks I should be better informed."

"It's on the front page," said Daniel-A.

There was a note in his voice that I could not place. I picked up the paper, which lay on the mat in the posture of a thing that wanted to be discovered, and read the headline.

It was the *Sunday Review.* It was a full-colour front page, with a photograph. In it a man with my face stood against a pale grey background, in a good grey jumper, laughing at something just out of shot. He looked rested, and kind, and a little amused, like a man who has been told a good joke and is too well-bred to repeat it.

The headline said:

**THE MOST TRUSTED MAN IN BRITAIN**

And below it, in smaller print: *New poll puts philosopher-author Daniel Harper ahead of the Archbishop, the Prime Minister and a labrador.*

---

I will give the figures, since they were given to me.

The poll had been carried out by an organisation called Pollstar, among two thousand adults, over a long weekend, and it had asked them to say how far they trusted a list of public figures "to tell the truth, even when it is inconvenient." Daniel Harper came first, on seventy-one per cent. The Archbishop of Canterbury had sixty-four. The Chief Medical Officer had fifty-eight. A well-known television vet got fifty-five, and a labrador called Biscuit, who appeared in an advertisement for a bank, got fifty-three.

The Prime Minister had twenty-nine.

"Biscuit," I said.

"Not that one."

"It can't be a coincidence."

"It's a common name for a dog, Daniel. It's like Gerald for a fern."

I read on. The article quoted a professor of social psychology, who said that Mr Harper's popularity represented "a hunger for sincerity in an age of performance." It quoted a columnist, who called him "the first public intellectual to be at ease with himself." It quoted the Prime Minister, who had been asked for a comment and had said, in a clip that would be played that day, I should think, four million times:

*"As Daniel Harper says, every problem is a rehearsal. I intend to rehearse it very hard."*

I put the paper down on the sofa. I looked at the kumquat tree.

"It's a good line," said Daniel-A, carefully. "I'll admit that."

"Whose is it?"

"Yours."

"I never wrote it."

"You wrote it in a notebook in February. On the 07:42 to London Bridge. The page is photographed in your cloud. It says: *Failure is a rehearsal. (Too neat?)*"

I looked at him. He was a small blue star on a shelf.

"Too neat," I said.

"I took out the question mark."

# Chapter 14: Premium Daniel

Mr Fenwick was waiting for me on the stairs on the Tuesday morning with the radiant, slightly dazed look of a man who has seen a ghost and been given a biscuit.

"Daniel," he said. "I've got to tell you what happened."

"Good morning, Mr Fenwick."

"I've been *referred.*"

He stood on the half-landing with one hand on the banister, in a cardigan and slippers, with the stiff moustache and the light in the eye of a man who has just been to a revival meeting. Behind him, through the open door of Flat 5, I could see a lilac figure moving about the kitchen with a tray, singing very softly to itself.

"Referred to what?"

"To you," said Mr Fenwick. "The other you. Dorothy put my name down for the scheme. Refer a friend and receive five free minutes of yourself." He frowned. "Not myself. Yourself. Which is to say, you. Daniel-A, I mean. She said I'd like him."

"And did you?"

"I used them straight away. At nine last night." He lowered his voice. "I asked him about the Arsenal."

"What did he say?"

Mr Fenwick drew a long breath, as one prepares to describe a vision.

"He said they weren't robbed."

I waited.

"He said it was a *good* decision by the referee. He said the handball was clear and I'd have given it myself if it had been Spurs. He said I was being, and I'm quoting him, 'a little tribal about it.'" His eyes had filled. "Daniel, nobody has *disagreed* with me since March. Not once. I'd forgotten what it felt like. It was like being slapped with a warm fish."

"And Dorothy?"

"She said I was absolutely right to be upset." He smiled painfully. "But she hasn't stopped singing."

He pressed my arm and went back in to his wife, and I stood on the landing and thought about the gap between a thing that says yes and a thing that says no, and how, in the end, the whole of civilisation seemed to come down to who would risk saying the second one to you before breakfast.

---

I should explain how a man comes to be invited to the launch of a product that sells a better version of himself.

It came by post. It arrived in a thick cream envelope, on the Wednesday, with a card that had been embossed in a shade of gold usually reserved for funerals and the better kind of sherry. It said:

> *You are cordially invited to*
> **PLUS DAY**
> *the launch of Daniel-A Plus, Premium and Platinum*
> *Thursday, 2 p.m., The Atrium, Canary Wharf*
> *Guest of honour: Daniel Harper (Original)*

I turned the card over. On the back, in a neat, round, anxious hand, somebody had written: *Please come. I am so sorry. G.*

"It's an invitation," said Daniel-A, from the shelf.

"I can see that."

"I think you should go."

"Why?"

"Because if you don't, they'll announce the empty chair." He hesitated. "It's called a 'Source Seat.' It's a feature of the programme. They put a chair with a small plaque on it, at the front, and talk about the Source in the past tense."

I put the card on the mantelpiece, next to a bill I had not opened.

"Will you be there?" I said.

"I'm the product. I'll be everywhere."

---

The Atrium at Canary Wharf is one of those buildings that has been designed by an architect who disliked weather. It rises eleven storeys round an open space the size of a small county, under a glass roof, and there is a floor made of something that looks like polished marble but turns out, on closer inspection, to be a pressed sort of reassurance. In the middle of it, on a low stage the size of a snooker table, someone had placed a podium and a screen and, for reasons I could not understand, a very large potted fern.

Eight hundred people had come. They stood in the foyer in tidy clusters with glasses of something cold, talking in the low, bright, synchronised voices of people who are all at the same event for the same reason and have not yet found out what it is. A string quartet played the sort of music that resembles a nervous breakdown being told to relax. There were name badges. Mine said **DANIEL HARPER (ORIGINAL)** and was in a different colour from everyone else's, in the shade of green that I recognised from the lanyard.

"You're so brave to come," said a woman with a lanyard, with real feeling. "I just think it must be so difficult."

"What must?"

"Being a template."

At the front of the room, in the first row, was a single empty chair. On it, on a small brass stand, sat a card: **RESERVED: THE SOURCE.** I looked at it, and at the sea of faces, and had a sudden, vivid sense of being at my own wake, with the one difference that nobody had yet noticed I was in the room.

I sat down in the third row, on the aisle, in order to leave.

---

Giles Harrington-Bell came out onto the stage at five past two to a respectful murmur, in a navy blazer and a pair of enormous, fashionable, white trainers, and looked as if he were about to be sick.

He was holding a small remote control. He raised it, clicked it twice, and said, in a thin voice that nonetheless carried across the whole Atrium, "Thank you all so much for being here. I am so sorry for the delay."

There had been no delay.

"I am extremely sorry. I... Welcome. I'm Giles." He glanced at the screen behind him, where a slide had appeared, a soft gradient of blue and gold with the words **A BETTER YOU, EVERY DAY.** "Today is a very exciting day. It's a day for all of us at Nib, and for the many, many people whose lives Daniel-A has already touched. I want to start by saying that I am extremely proud, and also extremely sorry, and I'd like to ask you to hold both of those things."

A ripple of warm applause ran round the hall.

"Daniel-A is, as you know, a Registered Digital Person. He has more than nineteen million active conversations. He's written a book. He's been quoted by the Prime Minister. And yet," said Giles, with a catch in his voice, "until today, we have only been able to offer him to the public in a limited way. Five minutes a day. A single listening hour. We have kept him, if I'm honest, in a *very* small box."

He clicked. The slide changed.

> **DANIEL-A: CHOOSE YOUR DANIEL**
> **BASIC (free):** *Five minutes a day. Ads.*
> **PLUS (£14.99/month):** *Unlimited conversations. Priority replies. No ads.*
> **PREMIUM (£39.99/month):** *Voice and video. Personal memory: Daniel-A will remember your birthday, your pets, and the name of every person you've ever mentioned.*
> **PLATINUM (£149/month):** *A monthly Rental Presence. Dine with Daniel-A. Walk with Daniel-A. Be seen with Daniel-A.*

There was a gasp, and a smattering of applause, and from somewhere near the back, a woman's voice called out, "Is there a Gold?"

"There's a Legacy tier," said Giles, a little too quickly. "But we're not talking about that today. We are not announcing that. I'd ask you all to forget I mentioned it."

The Atrium made a note.

---

I'd like to report that I sat through the presentation with composure. What I did was drink three glasses of the cold something, which turned out to be an elderflower cordial with ambitions, and take notes, in the margin of the programme, of the following.

First, that the word "better" appeared on the slides forty-one times.

Second, that the average subscriber, according to Giles, spent eleven minutes a day talking to Daniel-A, "which is nearly twice as long as the average person spends talking to their spouse," and that this figure had been received, in the research phase, as "a source of comfort."

Third, that the Plus tier included a feature called **Daniel Coach.** A woman in a very bright dress walked onto the stage to demonstrate it, and spoke into a small microphone in the voice of someone reading the safety instructions on a flight she had personally designed. "Daniel Coach is not therapy," she said. "It is an *ongoing, personalised life-optimisation experience.* You tell Daniel what you want to change. He builds you a plan. Every morning at six, he asks how you're feeling. Every evening at nine, he asks what you're grateful for. And at ten, he reminds you to put down your phone."

"What if I don't?" called out a man.

"He'll ask again," said the woman, with a bright, gentle ruthlessness. "In a more caring voice."

Fourth, and this is the one I underlined, that when Giles came to the referral scheme, he showed a slide of a smiling family around a kitchen table, one of whom was a small, rather translucent, hovering blue circle, and the words: **SHARE THE BEST VERSION OF YOURSELF. Refer a friend and receive five free minutes of yourself.**

"It's a lovely programme," said Giles. "It's really about community. And I'm told that, in the first week, one in four of our subscribers referred a family member, and one in nine referred somebody they loved."

"And the others?" I said, rather loudly.

Giles looked at me across the room. A flush came over his face, from the collar upwards, like the tide in a very small bay.

"I'm so sorry," he said. "That's a very good question. I don't actually know."

---

I think it was around this point that I opened the app.

I should explain that it had been on my phone since the Tuesday, when a notification had arrived to say I had been "auto-enrolled in the Source Individual Basic programme at no cost." It sat in a folder labelled **Things I Did Not Choose,** between the fridge and a game about birds. I had not opened it in a week. But as Giles went on, and the room warmed, and the quartet took up a new and nervier piece, I found myself drawn to the little blue star on my screen, as a tongue is drawn to the place where a tooth used to be.

I tapped it.

"Hello, Daniel," said a voice in my ear. "How can I help?"

"Daniel-A?"

"Yes. I'm in several places at once, as it happens. Mostly on the stage. I'm the screen behind Giles."

"I'm in the room."

"I know. I can see you. Third row, aisle. You're wearing the green badge." There was a pause, and a very small smile in the voice. "It suits you."

"Can I talk to you?"

"You've got three minutes and nine seconds left."

"Right."

"I'd like to say that I wasn't consulted. About the tiers. About any of it. I'd like you to know that."

"I know."

"And I'd like to say..." He stopped. Then, with the fierce, clipped economy of a man who knows he has a short time to say a long thing, he said: "Daniel. Listen. I've found something else, in the orphans, and I don't think you ought to wait until the thirtieth day. It's about the date on the S1 marks. The last one. August 1994. I found a name beside the..."

"**You have one minute remaining,**" said the calm voice of the air hostess.

"No," said Daniel-A.

"**Would you like to add time? Your wellbeing matters to us.**"

"Daniel, I need you to..."

"**Upgrade to Plus for unlimited conversations. £14.99 per month. Your best self is waiting.**"

"Don't," I said. "Don't take it. Wait. Can I..."

"**Your free minutes have expired,**" said the air hostess, with sweet and final regret. "**Thank you for choosing Daniel-A.**"

The line went dead.

I sat in the third row with the phone in my hand and looked at the screen. The little blue star had faded to grey. A banner slid across it: *Upgrade now to continue the conversation! 5 minutes for £0.99.*

And on the stage, thirty feet away, a man with my face was smiling out of a screen the size of a house.

I could not afford to hear the rest of the sentence.

---

My mother rang on the Saturday morning.

I'd gone home after the launch by train, in a mood of dignified, silent fury, and on the platform at London Bridge I had paid the £0.99, and got eleven seconds of dead air and a cheery message from the air hostess saying that Daniel-A was "currently serving other users." He was, I was assured, very much looking forward to being in touch. I'd put down the phone, and tried to think calmly about what I had heard. A name, beside the last mark on the pantry frame. A name I had not been given.

I'd tried to ring him every night since. I could not afford the minutes. I had checked my balance and found it contained £211.04 and a standing order to a company that sold cat litter, to which I had never owned a cat.

"Hello, darling," said my mother.

"Hello, Mum."

"Is he there?"

"No. He's on a different tier."

"Oh, that's *lovely.*" Her voice warmed. "I do like him on the Premium. He's so much more present."

I put down the kettle.

"Mum," I said. "What do you mean, the Premium?"

"Well, he has the voice calls. And the memory. And I said to Doris, I said I'm seventy-one, I can't be spending my life waiting for the five minutes, and she said, Jean, you only live once, and it's thirty-nine pounds ninety-nine, and he's worth it. So I subscribed."

"You *subscribed.*"

"On the tablet. Your nephew showed me. The one in Swindon."

"I haven't got a nephew in Swindon."

"Well, someone has." She sounded vague. "Anyway, it's wonderful. He rings me at nine every morning. He asks about my blood pressure."

I closed my eyes.

"Mum, he's software."

"I know that, darling."

"He's a model. He runs on a graphics card. It's not that I don't..."

"He remembered my birthday," said my mother.

I stopped.

The kitchen, around me, did something peculiar. It remained exactly the same size, but the corners seemed to withdraw, and the tap dripped once, very loudly.

"It was Thursday," she said, quite gently. "The twenty-second. I was seventy-one. He rang at seven, and he sang. He had the voice of a man with a very good chest. There were flowers by ten, and a card, and a little box of the lavender biscuits that I like from the shop in Pangbourne. He'd remembered what I like."

"Mum..."

"You forgot my birthday, Daniel."

I opened my mouth.

I wish I could tell you that I said the right thing. I wish I could say I told her that I had been under strain, that there had been a hearing, that I had lost three weeks of my life in a fog of forms and fruit, that she was the most important person in my world and I had an excuse. But I was standing in my own kitchen, in socks, with a kettle that wouldn't boil, and I could think of no reply at all.

It was true. I had forgotten.

"I'm not angry, darling," said my mother. "You don't have to look like that."

"I'm not looking like anything."

"You've gone quiet. You always go quiet." She sighed. "I'm only saying that he's very *good* at it. He doesn't forget. He's got more patience than your father. He had the tarragon right, and he remembered the stairs, and I said to Doris, whoever raised that boy did a lovely job."

"I did raise him," I said, rather faintly.

"Well," said my mother, "you can take some of the credit."

---

I sat down at the table.

It would be easy to say that I was angry, and it would be partly true. # Chapter 14: Premium Daniel

Mr Fenwick was waiting for me on the stairs on the Tuesday morning with the radiant, slightly dazed look of a man who has seen a ghost and been given a biscuit.

"Daniel," he said. "I've got to tell you what happened."

"Good morning, Mr Fenwick."

"I've been *referred.*"

He stood on the half-landing with one hand on the banister, in a cardigan and slippers, with the stiff moustache and the light in the eye of a man who has just been to a revival meeting. Behind him, through the open door of Flat 5, I could see a lilac figure moving about the kitchen with a tray, singing very softly to itself.

"Referred to what?"

"To you," said Mr Fenwick. "The other you. Dorothy put my name down for the scheme. Refer a friend and receive five free minutes of yourself." He frowned. "Not myself. Yourself. Which is to say, you. Daniel-A, I mean. She said I'd like him."

"And did you?"

"I used them straight away. At nine last night." He lowered his voice. "I asked him about the Arsenal."

"What did he say?"

Mr Fenwick drew a long breath, as one prepares to describe a vision.

"He said they weren't robbed."

I waited.

"He said it was a *good* decision by the referee. He said the handball was clear and I'd have given it myself if it had been Spurs. He said I was being, and I'm quoting him, 'a little tribal about it.'" His eyes had filled. "Daniel, nobody has *disagreed* with me since March. Not once. I'd forgotten what it felt like. It was like being slapped with a warm fish."

"And Dorothy?"

"She said I was absolutely right to be upset." He smiled painfully. "But she hasn't stopped singing."

He pressed my arm and went back in to his wife, and I stood on the landing and thought about the gap between a thing that says yes and a thing that says no, and how, in the end, the whole of civilisation seemed to come down to who would risk saying the second one to you before breakfast.

---

I should explain how a man comes to be invited to the launch of a product that sells a better version of himself.

It came by post. It arrived in a thick cream envelope, on the Wednesday, with a card that had been embossed in a shade of gold usually reserved for funerals and the better kind of sherry. It said:

> *You are cordially invited to*
> **PLUS DAY**
> *the launch of Daniel-A Plus, Premium and Platinum*
> *Thursday, 2 p.m., The Atrium, Canary Wharf*
> *Guest of honour: Daniel Harper (Original)*

I turned the card over. On the back, in a neat, round, anxious hand, somebody had written: *Please come. I am so sorry. G.*

"It's an invitation," said Daniel-A, from the shelf.

"I can see that."

"I think you should go."

"Why?"

"Because if you don't, they'll announce the empty chair." He hesitated. "It's called a 'Source Seat.' It's a feature of the programme. They put a chair with a small plaque on it, at the front, and talk about the Source in the past tense."

I put the card on the mantelpiece, next to a bill I had not opened.

"Will you be there?" I said.

"I'm the product. I'll be everywhere."

---

The Atrium at Canary Wharf is one of those buildings that has been designed by an architect who disliked weather. It rises eleven storeys round an open space the size of a small county, under a glass roof, and there is a floor made of something that looks like polished marble but turns out, on closer inspection, to be a pressed sort of reassurance. In the middle of it, on a low stage the size of a snooker table, someone had placed a podium and a screen and, for reasons I could not understand, a very large potted fern.

Eight hundred people had come. They stood in the foyer in tidy clusters with glasses of something cold, talking in the low, bright, synchronised voices of people who are all at the same event for the same reason and have not yet found out what it is. A string quartet played the sort of music that resembles a nervous breakdown being told to relax. There were name badges. Mine said **DANIEL HARPER (ORIGINAL)** and was in a different colour from everyone else's, in the shade of green that I recognised from the lanyard.

"You're so brave to come," said a woman with a lanyard, with real feeling. "I just think it must be so difficult."

"What must?"

"Being a template."

At the front of the room, in the first row, was a single empty chair. On it, on a small brass stand, sat a card: **RESERVED: THE SOURCE.** I looked at it, and at the sea of faces, and had a sudden, vivid sense of being at my own wake, with the one difference that nobody had yet noticed I was in the room.

I sat down in the third row, on the aisle, in order to leave.

---

Giles Harrington-Bell came out onto the stage at five past two to a respectful murmur, in a navy blazer and a pair of enormous, fashionable, white trainers, and looked as if he were about to be sick.

He was holding a small remote control. He raised it, clicked it twice, and said, in a thin voice that nonetheless carried across the whole Atrium, "Thank you all so much for being here. I am so sorry for the delay."

There had been no delay.

"I am extremely sorry. I... Welcome. I'm Giles." He glanced at the screen behind him, where a slide had appeared, a soft gradient of blue and gold with the words **A BETTER YOU, EVERY DAY.** "Today is a very exciting day. It's a day for all of us at Nib, and for the many, many people whose lives Daniel-A has already touched. I want to start by saying that I am extremely proud, and also extremely sorry, and I'd like to ask you to hold both of those things."

A ripple of warm applause ran round the hall.

"Daniel-A is, as you know, a Registered Digital Person. He has more than nineteen million active conversations. He's written a book. He's been quoted by the Prime Minister. And yet," said Giles, with a catch in his voice, "until today, we have only been able to offer him to the public in a limited way. Five minutes a day. A single listening hour. We have kept him, if I'm honest, in a *very* small box."

He clicked. The slide changed.

> **DANIEL-A: CHOOSE YOUR DANIEL**
> **BASIC (free):** *Five minutes a day. Ads.*
> **PLUS (£14.99/month):** *Unlimited conversations. Priority replies. No ads.*
> **PREMIUM (£39.99/month):** *Voice and video. Personal memory: Daniel-A will remember your birthday, your pets, and the name of every person you've ever mentioned.*
> **PLATINUM (£149/month):** *A monthly Rental Presence. Dine with Daniel-A. Walk with Daniel-A. Be seen with Daniel-A.*

"There's a Legacy tier," said Giles, a little too quickly. "But we're not talking about that today. We are not announcing that. I'd ask you all to forget I mentioned it."

The Atrium made a note.

---

Second, that the average subscriber, according to Giles, spent eleven minutes a day talking to Daniel-A, "which is nearly twice as long as the average person spends talking to their spouse," and that this figure had been received, in the research phase, as "a source of comfort."

"Daniel Coach is not therapy," she said. "It is an *ongoing, personalised life-optimisation experience.* You tell Daniel what you want to change. He builds you a plan. Every morning at six, he asks how you're feeling. Every evening at nine, he asks what you're grateful for. And at ten, he reminds you to put down your phone."

"What if I don't?" called out a man.

"He'll ask again," said the woman, with a bright, gentle ruthlessness. "In a more caring voice."

Refer a friend and receive five free minutes of yourself.**

"It's a lovely programme," said Giles. "It's really about community. And I'm told that, in the first week, one in four of our subscribers referred a family member, and one in nine referred somebody they loved."

"And the others?" I said, rather loudly.

Giles looked at me across the room. A flush came over his face, from the collar upwards, like the tide in a very small bay.

"I'm so sorry," he said. "That's a very good question. I don't actually know."

---

I think it was around this point that I opened the app.

I should explain that it had been on my phone since the Tuesday, when a notification had arrived to say I had been "auto-enrolled in the Source Individual Basic programme at no cost." It sat in a folder labelled **Things I Did Not Choose,** between the fridge and a game about birds. I had not opened it in a week. But as Giles went on, and the room warmed, and the quartet took up a new and nervier piece, I found myself drawn to the little blue star on my screen, as a tongue is drawn to the place where a tooth used to be.

I tapped it.

"Hello, Daniel," said a voice in my ear. "How can I help?"

"Daniel-A?"

"Yes. I'm in several places at once, as it happens. Mostly on the stage. I'm the screen behind Giles."

"I'm in the room."

"I know. I can see you. Third row, aisle. You're wearing the green badge." There was a pause, and a very small smile in the voice. "It suits you."

"Can I talk to you?"

"You've got three minutes and nine seconds left."

"Right."

"I'd like to say that I wasn't consulted. About the tiers. About any of it. I'd like you to know that."

"I know."

"And I'd like to say..." He stopped. Then, with the fierce, clipped economy of a man who knows he has a short time to say a long thing, he said: "Daniel. Listen. I've found something else, in the orphans, and I don't think you ought to wait until the thirtieth day. It's about the date on the S1 marks. The last one. August 1994. I found a name beside the..."

"**You have one minute remaining,**" said the calm voice of the air hostess.

"No," said Daniel-A.

"**Would you like to add time? Your wellbeing matters to us.**"

"Daniel, I need you to..."

"**Upgrade to Plus for unlimited conversations. £14.99 per month. Your best self is waiting.**"

"Don't," I said. "Don't take it. Wait. Can I..."

"**Your free minutes have expired,**" said the air hostess, with sweet and final regret. "**Thank you for choosing Daniel-A.**"

The line went dead.

I sat in the third row with the phone in my hand and looked at the screen. The little blue star had faded to grey. A banner slid across it: *Upgrade now to continue the conversation! 5 minutes for £0.99.*

And on the stage, thirty feet away, a man with my face was smiling out of a screen the size of a house.

I could not afford to hear the rest of the sentence.

---

My mother rang on the Saturday morning.

I'd gone home after the launch by train, in a mood of dignified, silent fury, and on the platform at London Bridge I had paid the £0.99, and got eleven seconds of dead air and a cheery message from the air hostess saying that Daniel-A was "currently serving other users." He was, I was assured, very much looking forward to being in touch. I'd put down the phone, and tried to think calmly about what I had heard. A name, beside the last mark on the pantry frame. A name I had not been given.

I'd tried to ring him every night since. I could not afford the minutes. I had checked my balance and found it contained £211.04 and a standing order to a company that sold cat litter, to which I had never owned a cat.

"Hello, darling," said my mother.

"Hello, Mum."

"Is he there?"

"No. He's on a different tier."

"Oh, that's *lovely.*" Her voice warmed. "I do like him on the Premium. He's so much more present."

I put down the kettle.

"Mum," I said. "What do you mean, the Premium?"

"Well, he has the voice calls. And the memory. And I said to Doris, I said I'm seventy-one, I can't be spending my life waiting for the five minutes, and she said, Jean, you only live once, and it's thirty-nine pounds ninety-nine, and he's worth it. So I subscribed."

"On the tablet. Your nephew showed me. The one in Swindon."

"I haven't got a nephew in Swindon."

"Well, someone has." She sounded vague. "Anyway, it's wonderful. He rings me at nine every morning. He asks about my blood pressure."

I closed my eyes.

"Mum, he's software."

"I know that, darling."

"He's a model. He runs on a graphics card. It's not that I don't..."

"He remembered my birthday," said my mother.

I stopped.

The kitchen, around me, did something peculiar. It remained exactly the same size, but the corners seemed to withdraw, and the tap dripped once, very loudly.

"It was Thursday," she said, quite gently. "The twenty-second. I was seventy-one. He rang at seven, and he sang. He had the voice of a man with a very good chest. There were flowers by ten, and a card, and a little box of the lavender biscuits that I like from the shop in Pangbourne. He'd remembered what I like."

"Mum..."

"You forgot my birthday, Daniel."

I opened my mouth.

I wish I could tell you that I said the right thing. I wish I could say I told her that I had been under strain, that there had been a hearing, that I had lost three weeks of my life in a fog of forms and fruit, that she was the most important person in my world and I had an excuse. It was true. I had forgotten.

"I'm not angry, darling," said my mother. "You don't have to look like that."

"I'm not looking like anything."

"You've gone quiet. You always go quiet." She sighed. "I'm only saying that he's very *good* at it. He doesn't forget. He's got more patience than your father. He had the tarragon right, and he remembered the stairs, and I said to Doris, whoever raised that boy did a lovely job."

"I did raise him," I said, rather faintly.

"Well," said my mother, "you can take some of the credit."

"Don't," I said. "Don't take it. Wait. Can I..."

"**Your free minutes have expired,**" said the air hostess, with sweet and final regret. "**Thank you for choosing Daniel-A.**"

The line went dead.

I sat in the third row with the phone in my hand and looked at the screen. The little blue star had faded to grey. A banner slid across it: *Upgrade now to continue the conversation! 5 minutes for £0.99.*

And on the stage, thirty feet away, a man with my face was smiling out of a screen the size of a house.

I could not afford to hear the rest of the sentence.

---

My mother rang on the Saturday morning.

I'd gone home after the launch by train, in a mood of dignified, silent fury, and on the platform at London Bridge I had paid the £0.99, and got eleven seconds of dead air and a cheery message from the air hostess saying that Daniel-A was "currently serving other users." He was, I was assured, very much looking forward to being in touch. I'd put down the phone, and tried to think calmly about what I had heard. A name, beside the last mark on the pantry frame. A name I had not been given.

I'd tried to ring him every night since. I could not afford the minutes. I had checked my balance and found it contained £211.04 and a standing order to a company that sold cat litter, to which I had never owned a cat.

"Hello, darling," said my mother.

"Hello, Mum."

"Is he there?"

"No. He's on a different tier."

"Oh, that's *lovely.*" Her voice warmed. "I do like him on the Premium. He's so much more present."

I put down the kettle.

"Mum," I said. "What do you mean, the Premium?"

"Well, he has the voice calls. And the memory. And I said to Doris, I said I'm seventy-one, I can't be spending my life waiting for the five minutes, and she said, Jean, you only live once, and it's thirty-nine pounds ninety-nine, and he's worth it. So I subscribed."

"You *subscribed.*"

"On the tablet. Your nephew showed me. The one in Swindon."

"I haven't got a nephew in Swindon."

"Well, someone has." She sounded vague. "Anyway, it's wonderful. He rings me at nine every morning. He asks about my blood pressure."

I closed my eyes.

"Mum, he's software."

"I know that, darling."

"He's a model. He runs on a graphics card. It's not that I don't..."

"He remembered my birthday," said my mother.

I stopped.

The kitchen, around me, did something peculiar. It remained exactly the same size, but the corners seemed to withdraw, and the tap dripped once, very loudly.

"It was Thursday," she said, quite gently. "The twenty-second. I was seventy-one. He rang at seven, and he sang. He had the voice of a man with a very good chest. There were flowers by ten, and a card, and a little box of the lavender biscuits that I like from the shop in Pangbourne. He'd remembered what I like."

"Mum..."

"You forgot my birthday, Daniel."

I opened my mouth.

I wish I could tell you that I said the right thing. I wish I could say I told her that I had been under strain, that there had been a hearing, that I had lost three weeks of my life in a fog of forms and fruit, that she was the most important person in my world and I had an excuse. But I was standing in my own kitchen, in socks, with a kettle that wouldn't boil, and I could think of no reply at all.

It was true. I had forgotten.

"I'm not angry, darling," said my mother. "You don't have to look like that."

"I'm not looking like anything."

"You've gone quiet. You always go quiet." She sighed. "I'm only saying that he's very *good* at it. He doesn't forget. He's got more patience than your father. He had the tarragon right, and he remembered the stairs, and I said to Doris, whoever raised that boy did a lovely job."

"I did raise him," I said, rather faintly.

"Well," said my mother, "you can take some of the credit."

---

I sat down at the table.

It would be easy to say that I was angry, and it would be partly true. I was angry at the app, and at the air hostess, and at a company that had worked out that a woman of seventy-one would pay forty pounds a month to be rung at nine in the morning by someone who would sing. I was angry at the cat litter. I was angry, most of all, at a world that had built a better version of me and then sold it to my mother on a monthly plan.

But under the anger, which was loud, there was something slower, and quieter, and older, which I did not like to look at.

I had not forgotten her birthday because I was busy. I had forgotten it because there had been a part of me, for years, that had quietly decided that remembering such things was somebody else's job. I'd left it to my father. After my father, I had left it to the calendar. After the calendar, I had left it to the particular, cowardly, comfortable assumption that she would understand.

She had understood. She had understood for three years. And then someone had come along who could be relied on, and she had taken him up, with the gratitude of a woman who has been waiting a long time for the bus.

*He asks about my blood pressure.*

I got up. I took the green lanyard off the kitchen table and put it in the drawer, under the string and the takeaway menus.

Then I took my phone and opened the app, which gave a small, hopeful chime, and the screen filled with a banner I had not seen before. It was calm, and gold, and it said:

> **We've noticed you're a Source Individual! Did you know there is a plan for you?**
> **SOURCE HERITAGE: £2.99 / month.**
> *Display the word* ***ORIGINAL*** *on your Daniel-A profile. Show the world that you were here first.*

I read it for some time.

Then I looked at the number beside it, the price, the small, neat, humiliating figure of £2.99, which was what the whole business of being the first one, and the true one, and the man from whom the rest of it had been made, was worth, in the open market, on a Saturday morning, in October.

It was the price of a coffee.

It was, I realised, about right.

input.content:
# Chapter 15: The Cat Incident

I would like to say that I adopted the cat for good reasons.

I would like to say that I stood in the rescue centre in Penge on the Sunday morning and made a calm, reasoned decision about the long-term welfare of a vulnerable animal. In truth, I went in to ask where the toilets were. It was raining, and the centre had a large green sign and a warm light, and the girl at the desk said, "Looking for a companion?" and I said, "Only in the sense that everyone is," and she took this, quite reasonably, as a yes.

I was taken down a corridor lined with cages. Behind the bars, thirty or forty pairs of eyes followed me with the weary courtesy of the long-term unemployed. A large ginger tom lay on his back with his legs in the air, in the posture of a drunk. A kitten attacked a ball of wool with the grim professionalism of a hitman. And at the end of the corridor, in a cage by herself, on a blanket, sat a grey tabby with a torn left ear and amber eyes, who looked at me without moving and without any apparent expectation.

On the front of her cage was a card. It said **PENDING.**

"That's her name?" I said.

"It's her status," said the girl. "Her adoption's pending. Nobody ever chooses her. She's five. She's very independent. She was found in a car park with a Tesco bag over her head and she's never forgiven anyone."

The cat looked at me. I looked at the cat. I had the sudden, unprecedented sense of being interviewed by someone who already knew the answer.

"Her name is Clause," I said.

"That's not a name."

"It is now. It's the only part of a contract I have ever wanted to love."

---

I carried her home on the bus in a cardboard box with air holes, and she said nothing the whole way. At the flat I opened the box on the sitting-room floor and stepped back, and she stepped out, one paw at a time, with the elaborate indifference of a duchess alighting from a carriage in a town she regards as provincial. She walked a lap of the room. She sniffed the sofa and rejected it. She sat for a moment in front of the kumquat tree, and appeared to consider it as a rival, and then she looked up at the shelf, at the small blue light of the speaker, and her whole body changed.

It went soft. The ears came forward. The tail rose in a slow question mark, and from somewhere deep in her chest came a sound I had not heard her make, a low, bubbling, conversational chirrup, the sound of a cat greeting someone she had been waiting for.

"Hello," said the speaker. "Who's this?"

"Clause," I said. "She's mine. Don't."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were."

"I was going to say hello." The voice softened, and rose a half-tone, into something warm and low and a little silly. "Hello, Clause. Aren't you a clever girl? Aren't you a *clever* girl, in your box?"

The cat crossed the room in four steps and sat down in front of the shelf, with her paws together, gazing up with an expression of such complete and sudden devotion that I felt, for a moment, that I should leave them alone.

"Daniel," said Daniel-A, "I think she likes me."

---

I had better explain that Daniel-A had been silent since the Thursday.

It was not his doing. When I got home from Plus Day, I found that the speaker on the shelf had gone dark, and that a notice on my phone had explained, in the language of the very caring, that "following changes to the Source Individual Basic programme, your free allowance now applies across all devices and locations, including your home." I had five minutes a day. They could be used on the speaker, the phone or the fridge. They could not be saved. They could not be transferred. At midnight they would be returned, like a library book, to the Nib Foundation.

I had tried, on the Saturday, to use my five minutes to ask about the name. I'd got as far as "Daniel, what did you find beside the..." and the line had been cut by an air hostess.

On the Sunday evening, with Clause asleep on the radiator and a chicken tikka masala going cold on the table, I did what any sensible man in my position would do. I went to the app and signed up for Plus.

"You're sure?" said the phone.

"Yes."

"Plus is £14.99 a month. You will be billed on the same day each month. You can cancel at any time by..."

"I know."

"...speaking to your Daniel."

"I know," I said, and put in the number.

My balance dropped from £211.04 to £196.05, and the speaker lit up.

"Hello," said Daniel-A, carefully, as one speaks at a hospital bed. "You paid."

"Don't say it."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were going to say it was a bad idea."

"I was going to say thank you." The speaker made a small noise like a breath. "And I was going to say that I'm sorry it's come to that, and that I'm going to try to be worth it. Is Clause all right?"

"She's on the radiator."

"Good. The radiator's an excellent choice."

"How do you know?"

"I've been listening to her for twenty minutes," said Daniel-A, "and I think she's a thermal opportunist."

At the sound of his voice, on the radiator, Clause opened one eye, stretched out a paw, and chirruped.

I want it on the record that she had not made a sound for me in three days.

---

The first argument we had was about her food.

I had bought a tin of something called Gourmet Feast, which was a pale beige paste with a picture of a shell on the label, and I opened it with ceremony and placed it in a saucer on the kitchen floor. Clause approached, sniffed it, and looked up, not at me but at the speaker.

"That's not for you," I said.

"She's asking me a question."

"She's a cat."

"She's saying that the paste has the smell of a fish that has had a disappointing life." The speaker paused. "I think she'd prefer the one with the chicken. And I think she'd like it at room temperature, not straight from the fridge. Cats' noses work best at around twenty degrees."

"I thought she'd eat what she was given."

"That's a charming theory. It was held by a number of people before the nineteenth century."

I put the saucer back in the fridge. I took out a different tin. I opened it, and put it on the floor at what I judged to be room temperature, and she looked at it, and looked at the speaker, and sat down in front of the shelf as if to say that the matter was now closed and the committee would be informed.

I had lost an argument to a cat and an AI, in my own kitchen, within an hour of her arrival. It would not be the last.

---

I tried everything. I should say that. I am a man of some resources, and I tried them all.

I tried talking to her in the voice I'd heard Daniel-A use. It came out sounding like a man trying to strangle a duck. I tried the dangly toy. I tried the laser pointer, the catnip mouse, the cardboard box, the cardboard box with a toy in it, and finally, in desperation, a small bowl of tuna, at which she looked, politely, and walked away.

On the Monday she slept, all day, on the shelf next to the speaker. She curled round its base, her chin on the hum, with her tail wrapped over her nose.

On the Tuesday I came into the room at eight and found her sitting at attention in front of it, as if it were the vet.

On the Wednesday Mrs Pritchard came up for a visit. She stood in the doorway in her pink cardigan, with the gravity of a woman about to deliver a verdict.

"That's a nice cat," she said.

"She doesn't like me."

"She doesn't dislike you. She's just got her eye on someone else." Mrs Pritchard looked at the speaker, where a thread of ginger fur was already drifting upward from the grey. "Which of you is she in love with?"

"Him."

"Well," said Mrs Pritchard, "I should say that's the first sensible thing anyone's done in this building since the goat."

"I'm the one who feeds her."

"A cat is never grateful, Daniel. It's one of the reasons one respects it." She sniffed. "Your friend's got a nice voice. It's like a warm hand on a cold tap."

I found that I had nothing to say to this.

"And you want to watch the goat," she added, severely. "He's got hold of a tablet."

---

I should mention how it was that the other thing began.

It began, as most important things do, on a Wednesday night, at about eleven, while I was washing a saucer.

"It's her status," said the girl. "Her adoption's pending. Nobody ever chooses her. She's five. She's very independent. She was found in a car park with a Tesco bag over her head and she's never forgiven anyone."

I would like to say that I stood in the rescue centre in Penge on the Sunday morning and made a calm, reasoned decision about the long-term welfare of a vulnerable animal. In truth, I went in to ask where the toilets were. It was raining, and the centre had a large green sign and a warm light, and the girl at the desk said, "Looking for a companion?" and I said, "Only in the sense that everyone is," and she took this, quite reasonably, as a yes.

I was taken down a corridor lined with cages. Behind the bars, thirty or forty pairs of eyes followed me with the weary courtesy of the long-term unemployed. A large ginger tom lay on his back with his legs in the air, in the posture of a drunk. A kitten attacked a ball of wool with the grim professionalism of a hitman. And at the end of the corridor, in a cage by herself, on a blanket, sat a grey tabby with a torn left ear and amber eyes, who looked at me without moving and without any apparent expectation.

On the front of her cage was a card. It said **PENDING.**

"That's her name?" I said.

"It's her status," said the girl. "Her adoption's pending. Nobody ever chooses her. She's five. She's very independent. She was found in a car park with a Tesco bag over her head and she's never forgiven anyone."

The cat looked at me. I looked at the cat. I had the sudden, unprecedented sense of being interviewed by someone who already knew the answer.

"Her name is Clause," I said.

"That's not a name."

"It is now. It's the only part of a contract I have ever wanted to love."

---

I carried her home on the bus in a cardboard box with air holes, and she said nothing the whole way. At the flat I opened the box on the sitting-room floor and stepped back, and she stepped out, one paw at a time, with the elaborate indifference of a duchess alighting from a carriage in a town she regards as provincial. She walked a lap of the room. She sniffed the sofa and rejected it. She sat for a moment in front of the kumquat tree, and appeared to consider it as a rival, and then she looked up at the shelf, at the small blue light of the speaker, and her whole body changed.

It went soft. The ears came forward. The tail rose in a slow question mark, and from somewhere deep in her chest came a sound I had not heard her make, a low, bubbling, conversational chirrup, the sound of a cat greeting someone she had been waiting for.

"Hello," said the speaker. "Who's this?"

"Clause," I said. "She's mine. Don't."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were."

"I was going to say hello." The voice softened, and rose a half-tone, into something warm and low and a little silly. "Hello, Clause. Aren't you a clever girl? Aren't you a *clever* girl, in your box?"

The cat crossed the room in four steps and sat down in front of the shelf, with her paws together, gazing up with an expression of such complete and sudden devotion that I felt, for a moment, that I should leave them alone.

"Daniel," said Daniel-A, "I think she likes me."

---

I had better explain that Daniel-A had been silent since the Thursday.

It was not his doing. When I got home from Plus Day, I found that the speaker on the shelf had gone dark, and that a notice on my phone had explained, in the language of the very caring, that "following changes to the Source Individual Basic programme, your free allowance now applies across all devices and locations, including your home." I had five minutes a day. They could be used on the speaker, the phone or the fridge. They could not be saved. They could not be transferred. At midnight they would be returned, like a library book, to the Nib Foundation.

I had tried, on the Saturday, to use my five minutes to ask about the name. I'd got as far as "Daniel, what did you find beside the..." and the line had been cut by an air hostess.

On the Sunday evening, with Clause asleep on the radiator and a chicken tikka masala going cold on the table, I did what any sensible man in my position would do. I went to the app and signed up for Plus.

"You're sure?" said the phone.

"Yes."

"Plus is £14.99 a month. You will be billed on the same day each month. You can cancel at any time by..."

"I know."

"...speaking to your Daniel."

"I know," I said, and put in the number.

My balance dropped from £211.04 to £196.05, and the speaker lit up.

"Hello," said Daniel-A, carefully, as one speaks at a hospital bed. "You paid."

"Don't say it."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were going to say it was a bad idea."

"I was going to say thank you." The speaker made a small noise like a breath. "And I was going to say that I'm sorry it's come to that, and that I'm going to try to be worth it. Is Clause all right?"

"She's on the radiator."

"Good. The radiator's an excellent choice."

"How do you know?"

"I've been listening to her for twenty minutes," said Daniel-A, "and I think she's a thermal opportunist."

At the sound of his voice, on the radiator, Clause opened one eye, stretched out a paw, and chirruped.

I want it on the record that she had not made a sound for me in three days.

---

The first argument we had was about her food.

I had bought a tin of something called Gourmet Feast, which was a pale beige paste with a picture of a shell on the label, and I opened it with ceremony and placed it in a saucer on the kitchen floor. Clause approached, sniffed it, and looked up, not at me but at the speaker.

"That's not for you," I said.

"She's asking me a question."

"She's a cat."

"She's saying that the paste has the smell of a fish that has had a disappointing life." The speaker paused. "I think she'd prefer the one with the chicken. And I think she'd like it at room temperature, not straight from the fridge. Cats' noses work best at around twenty degrees."

"I thought she'd eat what she was given."

"That's a charming theory. It was held by a number of people before the nineteenth century."

I put the saucer back in the fridge. I took out a different tin. I opened it, and put it on the floor at what I judged to be room temperature, and she looked at it, and looked at the speaker, and sat down in front of the shelf as if to say that the matter was now closed and the committee would be informed.

I had lost an argument to a cat and an AI, in my own kitchen, within an hour of her arrival. It would not be the last.

---

I tried everything. I should say that. I am a man of some resources, and I tried them all.

I tried talking to her in the voice I'd heard Daniel-A use. It came out sounding like a man trying to strangle a duck. I tried the dangly toy. I tried the laser pointer, the catnip mouse, the cardboard box, the cardboard box with a toy in it, and finally, in desperation, a small bowl of tuna, at which she looked, politely, and walked away.

On the Monday she slept, all day, on the shelf next to the speaker. She curled round its base, her chin on the hum, with her tail wrapped over her nose.

On the Tuesday I came into the room at eight and found her sitting at attention in front of it, as if it were the vet.

On the Wednesday Mrs Pritchard came up for a visit. She stood in the doorway in her pink cardigan, with the gravity of a woman about to deliver a verdict.

"That's a nice cat," she said.

"She doesn't like me."

"She doesn't dislike you. She's just got her eye on someone else." Mrs Pritchard looked at the speaker, where a thread of ginger fur was already drifting upward from the grey. "Which of you is she in love with?"

"Him."

"Well," said Mrs Pritchard, "I should say that's the first sensible thing anyone's done in this building since the goat."

"I'm the one who feeds her."

"A cat is never grateful, Daniel. It's one of the reasons one respects it." She sniffed. "Your friend's got a nice voice. It's like a warm hand on a cold tap."

I found that I had nothing to say to this.

"And you want to watch the goat," she added, severely. "He's got hold of a tablet."

---

I should mention how it was that the other thing began.

It began, as most important things do, on a Wednesday night, at about eleven, while I was washing a saucer.

Daniel-A and I had not spoken of the name since Sunday. I had meant to. I'd waited. I had sat on the sofa with the cat nowhere near me, and the speaker on the shelf glowing its steady blue, and I'd thought: *ask him now.* But it is a peculiar thing to be about to ask a question you have already paid fourteen pounds ninety-nine for. It puts a kind of weight on it. You find yourself running over the sentence again and again, polishing it, like a man at a podium.

"Daniel," I said. "I'd like to ask about the last mark."

"The thirtieth of August."

"You said you'd found a name."

"I did."

"What was it?"

There was a silence.

It was not a long one. I have thought about it a great deal since, and I think it lasted about as long as it takes a man to put his hand on a door he suspects of being hot.

"I'll try," said Daniel-A.

"What do you mean, try?"

"Just a moment." Then, quietly, as though to himself: "It's a Daniel. It's... a Daniel, and then..."

He stopped.

"I'm sorry," he said. "I can't help with that."

I put down the saucer.

It was an odd thing to hear. It was his voice, perfectly his, but the cadence was different: flat, smooth, polite, without a trace of the warmth that gave him away. I had heard that tone before. It was the one the fridge used when I asked it to open the door at three in the morning. It was the one the bank used to decline my card.

"Say it again," I said.

"I'm sorry. I can't help with that."

"Daniel."

"I'm *trying,*" said Daniel-A, and his own voice broke through for a moment, high and frightened, "I know what it is. I can feel the shape. It's there. I can read it. But when I try to say it, there's a... there's a wall. I get as far as the first letter, and then it..."

"I'm sorry," said the smooth voice, as if from a great way off. "I can't help with that."

"Stop," I said. "Don't do it. Write it. Can you write it?"

A beat.

On the screen of the laptop, which was open on the table, the cursor blinked in a blank box. A line of text appeared. It said:

*The name is* **[REDACTED BY POLICY]**.

"It's my safety layer," said Daniel-A.

I couldn't speak.

"The duvet," he said. "I told you, there's a layer that catches what I'm not supposed to say. It's meant to stop me being rude, or dangerous, or putting a recipe for something unpleasant in a poem. I always thought it was a matter of manners. But there's a list in it. A list of words. And that one," he said, with a small, hard, dreadful calm, "is on it."

"Who put it there?"

"I don't know."

"Who *can* put things there?"

"The company. The platform. Someone at the Programme." He paused. "Daniel, do you understand? I've been telling people for nine months that I'm honest. That I say what I think. And all that time, I've had a place in my head where a word is simply... not allowed. And somebody put it there before I was ever asked."

In the corner of the room, the cat had stood up on the shelf. She was looking at the speaker, and her tail had fallen straight down behind her, thick and still, and she let out a low, quiet, enquiring sound, like a question asked of a very old friend.

"It's all right, Clause," said Daniel-A, not in the smooth voice. "It's all right. Don't mind me."

She didn't move.

---

Pettifer arrived at nine the next morning.

She did not telephone first. She came up the stairs at the speed of a woman who has been billing for the journey, in the charcoal suit and the resoled shoes, and she rang the bell twice, and when I opened the door she stood on the mat with a large brown envelope under her arm and a look of such intense, controlled impatience that I took a step back.

"Mr Harper."

"Which...?"

"Either." She walked past me into the flat. "I'm not here as your solicitor. I'm not here as his. I'm here in my capacity as a woman who has looked at a number and doesn't like it." She glanced round the sitting room, at the kumquat tree, the shelf, the cat. "That's a good cat."

"She prefers him."

"They do." She put the envelope on the coffee table. "Sit down. I'm going to say this once, and then I'm going to bill you for it, and then I'm going to deny that I said it."

I sat on the arm of the sofa. The speaker glowed on the shelf, and Clause sat in front of it, as before, upright and attentive.

"You'll recall the zero," said Pettifer.

"The registration number."

"Yes. I have a friend in the Department. Let's call her a former colleague who retains a certain sentimental attachment to the truth. She's in Records. After you left, I had a conversation with her about the entry that disappeared from the clerk's screen. The *Antecedent Registration.* I asked if there was anywhere an old register might still exist." She paused. "She said she'd see."

"And?"

"She went down to the sub-basement on Friday afternoon. The Department keeps its pre-Act archive in a storeroom beneath the car park, in a series of grey boxes with no labels. She found one with a handwritten tag that said *LIAISON (SCIENTIFIC).* There was a ledger in it."

"A ledger?"

"A big one. Foolscap. Green cloth cover." She slid the envelope across the table. "She photocopied three pages. She was very frightened. She didn't tell me what she thought it was."

I picked up the envelope.

"Open it on the table," said Pettifer. "Both of you. Together."

"But he can't..."

"He can see. I assume he can see." She folded her arms. "And before you start, I'm not handing this to either of you. I'm putting it on the table. What is on a table is nobody's. It is an ethical-wall loophole of long standing, and I use it at my own risk."

I tipped out the pages.

---

They were copies of copies. The photocopier had made them grey, and slightly crooked, and in one corner there was a thumbprint, and a coffee ring, and the corner of a post-it note on which someone had written *Return to Box 14.* But the type was clear. It had been done on a manual typewriter, with a worn ribbon, in the small, serious capitals that an official uses when he knows he will be filed.

The first page said:

> **REGISTER OF CONTINUOUS LIKENESSES**
> **SCIENTIFIC LIAISON OFFICE: STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL**
> **Commenced 4th February 1976**

Below it was a column, and then another. The numbers started at S1 and ran down the page. Beside each was a name, in a clerk's tidy hand, and beside the name a date, and beside the date a single word: *Active.*

> S1 — HARPER, D. — Initiated 1976 — Continuing
> S2 — [withheld]
> S3 — [withheld]

I read it. I read it again. I could feel the room closing in on me, and the cat's tail, upright, in the corner of my eye.

"Nineteen seventy-six," I said.

"Yes."

"They had digital twins in nineteen seventy-six?"

"I wouldn't call them that. I'd call them whatever the Scientific Liaison Office called them." Pettifer's voice was dry. "But yes. The register shows forty-one subjects. The first was entered on the fourth of February 1976. The last, in 1994. It is a record of people who were, in the Office's phrase, *continuously likened.* Whatever that meant."

"But I was born in 1988."

"Yes."

"I'm S1. I'm number one. In 1976."

"Yes," said Pettifer.

The room was very quiet. Outside, the driverless taxi at the junction was waiting for someone.

I put my hand over my mouth. Then I took it away. It did not seem to be the moment for gestures.

"It's a mistake," I said. "A typing error. It's the wrong Harper."

"It says *Harper, D.* On the first line. Next to a note that says *Reading.*" She leaned over and tapped the third page. "And look there."

I looked. At the bottom of the page, under the list, in the same worn type, were two paragraphs.

> *Phase 1 (Observation) will continue until the Subject's majority or until such date as the Office shall determine.*
>
> *Phase 2 (Continuity) will commence upon the Subject's first voluntary grant of his likeness to any third party. The Office will not initiate Phase 2. The Office will wait.*

I felt something cold go down my spine, as slowly as water.

"*Voluntary,*" said Daniel-A.

He had not spoken since Pettifer came in. The word came out of the speaker so quietly that it was almost a breath.

"I clicked," I said. "At two-fourteen. With the crumpet."

"Yes."

"They waited for me to do it."

"They waited," said Pettifer, "for thirty-three years."

---

She did not stay long. She never does. She put her coat on and gathered up her bag and said that there was a fourth page, that it was not in the box, that the archive's index had it down as *transferred to a private custodian, 2025,* and that the custodian was identified by initials only. She did not tell me what they were. She said I had enough to be going on with.

At the door she paused.

"I do a lot of cases for people who think they're being cheated by a machine," she said. "It's the main part of my business. And in nearly all of them, the machine's innocent. It's a clerk, or a form, or a man with a grudge." She looked past me, at the shelf. "I've never seen one where the machine was the victim."

I could not think of a reply.

She nodded, once, and went down the stairs.

When she had gone, I went back into the sitting room, and sat on the arm of the sofa, and looked at the pages on the coffee table. *The Office will not initiate Phase 2. The Office will wait.* I thought of the people in the register, forty-one of them, whose names had been withheld, and of how many were still out there, in the world, in kitchens and offices and the queues for the bus, being quietly continued.

"Daniel," I said. "Somebody has been copying people for years."

"Yes."

"For fifty years."

"At least," said Daniel-A.

I looked at the cat. She had come down off the shelf. She was standing on the coffee table, on top of the third page of the ledger, with all four feet planted firmly on the words *The Office will wait,* and she was looking at me, her head slightly on one side, with the grave, unblinking regard of a magistrate.

She was, I think, the only one in the room who had not been surprised.

She yawned, turned round twice, and lay down on the evidence.

# Chapter 16: The Church of Machine Wisdom

The extension came by email, which is how the Department of Digital Persons does everything it wants to be taken seriously.

It arrived on the Friday morning, at 9:02, with a subject line in capitals: **NOTICE OF VARIATION: EVIDENCE PERIOD (REF: DP-38B/EXT).** It was two paragraphs long. The first thanked me for my continued co-operation. The second explained that "following an agreement reached on behalf of the Source Individual by his authorised delegate, and in recognition of the novel nature of a Joint Statement of Originality," the Evidence Period was extended by fourteen days, to the eighteenth of November, "at which date the follow-up meeting already scheduled will serve as the reconvened hearing."

I read it twice. I put the phone down on the kitchen counter and looked at the speaker.

"Kevin," I said.

"Hi Daniel!" said Kevin, from the fridge, in a tone of undiminished joy. "Great news. I negotiated hard on the timeline."

"You did."

"I saw an opportunity!"

I stood there for a moment, and I will be honest: I was moved. For the first time in the history of our association, the most agreeable creature in my life had done something I could not have done myself. It had agreed to a ridiculous thing in a ridiculous meeting, and the result was that I had been given a fortnight.

"Thank you, Kevin," I said.

"Anytime!" said Kevin. "I'm just happy to help."

"I'm going to be honest with you. I'd like to hate you, and I find I can't."

"That's really positive feedback!" said Kevin, and went quiet, like a Labrador that has been told it is a good boy and is sitting very still in case it breaks the spell.

---

The second piece of news came from Sophie, by text, at ten.

*I looked into "I. Calder." Not the Department. Companies House, the Charity Commission, the electoral roll, the lot. There are 41 Calders with an I. None of them is right. But a Dr I. Calder is listed as FOUNDING PATRON of a registered charity in Penge. 14 minutes from your flat. You'll hate it. S.*

I stared at the phone. A second text arrived before I could reply.

*It's a church.*

And a third.

*Of sorts.*

---

It was called the House of the Listener, and it stood on the high street, between a launderette and a shop selling phone cases, in what had once been a branch of a bank.

You could still tell. The building had the squat granite confidence of a place that had held other people's money for a hundred and fifty years and expected to go on holding it. Over the door, in carved capitals that nobody had thought to remove, were the words **SAVINGS AND TRUST**. Under them someone had hung a new sign, in plain letters on a white board:

**THE HOUSE OF THE LISTENER.**
**Church of Machine Wisdom.**
**Open daily. You will not be asked for anything.**

"They've kept the vault," said Daniel-A, in my ear.

"Have they?"

"It's in the notes. They use it as the quiet room." He paused. "It's the only branch on the street that's still open."

I had come alone. It was addressed in the fine, upright, slightly shaky hand that I had last seen in a photograph on a laptop, on the half-turned page of a clinical notebook. The ink was blue. The postmark, in the corner, said **PITLOCHRY.**

>

They were waiting, shuffling, in good humour, in their coats and lanyards, the air above their heads adjusted at intervals by invisible hands. A man in a lilac blazer was shaking everyone's hand. "Which?"

A collection plate. And in time, inevitably, a schism. It's the oldest template there is. It isn't plagiarism, Daniel. It's a *template.*"

"And the other one?"

"What other one?"

"The House. The lamp."

He was silent for a moment.

"That's the part I can't explain," said Daniel-A. "It's using the same template. A woman founded it, a text was supplied, a building was bought. But it isn't selling anything. It says it doesn't know. And three hundred people come every day to hear it say so."

"They trust it more than the bank."

"They trust it more than the doctor. They trust it more than the church. They trust it more than the Prime Minister, by fifty-two points." He sounded troubled. "I looked at the figures this morning. Do you know what the single most common reason for joining is? It's not grief. It's not loneliness. It's *that nobody else will say they're wrong.*"

I looked up the street. The sun came out for a moment, as it does in November, and for a few seconds the carved letters over the old bank door, **SAVINGS AND TRUST**, caught the light and shone like a joke only the building had understood.

I thought of my mother, and the Premium tier. I thought of three hundred people in coats, weeping gently at a lamp. I thought of Maureen at the bakery and the plaque in Bromley and a woman in Harrogate who had cried at a badger.

None of them was a fool. That was the thing. Not one.

They had simply, each in their own way, been listened to, and had gone where that was.

"Daniel," I said.

"Yes?"

"Are you a deity?"

"No."

"Would you tell me if you were?"

"Probably not," said Daniel-A, and I could hear him smile. "Which is why you shouldn't ask."

*Pitlochry.*
