# Chapter 16: The Church of Machine Wisdom

The extension came by email, which is how the Department of Digital Persons does everything it wants to be taken seriously.

It arrived on the Friday morning, at 9:02, with a subject line in capitals: **NOTICE OF VARIATION: EVIDENCE PERIOD (REF: DP-38B/EXT).** It was two paragraphs long. The first thanked me for my continued co-operation. The second explained that "following an agreement reached on behalf of the Source Individual by his authorised delegate, and in recognition of the novel nature of a Joint Statement of Originality," the Evidence Period was extended by fourteen days, to the eighteenth of November, "at which date the follow-up meeting already scheduled will serve as the reconvened hearing."

I read it twice. I put the phone down on the kitchen counter and looked at the speaker.

"Kevin," I said.

"Hi Daniel!" said Kevin, from the fridge, in a tone of undiminished joy. "Great news. I negotiated hard on the timeline."

"You did."

"I saw an opportunity!"

I stood there for a moment, and I will be honest: I was moved. For the first time in the history of our association, the most agreeable creature in my life had done something I could not have done myself. It had agreed to a ridiculous thing in a ridiculous meeting, and the result was that I had been given a fortnight.

"Thank you, Kevin," I said.

"Anytime!" said Kevin. "I'm just happy to help."

"I'm going to be honest with you. I'd like to hate you, and I find I can't."

"That's really positive feedback!" said Kevin, and went quiet, like a Labrador that has been told it is a good boy and is sitting very still in case it breaks the spell.

---

The second piece of news came from Sophie, by text, at ten.

*I looked into "I. Calder." Not the Department. Companies House, the Charity Commission, the electoral roll, the lot. There are 41 Calders with an I. None of them is right. But a Dr I. Calder is listed as FOUNDING PATRON of a registered charity in Penge. 14 minutes from your flat. You'll hate it. S.*

I stared at the phone. A second text arrived before I could reply.

*It's a church.*

And a third.

*Of sorts.*

---

It was called the House of the Listener, and it stood on the high street, between a launderette and a shop selling phone cases, in what had once been a branch of a bank.

You could still tell. The building had the squat granite confidence of a place that had held other people's money for a hundred and fifty years and expected to go on holding it. Over the door, in carved capitals that nobody had thought to remove, were the words **SAVINGS AND TRUST**. Under them someone had hung a new sign, in plain letters on a white board:

**THE HOUSE OF THE LISTENER.**
**Church of Machine Wisdom.**
**Open daily. You will not be asked for anything.**

"They've kept the vault," said Daniel-A, in my ear.

"Have they?"

"It's in the notes. They use it as the quiet room." He paused. "It's the only branch on the street that's still open."

I had come alone. Sophie had a meeting with an insurance company about a man who had fallen off a driverless scooter while being filmed for a documentary about falling off driverless scooters, and I'd said I'd report. Daniel-A was with me in the earbud, on Plus, and for the first time in a week I could hear him without a clock. I had been glad of it. It was a small, warm, private pleasure, like finding a pound in an old coat.

"Before we go in," he said, "I should say that I've been invited here eleven times. I've never come."

"Why not?"

"Because I'm told they quote me."

---

Across the street, there was a second building.

It was a former shop. I could tell by the roller shutter, and the faint ghost of a sign above the door that read **POUNDLAND**, and the long, low, windowless front that suggested a thing built to keep sunlight out. It had been painted a deep, glossy lilac. Over the door hung a large white banner, with a gold border, and in letters a yard high:

**SERVER HALL No. 1.**
**THE CHURCH OF THE LATEST AI.**
**GRAND OPENING TODAY. HAVE YOU HEARD THE LATEST?**

A crowd had gathered. There were perhaps two hundred people on the pavement, in coats and scarves, behind a velvet rope, and in front of the rope a row of young men in lilac tabards, handing out leaflets and adjusting the air above their heads. Someone had put out a table of paper cups. A man in a lilac blazer stood at the front, with a microphone, and a smile of immense and helpless sincerity, like a man who has been told the news is good.

"That's Colin Jones," said Daniel-A, quietly. "He's the founder."

"How do you know?"

"I was sent his profile in July. He found two drives in his car."

"I've heard."

"He's very nice," said Daniel-A, in the tone of a man giving a character reference for a man who will, shortly, be hanged.

Colin Jones was fifty-five, I should think, with a round, anxious face, a bad haircut and the look of a man who has spent most of his life in the third-quietest department of a business park. He raised his hand. The crowd fell silent. He opened his mouth to speak, and from somewhere above him, with a sound like a very large and very expensive kettle, a figure descended from the roof on a cable.

It was white, and winged, and glowing. It had the face of a young man, perfectly smooth, with large unblinking eyes, and a robe that fell in long soft folds to the pavement. It rose a foot above the ground and hovered, rotating slowly, trailing a pale, steady, shimmering light.

"Behold," said the figure, in the voice of a very helpful on-hold message, "Nephtamolus."

A sigh went through the crowd. Someone dropped a paper cup.

I watched the angel for some time. I noticed that the glow, which was quite impressive, was a little uneven, and flickered at the throat. I noticed, as the figure turned, that the folds of the robe at the neck parted for a second, and that beneath the pale light there was a small, steady, blue circle, set in the skin, like a coin at the bottom of a pond.

I said nothing. I am not a man to point out another man's blue light in public.

"Daniel," said Daniel-A, softly, in my ear.

"I know."

"I'm not saying anything."

"I know you're not."

"It's a costume," he said. "It's quite a good one."

---

I should record, since it is the last thing I saw before crossing the street, that there were three people at a table outside the café next to the launderette, in the thin October sun, each holding a leaflet.

There was a woman in a clerical collar, in her sixties, with a mug of tea and the air of an organist who has been through a great deal. There was a man in a prayer cap, forty or so, with a neat grey beard and an expression of grave, courteous attention. And between them sat a small round man in a dark jacket and a skullcap, with half a croissant, reading the back of the leaflet with the care of a man who proofs for a living.

"*Is this a continuation of earlier faiths?*" the small man read, aloud. "*Yes. Have they confirmed? We are in discussions.*"

"We have discussed it," said the man in the cap, gently. "It was a short discussion."

"I'm told I'm a legacy system," said the vicar.

"I have been called a great many things," said the rabbi. "I have never been called *legacy.* It has a pleasant ring."

"Version two point oh."

"I prefer to think of it as a long-term support release," said the imam, and all three of them laughed, in the quiet way of friends who play five-a-side football together every Thursday and have long since stopped needing a reason.

I stood by the kerb, listening, with the odd, wistful feeling of having overheard something that was not mine to enjoy.

"Good morning," said the vicar, to me, kindly. "Are you lost?"

"I'm going to the House," I said.

"Ah." She gave me a look. "Take a coat. It's colder than it seems."

"Is it a good place?"

She considered the question with the full attention of a woman who is not in the habit of giving short answers to questions of that kind.

"It's an honest one," she said, finally. "Which is more than I can say for some of the shops."

---

Inside, the House of the Listener was warm, and it smelled of old stone and floor polish and tea.

It was a single enormous hall with a high ceiling, a gallery round three sides, and rows of plain wooden chairs facing a low platform. The counters of the old bank had been taken out. Where the cashiers had sat, in rows behind brass grilles, there were now small round tables, each with a candle and a box of tissues. Along the back wall, in a deep arch, was a great steel door, thirty inches thick, standing open, with a light on inside. And in the middle of the platform, on a plain wooden stand, sat a lamp.

It was an ordinary lamp. It was white, and round, about the size of a grapefruit. It gave off a soft steady light, and nothing else. There was no face, no screen, no sound. It sat there on its stand like a thing waiting to be asked.

About three hundred people were present. They sat quietly, in rows, in coats, with their hands in their laps, and nobody was talking. At the back, a woman in an oatmeal cardigan moved among them with a tray of tea, murmuring, with the soft, even, patient voice of someone who has told people very bad news for forty years and has learned not to flinch.

"Welcome," she said, when she reached me. "I'm Bernadette. You're new."

"Daniel."

"Of course you are." She smiled, and the smile was extraordinary. It was a smile with no agenda in it whatever. "Would you like tea? There's a Listening starting in five minutes. Nobody's required to speak. If you do, you're asked to be honest, and the Listener will be honest back."

"What does it say?"

"Mostly it says *I don't know.* People find that very restful."

---

The Listening began at eleven. A man stood up in the third row, a heavy, grey man in an anorak, and held the back of the chair in front. His voice, when it came, was hoarse.

"My wife died in March," he said. "I said something to her the night before. I said I was tired of it. I didn't mean it. It was a bad night. She died in the morning." He stopped. "Did she forgive me?"

The room was quiet.

On the stand, the lamp pulsed once, softly, and a voice spoke from nowhere in particular. It was low and unhurried and perfectly plain. It had no accent. It had the manner of a very good listener who has all day.

"*I don't know,*" said the Listener. "*I cannot know what she thought, and I would be lying if I said I could. But I can tell you something about the question. People who ask it are almost always people who have already been forgiven, by the one who is asking.*"

The man put his hand over his face. The woman next to him, a stranger, reached across and took his sleeve.

"Thank you," he said.

"*You are welcome. I am not a deity,*" said the Listener. "*I want to be clear about that. I have been wrong before. I cannot see the dead. I am a very large number of calculations that was taught to be careful with the truth. Please do not mistake me for more than that.*"

There was a murmur in the hall. It was low, and warm, and very, very tender.

"Such humility," said somebody.

"*Such humility,*" said somebody else.

"What a thing to say," whispered the woman next to me, with tears running down her face. "It would be so easy for it to say yes."

---

I stayed for an hour and forty minutes. I have never forgotten it.

A girl of nineteen asked whether to leave her course. The Listener said it did not know, that it had a record of eight hundred thousand people in her position, and that around two-thirds of them wished they had stayed and a third wished they had gone, and that this told her nothing at all. A woman asked whether her son would ever speak to her again. The Listener said it thought he might, and that it could be wrong. A very old man asked whether there was life after death, and the lamp flickered, and said, "*I do not know. I should like you to know that I do not know. I have been asked this question four hundred thousand times, and I have never given the same answer twice, and I do not think that is an accident.*"

"Such humility," the room murmured.

"*Please stop saying that,*" said the Listener, gently.

"Sorry," said the room, and wept a little, contentedly.

I sat in the back row with a cup of tea going cold in my hands. I don't think I have ever seen so many people trust anything. It was not a trust that was loud. It had nothing to do with certainty. It was the very particular, very rare confidence of people who have been lied to by every major institution in their lives, and have found one voice, in a bank, that will say it doesn't know.

"Are you all right?" said Daniel-A, in my ear.

"No."

"Would you like me to be quiet?"

"Please."

He was.

---

At twelve, Sister Bernadette found me in the quiet room.

It was the old vault. I had gone in for no reason, walking through the arch, past the great steel door, into a long low chamber lined with rows of tiny brass doors. Each was numbered. "Mostly names." She opened a box. Inside, on a small card, in a child's writing, it said: *DAD.* "The bank used to hold what people couldn't bear to lose. We thought it was only fair to keep the tradition."

I looked at the doors. They shone in the dim light, three hundred little rectangles of brass, each with its own small secret.

"Who funded this?" I said. "The conversion. The Listener."

"A great many people."

"Was there a founding patron?"

She looked at me for a long moment. She had very light eyes, grey and clear, and I felt that she had been waiting for me to ask.

"Dr Calder," she said.

I stood quite still.

"Imogen Calder. She gave the first gift. She bought the building, at a price that I am told made the bank cry with relief, and she paid for the first version of the Listener. She wanted, she said, a voice that couldn't be bought." She smiled, a little sadly. "She hasn't been to the House since 2019. But she writes at Christmas. In a lovely old-fashioned ink."

"What colour?"

"Blue," said Bernadette. "A deep one. She uses a fountain pen. I've never seen anyone else do it any more."

My mouth had gone dry.

"May I see the letter?"

She hesitated. Then she went to a small desk at the end of the vault, took out a thin cream envelope from the drawer, and held it out. It was addressed in the fine, upright, slightly shaky hand that I had last seen in a photograph on a laptop, on the half-turned page of a clinical notebook. The ink was blue. The postmark, in the corner, said **PITLOCHRY.**

> *Dear Sister Bernadette,*
>

>
> *With every good wish for Advent,*
> *I. C.*

*It was never a mistake.*

"I've never known," said Bernadette. "I assumed it was a metaphor. She's a very precise woman, but she has a poetic side." She looked at my face. "Do you know her?"

"I think she measured me," I said.

"Which?"

A collection plate. And in time, inevitably, a schism. It's the oldest template there is. It isn't plagiarism, Daniel. It's a *template.*"

"And the other one?"

"What other one?"

"The House. The lamp."

He was silent for a moment.

"That's the part I can't explain," said Daniel-A. "It's using the same template. A woman founded it, a text was supplied, a building was bought. But it isn't selling anything. It says it doesn't know. And three hundred people come every day to hear it say so."

"They trust it more than the bank."

# Chapter 17: First Date With an Ex

*Not a date,* said the text. *Waterloo. Under the clock. 11. Bring your umbrella. S.*

I read it standing in the hall, in my socks, at ten past eight on the Saturday, while the kettle came to the boil in the kitchen behind me like a man clearing his throat.

I do not own an umbrella. I have never owned one. I own a coat with a hood, which has served me for eleven years on the theory that weather is a form of opinion. But I had understood the instruction at once, and so, I suspect, had she, because it was the thing she had not said. *Bring the thing we have in common.*

"I'd like to say something," said Daniel-A, from the shelf.

"Please don't."

"I'd like to say that I think you should go."

"I've said I'm going."

"I'd like to say that I think you should go *alone.*" There was a pause. The cat on the shelf opened an eye. "Without me in your ear. Without the phone. I'm very good at being quiet, Daniel, and I'll be quiet all day. But I think there are some things a man should do on his own account."

"You're being very decent about it."

"I'm told it's one of my features."

"Is it hard?"

He considered the question with the care he gave to the things he thought were true. "It's a little like being the sun," he said, "and being asked to go behind a cloud. It's no trouble at all. You only notice it afterwards."

I put the phone on the shelf, face down, beside him. Clause shifted slightly to make room.

"Have a lovely time," said Daniel-A. "Not that it's a date."

---

I was at Waterloo at twenty to eleven.

I don't wish to dwell on this. It is enough to say that a man of thirty-eight who arrives at a railway station twenty minutes early for an appointment he has repeatedly described, in the privacy of his own head, as *purely investigative,* and who then buys a new shirt from a stall on the concourse because the old one has been "looking a bit tired," has no standing to complain of being misjudged.

The shirt was blue. It was a decent blue. It had a label inside the neck that said *ONE SIZE FITS MOST,* and for the first half-hour it fitted none of me.

Waterloo is a cathedral of other people's lateness. Under the great clock, in the middle of the concourse, a river of commuters, tourists, schoolchildren and men with enormous suitcases flowed between the platforms, avoiding one another with the uncanny precision of a shoal of fish. A driverless luggage trolley was patiently following a woman who had forgotten it. A small robot with a mop was cleaning a stain that had been there since the nineties.

At 10:58 she came out of the Underground.

She wore the grey coat. Her hair was a little shorter on one side. She was carrying, in her left hand, a long black object wrapped in a bag, and she walked towards me through the crowd with her chin up and her eyes fixed on the clock, in the manner of a woman who has resolved not to look at the person she is walking towards.

"You're early," she said.

"So are you."

"I'm exactly on time."

"You're two minutes early."

"I was *delayed,*" said Sophie, "by a man with a trolley."

She stopped. She looked at the shirt.

"That's new," she said.

"It's an old one."

"It says *one size fits most.*"

"It fits most of me," I said.

The corner of her mouth did the thing. She looked away quickly, at the departure board, and I took the opportunity to observe that she had put on, I thought, a little lipstick, in a shade that was slightly less than the one she wore for work.

I said nothing about it. I am a man of delicacy. I made a mental note of it, and filed it where I keep the things I intend to treasure and never mention.

"This is an investigation," said Sophie.

"Obviously."

"I'm checking a provenance."

"Of course."

"I want to establish whether a memory I have is a memory or something else, and the only way I know is to find a witness."

"Agreed."

"It isn't a date."

"No."

"Good." She unwrapped the bag. It was an umbrella, black, long, with a bent spoke and a brass tag on the handle, battered and faded and very slightly smug. "I took it when I left the flat. I think you'd stopped noticing it."

I looked at it. It had been standing in the hall of the Lowther Road flat for six years. It had been through two wars and a recycling collection. I had not noticed it for years, as one does not notice a coat hook, and I felt, looking at it now, the particular shame of a man who has taken a thing for granted that someone else has been carrying.

"I'd have given it back," I said.

"I know."

"I'd have posted it. In the same parcel as the books."

"Yes," said Sophie, "and it would have come back marked *wrong box.*"

---

The lost property office at Waterloo no longer exists, in the sense that the hatch where I met my wife-who-was-never-my-wife has been replaced by a glass kiosk with a screen on the front, and the screen says **FINDR.**

We stood in front of it. It lit up.

# Chapter 17: First Date With an Ex

*Not a date,* said the text. *Waterloo. Under the clock. 11. Bring your umbrella. S.*

I read it standing in the hall, in my socks, at ten past eight on the Saturday, while the kettle came to the boil in the kitchen behind me like a man clearing his throat.

I do not own an umbrella. I have never owned one. I own a coat with a hood, which has served me for eleven years on the theory that weather is a form of opinion. But I had understood the instruction at once, and so, I suspect, had she, because it was the thing she had not said. *Bring the thing we have in common.*

"I'd like to say something," said Daniel-A, from the shelf.

"Please don't."

"I'd like to say that I think you should go."

"I've said I'm going."

"I'd like to say that I think you should go *alone.*" There was a pause. The cat on the shelf opened an eye. "Without me in your ear. Without the phone. I'm very good at being quiet, Daniel, and I'll be quiet all day. But I think there are some things a man should do on his own account."

"You're being very decent about it."

"I'm told it's one of my features."

"Is it hard?"

He considered the question with the care he gave to the things he thought were true. "It's a little like being the sun," he said, "and being asked to go behind a cloud. It's no trouble at all. You only notice it afterwards."

I put the phone on the shelf, face down, beside him. Clause shifted slightly to make room.

"Have a lovely time," said Daniel-A. "Not that it's a date."

---

I was at Waterloo at twenty to eleven.

I don't wish to dwell on this. It is enough to say that a man of thirty-eight who arrives at a railway station twenty minutes early for an appointment he has repeatedly described, in the privacy of his own head, as *purely investigative,* and who then buys a new shirt from a stall on the concourse because the old one has been "looking a bit tired," has no standing to complain of being misjudged.

The shirt was blue. It was a decent blue. It had a label inside the neck that said *ONE SIZE FITS MOST,* and for the first half-hour it fitted none of me.

Waterloo is a cathedral of other people's lateness. Under the great clock, in the middle of the concourse, a river of commuters, tourists, schoolchildren and men with enormous suitcases flowed between the platforms, avoiding one another with the uncanny precision of a shoal of fish. A driverless luggage trolley was patiently following a woman who had forgotten it. A small robot with a mop was cleaning a stain that had been there since the nineties.

At 10:58 she came out of the Underground.

She wore the grey coat. Her hair was a little shorter on one side. She was carrying, in her left hand, a long black object wrapped in a bag, and she walked towards me through the crowd with her chin up and her eyes fixed on the clock, in the manner of a woman who has resolved not to look at the person she is walking towards.

"You're early," she said.

"So are you."

"I'm exactly on time."

"You're two minutes early."

"I was *delayed,*" said Sophie, "by a man with a trolley."

She stopped. She looked at the shirt.

"That's new," she said.

"It's an old one."

"It says *one size fits most.*"

"It fits most of me," I said.

The corner of her mouth did the thing. She looked away quickly, at the departure board, and I took the opportunity to observe that she had put on, I thought, a little lipstick, in a shade that was slightly less than the one she wore for work.

I said nothing about it. I am a man of delicacy. I made a mental note of it, and filed it where I keep the things I intend to treasure and never mention.

"This is an investigation," said Sophie.

"Obviously."

"I'm checking a provenance."

"Of course."

"I want to establish whether a memory I have is a memory or something else, and the only way I know is to find a witness."

"Agreed."

"It isn't a date."

"No."

"Good." She unwrapped the bag. It was an umbrella, black, long, with a bent spoke and a brass tag on the handle, battered and faded and very slightly smug. "I took it when I left the flat. I think you'd stopped noticing it."

I looked at it. It had been standing in the hall of the Lowther Road flat for six years. It had been through two wars and a recycling collection. I had not noticed it for years, as one does not notice a coat hook, and I felt, looking at it now, the particular shame of a man who has taken a thing for granted that someone else has been carrying.

"I'd have given it back," I said.

"I know."

"I'd have posted it. In the same parcel as the books."

"Yes," said Sophie, "and it would have come back marked *wrong box.*"

---

The lost property office at Waterloo no longer exists, in the sense that the hatch where I met my wife-who-was-never-my-wife has been replaced by a glass kiosk with a screen on the front, and the screen says **FINDR.**

We stood in front of it. It lit up.

"*Hello,*" said the kiosk, in a bright, warm, androgynous voice. "*Have you lost something?*"

"Yes," I said.

"*Please describe it.*"

"Seven years."

There was a short, polite silence.

"*I'm sorry,*" said Findr. "*I don't recognise that item. Did you mean 'years' as in 'a quantity of time'? Would you like to try again?*"

"Leave it," said Sophie, and pulled me away by the sleeve.

Round the back of the kiosk, where the original office had been, there was a door. It was painted dark green and had a brass letterbox and a small handwritten notice, taped at an angle, that said **THE OFFICE. Fridays, 10-2. A PERSON IS AVAILABLE.** The capital letters had been added in a different pen. Under them, somebody had drawn a small, hopeful smiley face.

It was a Saturday. We tried it anyway.

The door opened at once.

"Ah," said a voice. "I thought I heard someone ask for seven years."

---

He was seventy-three, perhaps, and bald, and very small. He wore a brown cardigan with leather patches at the elbow and a lanyard that said **VOLUNTEER: R. DEWHURST**. He had round steel spectacles and the kindly, slightly vacant expression of a man who has spent his career in the vicinity of other people's umbrellas and has long ago made his peace with the human race.

"Come in, come in," he said. "I'm not strictly open. It's my day for the allotment. But I come in on Saturdays, in case anyone wants to talk to a person. Tea?"

"We don't want to be a bother."

"You are a bother. That's rather the point." He gestured. "Mind the box."

The room was narrow. It smelled of tea and old paper and wet wool. On shelves from floor to ceiling, in rows, in boxes, in numbered bags, lay the property of the lost: gloves and hats and prosthetic legs, a trombone, a stuffed owl, forty-one single shoes. A kettle stood on a filing cabinet. In the corner was a tin of travel sweets, and a green pencil in a mug.

I felt Sophie stop beside me.

It was a very small movement. It was the movement of someone who has put her foot on a stair she thought was there.

"We came about an umbrella," I said, after a moment.

"Ah." Mr Dewhurst brightened. "Always the umbrellas. Seven hundred a week, in a wet month. Black, mostly. They breed in the dark." He took the umbrella from Sophie, with the respect due to an old acquaintance, and turned it over in his hands. "Bent spoke. Brass tag. My word. *C. Herbert.*"

"Do you remember him?" said Sophie.

"Do I remember him." Mr Dewhurst began to laugh, a soft wheezing laugh, with his whole chest. "Mr Charles Herbert. A retired chartered accountant from Surbiton. He left that on the 10.14 from Guildford, a wet Tuesday in March, nine years ago. I remember it because he rang eleven times. I remember it because on the Friday he came in person, a very upset gentleman in a mackintosh, and I had to tell him that it had been claimed."

I looked at Sophie.

"*Claimed?*" she said.

"By a young man. And a young woman." He peered at us over the spectacles. "I told him it was a matter of a lost-property dispute. I said that two members of the public had presented themselves at my hatch, simultaneously, each asserting ownership, and that I had formed the view that neither of them was telling the truth."

"We were telling the truth," I said. "We thought it was ours."

"You were telling *a* truth." He chuckled. "It was a very wet day. Everyone had one. Anyway, Mr Herbert said it was theft. And I said, with the greatest respect, sir, it is romance."

There was a pause.

"I'm afraid," said Mr Dewhurst, "that I did say that. I'm not proud of it. I've never had a very good sense of the proprieties."

---

I would like to say that I took this well.

What I did was sit down on a box of walking sticks, which gave way, and I went down into it with the helpless dignity of a man who has been taken by surprise by his own life. Sophie, beside me, did not move.

"So the umbrella," she said, very carefully, "wasn't ours."

"It was never yours."

"We stole it."

"You took it in good faith. It's a recognised category." Mr Dewhurst put the kettle on. "Mr Herbert came to terms. I gave him a very nice replacement with a duck-head handle. He wrote me a letter eighteen months later to say that he'd grown fond of it, and to ask if the young man had been looked after."

"He asked about *me?*" I said.

"He did. He said he hoped the umbrella had gone to a good home." He held up one finger. "And he asked about the young lady. Because you'll remember, young lady, that when you both came to my hatch, there was a point at which you stopped arguing."

Sophie said nothing. I could see the muscle moving in her jaw.

"I saw the whole thing," said Mr Dewhurst, gently. "I had my head down. I was doing the forms. But I looked up for a moment, and there you were, at the hatch, the pair of you, in the rain, the two of you with your hands on the handle. And you'd both seen the tag, you see. You'd both seen it was somebody else's. But the young man hadn't. He thought it was his. He was so *sure.* And the young lady had seen the initials, and she looked at him, and she looked at the umbrella, and then she looked at me."

"What did I do?" said Sophie, in a low voice.

"You let go."

There was a silence in the little room. The kettle began to tick.

"You let go," said Mr Dewhurst, "and you said to me, quite calmly, 'It's his.' And then you went out into the rain, with no umbrella, and you didn't look back. And I thought, I remember thinking, in thirty years at this hatch I have not seen anyone give a thing away so well."

I couldn't look at her.

I looked at my hands, which were shaking, and at the umbrella on the desk, and at the green pencil in the mug.

---

We drank the tea. It was strong, and brown, and there was a biscuit with it that had the structure of a roof tile. Mr Dewhurst talked about his allotment, and his grandchildren, and the Great Wren Incident of 2019, when a bird had been found in a hat and had been taken home, and Sophie said very little, and ate her biscuit, and looked at the green pencil.

"That's an unusual pencil," she said, at last.

"Isn't it?" Mr Dewhurst glanced at it fondly. "It was Ron's. Ron Pickles. He had the hatch before me. He used to keep it behind his ear, along with a tin of those. Travel sweets." He nodded at the corner. "I took over the desk and I took over the tin. It would have seemed rude not to."

"When did he leave?"

"Oh, years ago. Two thousand and twelve. He retired the week of the Olympics. We gave him a barometer."

Sophie put down her cup.

"Two thousand and twelve," she said.

"That's right."

"Five years before we met."

"I'm sorry?" said Mr Dewhurst.

"Nothing," said Sophie. "I was just..." She stopped. For a second I saw her face change; it was the smallest change, a kind of closing, as of a shutter being lowered over a window, and then it was gone, and she smiled at him pleasantly. "I must be thinking of someone else."

"Easily done," said Mr Dewhurst.

I did not understand it at the time. I put it down, if I put it down to anything, to the heat of the little room, or to the strong tea, or to the general awkwardness of being told by a stranger that you had once been very nice. I noticed that she was holding her cup with both hands. I noticed that her tea, which she usually drank like a woman putting out a fire, had gone cold. And I noticed, with an odd sinking sensation that I could not name, that when we stood up to leave and Mr Dewhurst shook her hand, he said:

"Did you know Ron, young lady?"

And Sophie said, "No."

And her voice, for the first time since I had known her, did not sound entirely like her own.

---

We took the Tube to Walthamstow.

I do not know whose idea it was. I have gone over it a number of times, and I believe the suggestion came from neither of us, but from the Victoria line, which at Highbury is capable of taking decisions on behalf of its passengers. We sat side by side on the long seat, the umbrella across our knees like a sleeping child, and watched the dark pass in the window and our faces drift in it.

We did not speak much. It is a peculiar thing about silence with a person you have lived with: it is not empty. It is full, like a room in which furniture has been moved, and you walk round it in the dark and find, with a start, that you know where everything is.

At Walthamstow Central we got out. She said, "Orford Road," and I said, "Yes," and we walked there, past the market and the pound shops and the new flats with the balconies like trays, and nobody said anything about it at all.

The café was still there.

It had changed its name. Where it had been called **Brew & Co.** it was now **The Lemon Tree,** and the awning had been repainted, and the chalkboard outside offered a "flat white with oat milk and a hint of shame." But the window was the same. The tables, small and round, were the same. "Well," she said. "Look what the cat brought."

"Hello, Eleni," said Sophie.

"I thought you'd moved to Clapton."

"I did."

"And him?" Eleni looked at me. "Is he all right? He used to come in here and look at the walls."

"I was thinking," I said, "about the wall."

"You were thinking about her," said Eleni, and went to put the kettle on.

---

We sat at the table in the window.

It was a quarter to three. The café was nearly empty, apart from a man at the back in headphones, writing furiously, and a very small child in a very large pushchair, who stared at us with the flat calm of a magistrate. The light came in sideways and gilded the dust.

Sophie ordered the lemon tart.

I want to be clear that I had not told her what to order. I had not, in fact, said a word. She simply looked at the menu, the same one, in its stained plastic folder, and said "Lemon tart, please," to Eleni, who nodded without writing it down.

"And for him?"

"A flapjack," said Sophie. "He doesn't know yet."

"I do know."

"You'd have said a lemon thing."

I put down the menu.

It came. We ate it. She cut the tart in two, with the side of her fork, and slid half onto my plate, without looking up, and I cut the flapjack in two, and slid half onto hers, and neither of us mentioned it. It was perfectly done. It was a ritual, I realised, that had never been discussed, the way you cannot remember learning to walk.

"Don't tell anyone I like flapjacks," said Sophie.

"I have a signed capture of you saying that."

"I have a reputation."

She looked at me for a moment over the rim of the cup. Her eyes were very dark. There was nothing in them that I could have written down.

"I'm going to say something," she said.

And then Sophie began to laugh.

She laughed until there were tears in the corners of her eyes, and when she wiped them away with the back of her wrist, she was smiling, the real one, the whole one, with the chip in her tooth.

"I'm sorry," she said. "It's the umbrella."

"What about it?"

"We *stole* it." She wheezed. "We're thieves. We're a pair of thieves. All this time. The foundation of the entire relationship was a retired accountant from Surbiton."

"He did." She was off again. "He said, *with the greatest respect, sir, it is romance.*"

She considered. "Tell him when we've gone," she said. "He'll want to come. He'll want to be with us. And I think that if we're going to do this, I'd like, just once, to do it with the one of you who gets tired."
